PREFACE 

TH HIS book is written with the object of presenting to college students and business men a practical survey of law from the standpoint of a business man. The introduction describes such general matters as the sources of law; law distinguished from equity; grounds of equity jurisdiction; criminal and civil law; the grades, kinds, and functions of courts, both state and 

Federal; the steps in a lawsuit; business law. The text presents fundamental principles of ten subjects of law, almost two thirds of the subjects that would be covered by a student at law school. Some of the leading principles in the text have footnote references to cases bearing upon those principles, to be found in the second half of the book. The 

Uniform Sales Act, the Uniform Partnership Act, and the

Negotiable Instruments Law have been so widely adopted by the states that these laws have been included in their entirety, following the cases. The reader may find the inclusion of these laws useful, not only for the purpose of supplementing the text, but also for the purpose of checking the law in situations which may arise subsequent to the study of the text. A compilation of forms has also been included at the end of the book in order that the reader may have before him some of the more important instruments and documents referred to in the text. While the student may find many of these forms useful in his business career, the author wishes to remind him that the laws of the states vary as to the form and requisites of legal papers and that he should therefore consult a lawyer before executing important documents. 

The method employed by the author in writing the text has been that of stating as concisely and clearly as possible the leading, practical principles of the subjects treated, illustrating them with simple examples when they are not self-evident. 

This method has been employed instead of the common V

vi 

PREFACE 

method of burying principles in wordy explanations of the points involved, because the author believes that a student of business law has so much ground to cover in so short a period that he should not be obliged to spend his time digging out of verbiage in the text the essential principles he is expected to grasp and retain. He may employ this time much more profitably in analyzing the fundamental principles and pondering their application to practical situations. 

This book is adapted to the text system of study, supplemented by the case system. While the author concedes the superiority of the case system, now used in the law schools of higher standing, over the text system, in training students who are to become lawyers, he feels that extracting principles from cases requires considerable time-time that is well spent if the student is to make the determination of law from cases his life's work. But were the student of business law to study exclusively from cases, he would be able, in his limited time, to cover thoroughly no more ground than about one half of the subject of contracts; and the case system, in such limited time, would utterly fail to serve its purpose of developing a legal mind. For the student of business law, it is more important to cover the eight or ten subjects presenting principles likely to be encountered in business than to attempt the development of a legal mind. 

And yet the student of business law would utterly fail to grasp the significance of common law if he did not have some contact with cases discovering how legal principles are extracted from cases, learning how these legal principles are applied in actual cases, ascertaining the grounds upon which courts base their decisions, reading the enlightening opinions of courts deciding actual cases. It is for this reason that the author has supplemented his text with carefully selected cases of the courts of many different states. These cases, it should be pointed out, are not in most instances reproduced in their entirety. As originally published in the state reports, they are generally much longer than the extracts given in this text. 

To promote economy of space and economy of the student's time, the author has reproduced from the original cases only

PREFACE 

vii those facts and portions of opinions which bear directly upon the points for which the cases are cited. Procedural points in the cases have in the main been omitted. Consequently, the reader should appreciate that they are more readable and easier to analyze than the ordinary run of cases he would be obliged to consult in investigating points of law in the state reports.

The principles of law set forth in this text are intended to represent those sound, leading principles most widely adopted in the states. In respect to principles about which there is a conflict of authority, the author has endeavored to present only those supported by the weight of authority instead of stating too frequently that some states hold one view and other states another. It is felt that the latter method of presenting principles of law, necessary as it is at times, tends to weaken materially the interest of the student of law. 

In cases in which there is no clear weight of authority or in which there is an important minority authority, the author has alluded to the conflict of authority in the states. 

This method of presentation is pointed out so that the reader in a particular state will not assume that all the principles set forth in this book are necessarily good law in his state. As to some of the principles, his state may not be in accord with the so-called general principles of American law. 

If the reader is studying this book under classroom guidance, his instructor will undoubtedly point out to him any discrepancies between the principles of this text and the law of his particular state.

The view is sometimes expressed that a business man should not study law because it may influence him to rely on his inadequate learning instead of consulting a lawyer. The observation of the author, from both practice and classroom instruction, is that this view is erroneous. The person who as had no training in law whatsoever is generally totally ignorant of the importance of legal questions that confront him. Not until he has made some costly error by proceeding in ignorance of his legal rights and liabilities does he appreciate the wisdom of securing expert advice. The person with

viii 

PREFACE 

training in law, on the other hand, is more apt to perceive the importance of legal questions that arise. His study has impressed upon him the complexity of law and the necessity of checking carefully each set of facts in the light of all the existing law applicable thereto. In consequence, he is more likely to secure expert guidance when legal questions confront him. Also, in the countless legal situations that inevitably arise in the life of everyone, when there is not sufficient time to consult a lawyer or when the matter does not at first sight appear sufficiently important to warrant consulting a lawyer, the person who has studied law finds that his study stands him in good stead.

INTRODUCTION ·

INTRODUCTION 

§ 1. Law defined. The term law is used in a variety of senses. Employed in the sense attached to it when we speak of the study of law, the term may be defined as follows: 

Law is the system of principles and rules of an organized society (such as the state), governing the conduct of its members. More specifically, law consists of those rules which the courts will recognize and enforce in the decision of cases brought before them. § 2. Sources of law. The principal sources of law in the 

United States are as follows: 

Constitutions. A constitution is the organic and fundamental law of a nation or a state. In American law, a constitution is a written instrument, drawn by the people of a state or of the United States, establishing rules for the departments and the officers of the government and commonly defining the fundamental rights of citizens. The 

United States has a constitution, as has each state. The 

United States Constitution is considered a grant to the Federal Government by the states of the powers enumerated therein. 

Such powers as are not granted, the states are deemed to retain. Thus, Congress does not have power to legislate except when the power is conferred expressly, or by reasonable implication, in the Federal Constitution. For example, the Federal Constitution gives Congress power to "regulate commerce with foreign nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian tribes." Under this provision, Congress may regulate interstate commerce, but it has no power to regulate intrastate commerce. That power is reserved by the states. Similarly, the states, having given Congress power to regulate interstate commerce, may not themselves regulate it. 3

INTRODUCTION 

The provisions of a constitution control until they are changed by the authority which established them, and any act of a legislative body or any decision of a court which violates such provisions is null and void. A law is said to be unconstitutional when it violates a provision of a state constitution or of the Federal Constitution.

Statute law. The statute law of a particular jurisdiction consists of the statutes enacted by the legislature. Thus, Congress enacts statutes for the United States; state legislatures enact statutes for their respective states; and legislative bodies of cities and towns, for their subdivisions of the state. The statutes of a state are generally embodied in several compact volumes, compiled as of a certain date and supplemented by annual volumes of legislative enactments since that date, showing any additions to, or amendments of, the statutes in the general compilation. 

A number of uniform laws, such as the Negotiable Instruments Law, the Sales Act, and the Partnership Act, have been drafted by a commission, the members of which are known as the Commissioners on Uniformity of Legislation. These uniform laws have been enacted as statutes by the legislatures of many states.

Except for the study of these uniform laws, the student of law spends but little time upon statutes. He studies chiefly common law, principally for the following reasons: (1) Statute law may be easily ascertained, when the need arises, by reference to a few books containing statutes; whereas ascertaining principles of common law involves not only extensive investigation among many hundreds of books, but also skill in applying the principles found to the case presented. (2) The principles of common law of a state are infinitely more numerous than its statutes. 

Common law. Practically speaking, common law consists of the principles embodied in decisions of appellate courts. Thus, if the Supreme Judicial Court of Maine, in an appeal raising the question of the right of John Smith, a minor, to avoid a certain contract into which he had entered with one Jones, decides in favor of Smith on the ground that

INTRODUCTION 

5. he is a minor, this decision embodies the general principle that a minor may avoid his contract. This principle becomes a part of the common law of the State of Maine. 

Principles established by an appellate court are regarded as precedents in the jurisdiction for which the appellate court functions and are applied in similar controversies arising. Thus, if the Supreme Judicial Court of Maine should decide in the case of Smith v. Jones that a minor has the right to avoid his contract, as described in the preceding paragraph, all courts of Maine would render a similar decision if subsequently one Brown, a minor, sued for breach of contract, seeks to avoid liability on the ground of minority. 

In such a case, if a lower court in Maine refused to follow the principle established in Smith v. Jones and rendered judgment against Brown, Brown could appeal the case to the Supreme Judicial Court, which would reverse the judgment of the lower court in conformity with the precedent it had established in Smith v. Jones. The purpose of an appeal is to correct errors committed by the lower courts in the trial of cases.

The decisions of an appellate court are not binding upon the courts of another jurisdiction. Thus, the law of Maine giving a minor the right to avoid his contract, as established in the hypothetical case of Smith v. Jones, would not be regarded as controlling upon the courts of Rhode Island. 

But if the appellate court of a state has not previously decided a point of law, it will accord weight to the decisions of appellate courts in other states, the weight depending upon the merit of such other appellate courts, the number of such state courts reaching a similar conclusion, and the soundness of the reasoning supporting the conclusion. Thus, let us suppose the appellate court in Rhode Island has never decided the question of whether a minor has the right to avoid his contract, and the question is presented for the first time in the case of X v. Y, appealed from a lower court. If the appellate courts of forty other states have decided, in accord with Maine law, that a minor has the right to avoid his contract, while five states have decided contra, the Rhode Island court

INTRODUCTION 

will be considerably influenced by the weight of authority in permitting a minor to avoid his contract.

This classification also represents the order of priority when these three types of law conflict. A statute must not be contrary to a provision of the constitutions; a court decision must not be contrary to a statute. A principle established in a court decision is superseded by a subsequent statute providing to the contrary. 

§ 3. Courts of equity distinguished from courts of law. 

A court of equity is a court which exercises jurisdiction generally for the purpose of affording relief in certain cases in which a party has no adequate remedy in a court of law. 

The first courts in England were courts of law. As common law developed in England, it gradually became more crystallized and less flexible. Guided by precedents, the law courts would hear cases, coming within certain well-defined classes, in which relief had previously been given, but not cases outside these classes. Thus, a law court would award money damages to a party injured by a breach of contract, but it would not order the party committing such breach to perform his contract, although in certain cases justice might require such relief. In consequence of the deficiencies of the law courts, there evolved in England a high court of chancery (court of equity), the purpose of which was to afford relief and to administer justice in cases for which there was no adequate remedy at law. The term equity was employed because it was descriptive of the fairness and the natural justice which inspired the founding, and invoked the jurisdiction, of courts of equity.

The states of this country adopted equity jurisprudence along with the common law of England. In most states one court will hear both law and equity cases; in some states courts of equity are separate and distinct from courts of law; and in a few states the distinction between law and equity has been abolished.

The rules followed in both courts of equity and courts of law are rules of law. The two sets of rules, though distinct, are not to be regarded as independent systems of law. The

INTRODUCTION 

7 rules of equity are merely a supplement or an appendix to the common law. They assume the existence of the common law, and add something to it. Principles of equity, like principles of common law, have the force of precedents and are binding upon the court which establishes them. 

§ 4. Grounds of equity jurisdiction. The cases in which equity jurisdiction is entertained generally fall into three classes: (1) Cases in which the subject matter is equitable, as in a controversy relating to the administration of a trust. (2) Cases in which a particular relationship exists, as in suits between partners and coöwners of real estate. (3) Cases in which there is a remedy at law, but the remedy is not plain, adequate, and complete. Some illustrations of this class of cases follow: A party seeks to reform a written instrument because of mistake; to rescind, cancel, or set aside contracts obtained by fraud; to obtain specific performance of contracts for the sale or purchase of land, or for the sale of an article of intrinsic or sentimental value, such as a rare painting; to enjoin (forbid) a party to a contract to break his contract in certain cases-for example, an employee agrees that for one year following termination of his employment he will not engage in the same business in a certain locality; to enjoin the commission of threatened tortsfor example, a person threatens to cut down a tree on the land of another; to reach and apply property of a debtor which cannot be attached at law-for example, a debtor is alleged to have conveyed property to another with the intent to defraud creditors; and so forth.

Many principles recognized by courts of equity are founded upon such maxims as: "Equality is equity"; "Equity regards substance rather than form"; "Equity looks upon that as done which ought to have been done"; "Equity suffers not a right without a remedy"; "Equity delights to do justice and that not by halves"; "He who comes into equity must come with clean hands"; "He who seeks equity must do equity."

INTRODUCTION 

§ 5. Criminal and civil law.-Criminal law is that division of law which treats of violations of duties an individual owes to the community. Thus, the crime of murder is a violation of the duties the murderer owes to his community, and the law pertaining to this crime and its punishment is known as criminal law.

Civil law is that division of law occupied with the exposition and enforcement of civil rights. Thus, if a party to a contract breaks such contract, the law regulating the right of the other party to sue for damages is known as civil law. 

The Courts 

§ 6. In general.—A court is an organ of government, the function of which is the application of law to controversies brought before it, and the public administration of justice. 

It is manifest that in any society controversies will arise between its members. Perhaps a member will commit an offense, such as stealing the property of another member (larceny), which will endanger the welfare of the group as a whole; or perhaps a member will violate the civil rights of another member, as by breaking a contract into which he has entered (breach of contract) or by making defamatory statements about another (slander). In the controversies which will inevitably arise in any community, the necessity of having a department of government that will adjudicate the disputes between members, and between the community and its members, is obvious. Without such a department, there would be no security for either the community or the rights of its members; members would take into their own hands. offenses against the community and violation of private rights, and such action would result in chaos and more serious offenses than those the injured members seek to avenge. 

A judge is a public officer appointed by a community to preside over, and to administer the law in, a court of justice. 

The powers of a judge depending, of course, upon the particular court over which he presides are far-reaching. 

In accordance with law, he may deprive a person of his liberty; he may sentence a person to death; he may award a

INTRODUCTION 

9 person's property to another; he may prevent a person from carrying on his business; he may separate a person from his spouse; he may deny one the custody of his children. The justification for conferring such extensive powers upon judges is the interest of the community in preventing and punishing offenses against it and in protecting the rights of its members. 

§ 7. State courts.-The courts of the states vary with respect to grades, jurisdiction, and names. In general, the courts of a state may be roughly divided into the following three grades: 

District courts; also called municipal, city, county, and justice of the peace courts. These courts have jurisdiction over certain cases arising within a particular section, as a city or one of several districts into which a county has been subdivided. Both civil and criminal cases are tried in these courts, but jurisdiction in civil cases is usually limited to suits involving less than a certain amount, as $5,000, and jurisdiction in criminal cases is usually limited to the less serious crimes. These courts are presided over by a judge sitting without a jury. The constitutional right of defendants in these courts to a trial by jury is preserved by permitting defendants to appeal an adverse decision to a higher court with jury.

Superior courts; in various states also called circuit and district courts. These courts have jurisdiction in a particular county or, in some states, in cases arising anywhere in the state. Both civil and criminal cases are tried in these courts, without limitation as to the amount involved or the seriousness of the crime. These courts sit with and without a jury. Cases may be entered in these courts originally, or may be carried there from lower courts by removal or appeal. 

In most states courts of this grade hear both equity and law cases; in a few states, however, this grade of court is divided into law courts and equity courts. In this grade, also, are probate courts, which have jurisdiction over such matters as the settlement of estates of deceased persons, divorce, appointment of guardians and conservators, and so forth.

INTRODUCTION 

Courts of this grade and those of the first are known as trial courts.

Supreme court; also called in various states court of appeals, supreme court of errors, supreme judicial court, supreme court of appeals, and so forth. This is the highest court in a state and, unlike the courts in the first and second classes, it is not a trial court. Cases are not usually originally entered in this court. They are carried there by appeal from the lower, or trial, courts. Generally, there is only one such appellate court in a state, and it is composed of a number of justices, commonly five or seven. The function of this court is to review the record of the proceedings in the lower court, at the request of a party (appellant) aggrieved by a decision there, for the purpose of determining whether any error was committed by the judge in the trial of the case. If the appellate court finds that there was no error, it affirms the judgment of the lower court or dismisses the appeal; if it finds that error was committed, it reverses the judgment of the lower court, usually ordering a new trial. 

The decisions of an appellate court are embodied in opinions written for the court by one of the justices whose name is found at the beginning of the opinion. The opinions of the supreme court of a particular state are compiled chronologically in a set of reports, such as California Reports, New York Reports, and the like. References to cases appearing in these reports are in such form as 122 Cal. 403. This means that the case referred to will be found on page 403 in Volume 

122 of the California Reports.

Generally, only the decisions of the appellate court of a state are printed and have the force of law. The decisions of such courts, since inception, constitute in the main the common law in force in a particular state. The decisions of the lower, or trial, courts are not usually compiled in reports and do not have binding force as precedents. 

§ 8. Federal courts. The jurisdiction of Federal courts embraces the following persons and matters: (1) Cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls; controversies in which the United States is a

INTRODUCTION 

11 party; controversies between two or more states, between a state and citizens of another state, between citizens of different states, and between a state or the citizens thereof and foreign states, citizens, or subjects. (2) All cases in law and in equity arising under the Constitution, the statutes, and the treaties of the United States; and all admiralty and maritime cases. 

There are three grades of Federal courts, as follows:

United States District Court. The country is divided into some eighty-nine districts, each of which contains a United States district court. Many of the states comprise a single district, while some of the larger states are divided into a number of districts. New York has four such districts. The district court is the trial court of the Federal system and is the lowest of the system. Appeals from its decisions may be taken to higher courts.

Examples of cases tried in the district courts are such crimes as violations of the Federal prohibition law, of the internal revenue law, and of postal and copyright laws; proceedings in bankruptcy; civil suits between citizens of different states.

Circuit Court of Appeals. The United States is divided into ten circuits, in each of which is one of these courts. A circuit court of appeals reviews, on appeal or writ of error, decisions of district courts within its circuit. Its decision is final in a large number of cases, such as controversies between aliens and citizens, suits between citizens of different states, and cases arising under patent, revenue, and criminal laws. 

The opinions of the circuit courts of appeals and the district courts are compiled in what is known as the Federal Reporter. A reference to a case in these reports is in such form as 194 Fed. 26.

United States Supreme Court. This is the highest court in the Federal system. It hears appeals in certain cases directly from district courts, as in a case involving the constitutionality of a Federal statute; from certain decisions of the circuit courts of appeals; from certain decisions of the appellate courts of

INTRODUCTION 

states. The opinions of the United States Supreme Court are published in volumes known as the United States Reports. 

In addition to the foregoing, there are special Federal courts, as the Court of Claims, the function of which is to hear claims against the Federal Government. § 9. Steps in a lawsuit.-A person bringing suit is known as the plaintiff. A person against whom the suit is brought is known as the defendant. The following steps mark the progress of a case in court:

Service of summons upon the defendant. A summons is a writ directed to the sheriff or other proper officer requiring him to notify the person named (defendant) that an action has been commenced against him in the court from which the writ issues and that he is required to appear on a day named and to answer the complaint in such action. The summons is prepared by the attorney for the plaintiff and is given to a sheriff or constable for service upon the defendant. 

Service is usually made when a copy of the writ is either handed to the defendant, called service in hand, or left at the last and usual place of abode of the defendant. If the defendant is outside the state but has property within the state, service may sometimes be made by a notice of the writ published in a newspaper. Unless a summons is served upon the defendant as directed by statute, the defendant is not brought within the jurisdiction of the court and the plaintiff will be unable to recover judgment against him. The officer serving`a copy of the writ on the defendant indorses on the back of the original writ a statement of the service, including time, place, and kind of service, and either files it himself in the office of the clerk of court on the date named in the writ or gives it to the plaintiff's attorney for such filing. 

Filing of pleadings. The pleadings consist of written statements filed by the plaintiff and the defendant in the office of the clerk of court. Those of the plaintiff are generally called a declaration; those of the defendant, an answer. The plaintiff must file his declaration on the date named in the writ; the defendant must file an answer within a certain

INTRODUCTION 

13 number of days later, the time being governed by statute or rules of court. If the defendant files no answer, he is defaulted and the plaintiff recovers judgment without the necessity of trying his case. Sometimes a defendant files a demurrer instead of an answer. A demurrer is an allegation that even if the facts stated in the declaration are taken as true, still the declaration does not state a cause of action upon which the plaintiff can recover, or is otherwise defective as a matter of law. If the court overrules the demurrer, the defendant must file an answer. If the court sustains the demurrer, the defendant prevails in the suit unless the court permits the plaintiff to correct, by amendment, the defect in his declaration. The foregoing are the most common pleadings, but there are others that the parties may file, depending upon the circumstances of the case and the laws of the particular state. 

Trial. Since the answer of the defendant is always a denial of the facts alleged in the plaintiff's declaration, trial of the case is necessary to determine the issues. Either party may mark a pending case for trial. In a lawsuit, trial takes place before a judge and a jury, if either party claims the right to trial by jury. If such right is not claimed, trial takes place before a judge only. In suits of equity, a party is not entitled to trial by jury as a matter of right, although such a trial may be granted in certain cases. If trial is by jury, all questions of fact are submitted to the jury for determination in the light of instructions by the judge. as to the law applicable to the case. If trial is not by jury, the judge hearing the case makes both findings of fact and rulings of law. The decision of a jury is known as a verdict. The decision of a court based either upon its findings of fact where there is no jury, or upon the verdict where there is a jury, is known as a judgment. A judgment is the final determination by the court of the rights of the parties in the suit. The judgment of a court of equity is called a decree. 

Appeal. The unsuccessful party in a trial has the right to appeal to an appellate court for the purpose of having such court review the record in the lower court. If the appellate court concludes that the lower court has erred in its

INTRODUCTION 

judgment or committed materially prejudicial error in any of its rulings made during the trial of the case, it will reverse the judgment and order a new trial, or direct entry of judgment for the appellant, as justice may require. If the appellate court finds that the record does not disclose materially prejudicial error, it will affirm the judgment of the lower court. 

Appeals are commonly based upon such grounds as a ruling of the lower court in which it excluded certain evidence; refusal by the lower court to direct á verdict at the request of a party, or to instruct the jury as requested by a party; improper instruction of the jury; denial of the motion of a losing party for a new trial; claim that the verdict is against the evidence. 

Upon appeal, the court will not reverse findings of fact by the jury, or by the judge sitting without jury, unless they are plainly wrong or there is no evidence to warrant such findings. · Only a small percentage of the cases tried in the lower courts are appealed, owing chiefly to the belief of defeated parties that the record does not disclose such errors as would cause the appellate court to reverse the judgment, and partly to the expense and the time required for preparing briefs and arguing the case before the appellate court. If a case involves a sum of only a few hundred dollars, it is hardly worth the while of the defeated party to appeal, even though he may have excellent grounds for carrying up the case. 

10. Business law. The term business law is ambiguous. 

In law there is no such classification as "business law." In business the term is understood to refer to those divisions of law, such as contracts, agency, and the like, which present principles that a person is most likely to encounter in the business world. Business law is not, as some persons believe, an inferior division of law; nor is it a clearly specialized field of law. Business law is the same law that a student at law school learns, except that it is not so comprehensive. But a complete course in business law is far more comprehensive, and covers much more of the ground covered at law school than most persons imagine.

The difference between business law and law-school law can be better grasped by a comparison of the subjects treated

INTRODUCTION 

15 by each.

A complete course in business law would ordinarily cover the following subjects: (1) contracts, (2) agency, (3) sales, (4) bailments, (5) negotiable instruments, (6) partnerships, (7) corporations, (8) bankruptcy, and perhaps (9) real property, including landlord and tenant and real estate mortgages. At law school these nine subjects would be presented, in addition to the following, subject to variations at different schools: (10) criminal law, (11) torts, (12) wills, (13) trusts, (14) equity, (15) civil procedure, (16) evidence, and (17) constitutional law.

In the subjects that are generally treated both in a college course in business law and at law school, the student of business law, despite the limited time he can devote to the study of law, should learn nearly as much law as the student at law school, because the former studies from a text, a secondary source, rather than from cases, a primary source. Extracting principles from cases occupies far more time than reading the principles collected from the cases and arranged in text form by a textbook writer.

PART I TEXT

CONTRACTS

CONTRACTS CHAPTER I GENERAL MATTERS § 1. Definition.-A contract is an enforceable agreement between two or more competent persons, embodying an offer by one person to do or not to do a certain thing and an acceptance by another.

This definition, like most definitions, fails adequately to define so comprehensive a term as contract. The reason is that it is impossible to compress into one sentence all the requirements and circumstances attending the formation of a valid contract. Only by a thorough study of the law relating to the formation of contracts can one hope to understand what is meant by the term contract. 

§ 2. Essential elements of a contract. The following elements are essential to the creation of a binding contract: (1) Mutual assent (offer and acceptance). (2) Consideration. 

(3) Legal subject matter. 

(4) Competent parties."

The study of contracts is based in large part upon a consideration of each of these elements and of matters naturally relating to them. These points will be treated in the chapters that follow. § 3. May be oral or written.-Generally speaking, a contract is enforceable whether it is made orally or in writing. 

A common misconception as to the law of contracts is that an agreement is not binding unless it is in writing. This misconception is probably due to the following: (1) The erroneous belief that facts may be established by written evidence only; that since testimony of one witness may be contradicted by 21

CONTRACTS 

testimony of another witness, credence cannot be given the testimony of either one. This belief is not correct. A court is not precluded from believing testimony of one witness by the fact that there is a conflict of testimony. The conflict merely gives rise to a question of fact: namely, which witness is telling the truth. An oral contract may be enforced if the court accepts as true the testimony of the party who seeks to establish the contract. (2) The fact that some contracts are not enforceable unless they are in writing. As will appear in a later chapter, statutes of frauds in various states do provide that certain contracts shall not be enforceable unless they are in writing and are signed by the party to be charged or his agent; for example, contracts not to be performed within a year, contracts to answer for the debt, default, or misdoings of another. However, the requirement that certain types of contracts must be in writing to be enforceable should not lead one to believe that all contracts must be in writing. § 4. Formal and simple contracts.-A formal contract is one in writing and under seal. Such contracts are also called specialties. Commonly, contracts are executed under seal by pasting a round, printed seal, about one-half the size of a postage stamp, on the contract following the signature. Most states, however, require a simpler procedure for sealing: in some it is sufficient if, after the signature, the word seal or the letters L. S., the abbreviation of Locus Sigilli, meaning place of the seal, appear; in others a mark, blot, or flourish intended to be a seal is sufficient; in still others there need be only a recital that the instrument is a sealed instrument.

A simple contract is one not under seal. It may be in writing,¹ it may be oral, or it may be merely implied. Simple contracts are also referred to as parol contracts. 

§ 5. Express and implied contracts. An express contract is one the terms of which are stated in distinct and explicit language, either orally or in writing. An implied contract is one the terms of which are not stated by the parties, but are inferred by law as a matter of reason and justice from the acts 

¹ Form of Simple Written Contract, p. 487.

GENERAL MATTERS 

23 or conduct of the parties and the circumstances surrounding the transaction. A contract may be express in part and implied in part.

Implied contracts are sometimes subdivided into two classes: those implied in fact and those implied in law. The definition of implied contracts just given refers to contracts implied in fact. The following is an illustration of an implied contract: A constructs a fence on B's land with the expectation that B will pay for it, and B, knowing about the construction and about A's expectation of payment, nevertheless permits him to construct the fence without objection. The court will infer a promise by B to pay A for the fence.2 

However, a contract to pay for a benefit conferred will not be implied if the party receiving the benefit does not know that it is being conferred, or, knowing about it, raises objection. 

A contract implied in law is one in which an obligation is imposed upon a person, irrespective or even in violation of his intention to enter into a contract, because it is just that such obligation should be imposed upon him. For example, a husband who neglects to provide his wife with necessaries may be liable upon a contract implied in law for the value of necessaries supplied her by someone else. But obligations of this kind are not properly contracts at all, because they are imposed even contrary to the intentions of the parties. Such obligations are more correctly described as "quasi" contracts, which is the better name, since it indicates that the obligation is not a true contract, and avoids confusion with contracts implied in fact, which are real contracts. § 6. Executed and executory contracts.-An executed contract is one the terms of which have been carried out; for example, A enters into a contract with B to sell a suit, and A delivers the suit and B pays for it. An executory contract is one the terms of which have not been carried out; for example, A enters into a contract with B to sell a suit, and A has not delivered the suit nor has B paid for it. A contract may be partly executed and partly executory. 

2 Day v. Caton, p. 303.

CONTRACTS § 7. Bilateral and unilateral contracts. A bilateral con tract is one in which promises are made by both parties. The following is an illustration: A promises to sell B a suit for $30 and B promises to pay A $30 for the suit. A unilateral contract is one in which there is a promise on one side only and an act on the other side; for example, A promises B that he will pay B $10 if he jumps a certain fence and B jumps the fence.

Offers are sometimes classified as bilateral and unilateral. 

A bilateral offer is one which calls reasonably for acceptance in the form of a promise; a unilateral offer is one which calls reasonably for acceptance by performance of an act requested. 

For example, the offer "I will pay you $5,000 if you will build a house in accordance with these plans" would be bilateral. 

It calls reasonably for a promise on the part of the offeree, since the offeror would naturally wish to know in advance of performance whether the offeree was going to accept the offer. But the offer "I will pay you $10 if you jump that fence" would be unilateral, since it calls only for an act. The offeror would not be interested in obtaining the promise of B to jump the fence, but only in his jumping the fence. § 8. Divisible and indivisible contracts. A divisible contract is one divided on both sides into stated installments, an installment on one side being equivalent to an installment on the other side; for example, A enters into a contract with 

B whereby A is to sell B his radio for $25, his piano for $200, and his victrola for $75. Divisible contracts are also called "severable."

An indivisible contract is one the consideration for which is entire on both sides; for example, A enters into a contract with B to sell B his radio, piano, and victrola for $300. 

Indivisible contracts are also referred to as "entire." The question whether a contract is divisible or indivisible is primarily one of the intention of the parties. 

§ 9. Void, voidable, and unenforceable contracts.-A 

void contract is one under which no legal obligation exists. 

An example is a contract the terms of which violate an existing statute.

GENERAL MATTERS 

25 A voidable contract is one that may be rescinded by one of the parties. For example, a contract entered into by a minor is voidable, since the minor may rescind it. Unless rescinded, however, a voidable contract is binding upon both parties. 

A contract may also be unenforceable, for some reason, by one or both of the parties, although it is neither void nor voidable. For example, a contract within the Statute of 

Frauds is not void, but it is unenforceable by either party unless the requirements of the Statute have been met. 

§ 10. Capacity to contract. All persons, with the exception of some for whom guardians or conservators have been appointed, are competent to enter into contracts. However, certain persons, such as minors, insane persons, and drunkards, while competent to enter into contracts, may avoid their contracts if they so elect. This subject will be considered in a later chapter.

CHAPTER II MUTUAL ASSENT Offer and Acceptance 

§ 1. Necessity of mutual assent.-A contract cannot arise without mutual assent: that is, without agreement of the parties to all of its terms. Courts have referred to this essential of contracts as “the meeting of the minds of the parties." 

However, only the expressed assent of the parties governs in determining whether there is mutual assent. The secret, uncommunicated intent of a party is unimportant. § 2. Mutual assent expressed by an offer and an acceptance. The assent of one party to a contract is expressed by an offer; the assent of the other party is expressed by an acceptance of the offer. 

3. What constitutes an offer and an acceptance.-An offer is a proposal made by one party to another; for example, A says to B: "I will sell you my radio for $30." An acceptance is the assent of one party to the proposal of another; for example, B replies to the aforementioned offer of A: “I accept your offer." A person who makes an offer is called an offeror; a person to whom an offer is made, an offeree. 

If the offeree accepts the offer, he is also called acceptor. an An offer may consist of a promise, as stated in the preceding paragraph, or it may consist merely of an act. For example, if B were a customer in A's store and A, without saying anything, tendered B a radio on which there was a price tag of $30, this act might be construed as constituting an offer. 

The test for determining whether a promise or an act is an offer is whether a reasonable person in the position of the other party would so construe it. 26

MUTUAL ASSENT 

27 Similarly, an acceptance may consist of a promise or an act, and the test is the construction by a reasonable person in the position of the offeror. Offer § 4. Offer must be definite.-An offer must be definite with respect to its terms, if it is to be a valid offer. For example, a promise by A to sell oil to B on favorable terms in order that B can successfully compete with other parties selling in the same territory is too indefinite to constitute an offer.

However, an offer the language of which appears indefinite may nevertheless be held definite in the light of all the circumstances and the legal construction placed upon the language. 

Thus a promise to pay "what the services are worth" has been held a promise to pay reasonable compensation. 

Also, an offer must be made with an intent to create legal relations. For this reason, agreements made in jest, social engagements, and the like, are not contracts. § 5. Preliminary negotiations are not offers. Preliminary negotiations must not be confused with offers. By preliminary negotiations is meant the great variety of overtures, statements of property for sale, and advertisements and circulars stating that the seller has certain goods he desires to sell at a certain price.

Such preliminary negotiations are generally construed as invitations to those receiving them to make an offer. Consequently, no contract will arise until the negotiations result in an offer and in an acceptance of the offer by the offeree. 

On the other hand, language resembling preliminary negotiations may be held an offer. In each case the question is one of intent: Is some performance promised in positive terms, in return for something requested? § 6. Offer must be communicated. An offer must be communicated to the offeree, to be valid. For example, A writes an offer to B on a piece of paper. A leaves the paper 

1 Moulton v. Kershaw, p. 304.

CONTRACTS 

on his desk, intending to deliver it to B the next day. If B should see the paper before delivery without the knowledge, or through no fault, of A, and should accept the offer, no contract would result.

An offer must be communicated by the offeror or his agent. 

An offer is not valid if the offeree learns of the offer from some other source. § 7. Duration of offer.-An offer continues until it lapses, is revoked, is rejected, or is accepted. While an offer continues, an acceptance of it will create a contract. 

After an offer terminates, an acceptance is without effect. § 8. Offer may lapse.—An offer lapses upon the expiration of a reasonable length of time after it is made. What is a reasonable length of time is a question of fact to be determined by the jury in the light of all the circumstances under which the offer is made.

An offer also lapses upon expiration of the period fixed by the offeror for continuance of his offer. § 9. Offer lapses upon death or insanity.--An offer terminates upon the death or insanity of either the offeror or the offeree. An acceptance by the offeree or his representatives after death or insanity is without effect.

Since an offer and an acceptance create a contract, death or insanity of either party after an acceptance does not affect the validity of the contract The effect of death or insanity upon performance of a contract will be considered in a later chapter. § 10. Offer may be revoked by offeror.-An offer may be revoked by the offeror any time prior to acceptance. However, a revocation will not be effective unless it is communicated to the offeree.

An offer may be revoked prior to acceptance even though the offeror has promised the offeree to keep the offer open a specified length of time. If the promise is not supported by consideration, it is clear that the offeror is under no liability if he fails to perform his promise. If the promise is supported by consideration furnished by the offeree, this constitutes a contract, binding upon the offeror, to keep the offer open.

MUTUAL ASSENT 

29 His revocation of the offer under such circumstances would be a breach of contract, rendering him liable in damages to the offeree. Such contract to keep an offer open for a specified length of time is called an option contract.

An offeror may revoke an offer made to the public generally by giving the same publicity to the revocation as he gave to the offer. The reason is that it would be impossible to give individual notice of revocation to everyone who had knowledge of the offer, and public offers would not be made unless some practicable method of revocation were provided. 

A unilateral offer may be revoked any time prior to completion of the act requested. The reason is that a unilateral offer is not accepted until completion of the act requested. 

§ 11. Offer terminates upon rejection.-An offer termi nates upon rejection by the offeree. An acceptance subsequent to rejection is without effect.

An attempted acceptance which alters, qualifies, or adds to the terms of the offer is held to be a rejection, terminating the offer. Such attempted acceptance is called a counter offer, and no contract can result until acceptance of the counter offer by the original offeror.

However, a mere inquiry by the offeree does not terminate an offer. Nor does the addition of terms in an acceptance, requested as a favor, terminate the offer or affect the validity of the acceptance. In any particular case the test is whether the acceptance is conditioned upon the term requested. § 12. Offer terminates upon acceptance. An offer terminates upon acceptance by the offeree. A valid acceptance creates a contract. § 13. Terms of offer.-As a rule an offeree is bound only by the terms communicated to him as a reasonable man. 

Thus, when terms are printed upon receipts, bills of lading, letterheads, and the like, the question of whether the terms appearing thereon are part of the contract depends upon whether the offeree should, as a reasonable man, read them and consider them a part of the proposed contract. 

In one case it was held that a shipper was bound by a provision legibly stamped upon a bill of lading handed to him by

CONTRACTS 

the carrier, but not read by him. In another case a printed notice on the top of each page of a hotel register disclaiming liability for valuables not deposited in the office safe was held not to bind the guests who signed the book unless their attention was called to it. 

Acceptance 

§ 14. In general. An acceptance must coincide with the terms of the offer.2 As is previously explained, an acceptance which varies the terms of an offer is invalid and amounts to no more than a counter offer. § 15. Acceptance of unilateral and bilateral offers.-A unilateral offer is accepted by completion of the act requested. 

A bilateral offer is accepted by a promise to do what is requested in the offer. § 16. Communication.-An acceptance must be communicated to the offeror by the offeree or his agent, if it is to be valid. § 17. Time acceptance takes effect. An acceptance takes effect when it is received by the offeror or when it is placed within the means of communication authorized by him, whichever occurs earlier.

An offeror may authorize a certain means of communication expressly or impliedly. He authorizes a certain means expressly when he designates that means in his offer. For example, A writes to B: "I will sell you my car for $400. 

Please let me know by telegraph." If B sends his acceptance by telegraph, his acceptance takes effect and a contract is created as soon as B gives his acceptance to the telegraph company for transmission. If B uses an unauthorized means of communication in this case, as by mailing a letter of acceptance, the acceptance is still valid if the offer remains open sufficiently long, but the acceptance does not take effect until the letter is received by the offeror.

An offeror authorizes a means of communication impliedly. when he uses a certain means himself. For example, A writes 

2 Williams v. West Chicago St. R. Co., p. 305.

MUTUAL ASSENT 

31 to B in a letter: "I will sell you my car for $400." If B mails his acceptance, the acceptance takes effect when the letter, properly stamped and addressed, is posted, and the contract comes into existence at that time. However, if B selects some other means of communication, acceptance does not take effect until it is received by the offeror. Also, implied authorization of a certain means may appear from circumstances other than the use of a certain means by the offeror, as when an offeror communicates his offer orally and it is within the contemplation of the parties that the acceptance will be sent by mail. 

The reason for the rule that an acceptance takes effect when it is placed within the means of communication authorized by the offeror is that, by authorization, such means become the agent of the offeror, and the offeror is deemed to receive the acceptance when it is given to his agent. But unauthorized means are the agent of the offeree, and consequently the offeror does not receive the acceptance until it is delivered to him. Thus, it appears that this rule is based upon a presumption, and the presumption may be overcome by circumstances indicating a contrary intention. For example, if A wrote to B: "I will sell you my car for $400; your acceptance must reach me within a week," an acceptance by mail would not take effect until it reached A. 

The importance of determining when the acceptance takes effect is that, until that time, the offer may be revoked or may lapse, but not afterwards; nor may the offeree withdraw his acceptance once it has taken effect. 

The foregoing rules are not law in all the states, but represent the great weight of authority. § 18. Silence as acceptance.-Silence cannot be construed as an acceptance, generally speaking. If A sends B three neckties without B's request, with the statement that B is to send the price of the ties or return them within a week after receiving them, B's failure to send the price or return the ties cannot be construed as an acceptance. A does not have 

3 Prescott v. Jones, p. 306. 3

CONTRACTS 

the right to require B to do an act under the penalty of having his silence construed as an acceptance. On the other hand, if B wears the ties, sells them, or gives them away, these acts may imply an acceptance on the part of B. 

However, circumstances may impose a duty upon the offeree to reject the offer or to have his silence construed as an acceptance. For example, if B requests A to send him three neckties on approval for a week, and B retains the ties beyond a week without paying for them, his retention may be construed as an acceptance. The circumstance of the ties, being sent at B's request imposes a duty upon him to reject the offer by returning the ties, if he does not wish to be bound by a contract.

Also, as is pointed out in Chapter I, silence will be construed as an acceptance when a benefit is conferred upon one with his knowledge of an expectation of payment. Here, also, the circumstances impose a duty upon the person receiving the benefit to reject the offer. But silence cannot be construed as an acceptance if the person receiving the benefit has no knowledge of it.

CHAPTER III CONSIDERATION § 1. Necessity of consideration. As is stated in Chapter 

I, consideration is an essential element in a contract. A gratuitous promise is not enforceable. For example, if A says to B, "I will pay you $100," A is not bound by his promise because it is not supported by consideration. It is called a nudum pactum. Even though there were mutual assent to this proposal as a result of B's saying “All right,' the agreement would not be binding because of the absence of consideration. 

1 Hamer v. Sidway, p. 307. § 2. Promises under seal.—A promise in writing under seal is binding without consideration. It is said that the seal imports consideration. However, this rule has been changed in many states, with the abolishment of seals. § 3. Consideration defined.-Broadly speaking, consideration may be defined as the waiving of, or a promise to waive, a legal right at the request of another.¹ In other words, a party gives consideration when he sustains some legal detriment as a result of an act, or a promise to do an act, which he is not legally bound to perform. For example, if A says to B, "I will sell you my car for $100," A is promising to waive a legal right in his promise to sell his car, which he is not otherwise legally bound to do. If B replies, "I accept your offer,' he is promising to waive a legal right in his promise to buy the car for $100, which he is not otherwise bound to do. Thus the promise of each is supported by consideration. 

Consideration is sometimes spoken of as something which is a benefit to the promisor or a detriment to the promisee. 

But since a benefit to the promisor would ordinarily result 

34

CONSIDERATION 

35 from the promisee's waiving, or promise to waive, a legal right, we need not go into this aspect of consideration. § 4. Adequacy of consideration.-Consideration need not be adequate, generally speaking. In determining whether a promise is supported by consideration, the court merely ascertains whether or not the promisee has waived, or promised to waive, a legal right at the request of the promisor. It is clear that if the court were to hold as insufficient, consideration unequal in value to that furnished by the promisor, it would spend most of its time in a futile effort to compute the value of consideration. Consequently, it may often happen that there is a material difference in the values of the considerations furnished by the parties. 

However, consideration will be held inadequate when it is of the same kind as that promised by the other party and is less in amount. For example: A says to B, "I will pay you $100 if you will give me $1," and B replies, "I accept your proposal." § 5. Past consideration.-Past consideration is the waiving of, or a promise to waive, a legal right that occurs prior to the promise sought to be enforced, and is insufficient to support a promise. For example, A, without B's knowledge, paints B's camp. Subsequently, B learns of this, and promises to pay A $50 for painting the camp. B's promise would not be enforceable because it is supported only by past consideration. Consideration, to be sufficient, must be an inducement to the other party to enter into a contract. 

However, in the above case, if B knew that A was painting his camp with the expectation of being paid, the court might imply a promise on the part of A to pay for the work, and a subsequent express promise by B to pay a certain amount might be enforced as defining the extent of his obligation. 

§ 6. Moral consideration. Moral consideration is the moral obligation of the promisor to perform his promise, and is insufficient to support a promise. 

§ 7. Contractual obligation as consideration. The per formance of, or promise to perform, a contractual obligation is not consideration. The reason is manifest. If there be a 

---

CONTRACTS 

contractual obligation, a person is not waiving a legal right when he performs or promises to perform the obligation. 

However, if in addition to the performing of, or a promise to perform, a contractual obligation, there is a waiving of, or a promise to waive, a legal right, this situation will constitute consideration. For example, A and B enter into a contract whereby B is to build A a house for $10,000, by June first. If B refuses to complete the house unless he is paid $2,000 in addition to the contract price, A's promise to pay the additional $2,000 will not be enforceable even if B completes the house, because B is merely performing a contractual obligation; but if A promises to pay $2,000 additional for B's promise not only to complete the house, but to complete it one month earlier than previously agreed, A's promise is enforceable, because B is promising to waive a legal right in agreeing to complete the house at an earlier date. 

When a contract is rescinded by mutual agreement, the promise of a party to perform, or his performance of, his prior contractual obligation will be consideration. The obligation having been discharged, his new promise to perform is a promise to waive a legal right. In this connection it is pointed out that any contract, even the most formal, may be modified or rescinded by subsequent mutual agreement of the parties. This subsequent agreement will be binding even though it is oral. § 8. Payments received in full settlement. When a claim is liquidated—that is, ascertained, the promise of a creditor to accept in full settlement less than the amount of his claim is not binding upon him. The reason is that since the debtor is legally bound to pay the full claim, his payment of, or his promise to pay, a part is not consideration for the promise of the creditor to accept it in full settlement; the debtor is not waiving or promising to waive a legal right. It is immaterial whether the promise of the creditor is made expressly in writing, as when a receipt for payment in full is given the debtor, or orally; or whether the promise is implied from the creditor's conduct in accepting a payment that is stated by the debtor to be made in full settlement, as in

CONSIDERATION 

33 37 32 indorsing and cashing a check upon which is noted "in full settlement." A debtor, if he desires, can impose upon his payment the condition that the creditor receive it in full settlement, but that condition will not be binding unless the creditor's promise is supported by consideration. 

However, when the claim is unliquidated or is honestly disputed, the promise of the creditor to accept less than the amount of his claim in full settlement is binding upon him. 

The reason is that since no definite amount is due, a payment of, or a promise to pay, a part is the waiving of a legal right; and the court does not inquire into the adequacy of the amount under the general rule. In many states it is immaterial that the part paid is admittedly due, but in a few states the payment of such part is not a discharge of the balance.

The promises of creditors who are parties to a composition agreement with a debtor, wherein they agree to accept less than the amounts of their claims, are binding upon them. 

The consideration for each promise consists of the promises of the other creditors. 2 

§ 9. Duty imposed by law as consideration.-Performance of, or a promise to perform, a duty imposed by law is not consideration for a promise. Since a duty to perform is imposed by law, the person who performs or promises to perform it is not waiving a legal right; but if a person upon whom a duty is imposed by law does something in excess of what is required by law, this act may constitute consideration. 

For example, since a fireman has a duty by law to extinguish fires, his efforts to extinguish a fire would not be consideration for a promise to reward him therefor; but if a reward is offered for the capture of the person setting the fire, and the fireman captures him, the capture is consideration for the promise to reward. 

2 Lees v. Colgan, p. 308. § 10. Promises to forbear bringing suit.-A promise of a creditor to forbear suing on his claim for a certain length of time, or never to sue, is consideration for a promise of the

CONTRACTS 

debtor. The creditor, in agreeing to forbear bringing suit is waiving a legal right. § 11. Promise of bankrupt to pay a claim discharged by bankruptcy. A promise of a bankrupt to pay a claim discharged by bankruptcy proceedings is enforceable though not supported by consideration. Generally, however, according to statute, the promise is not enforceable unless made in writing. 

The reason this promise is enforceable without consideration is that the original debt is not in reality discharged by bankruptcy; the creditor is merely barred from suing upon the debt by reason of bankruptcy. The new promise by the bankrupt is construed as a waiver of his right not to be sued. 

The protection of the Bankruptcy Act having been waived by the bankrupt as a result of his promise, the creditor may sue upon the original debt. § 12. Promise to pay a debt upon which Statute of Limitations has run.-A promise by a debtor to pay a debt upon which suit is barred by the Statute of Limitations is enforceable without consideration, because the promise is a waiver by the debtor of the protection afforded by the Statute of Limitations. The mere running of the Statute does not discharge the debt; it merely bars suit by the creditor to enforce the debt. 

The promise must be in writing in most jurisdictions. 

An unqualified acknowledgment of the debt or a part payment by the debtor has the same effect as a promise, in that it waives the protection afforded by the Statute of 

Limitations. 

Also, the effect of a new promise, an unqualified acknowledgment, or a part payment by the debtor during the period the Statute is running, is to start the Statute running again from the date thereof.

The Statute of Limitations is a statute which states during what period of time a person may sue upon a claim. The 

Statute also limits the time during which a person may be prosecuted for a crime. The period of limitation varies with the kind of claim, and the statutes of states are not uniform in this respect. Ordinarily, a claim arising out of a contract

CONSIDERATION 

39 may not be sued upon after six years from the time the cause of action accrued.³ 

§ 13. Charitable subscriptions. A charitable subscrip tion is enforceable only if supported by consideration. A promisee who incurs expense in accomplishing a purpose for which a charitable subscription is made, furnishes consideration for, and may enforce, the subscription. In a few jurisdictions it is held that the promise of each subscriber is supported by the promises of the others, but this doctrine seems unsound, since subscriptions are not ordinarily given in exchange for one another.
