CHAPTER IV VOIDABLE CONTRACTS 

§ 1. Contracts of minors. A minor may avoid his contract. This right is conferred upon a minor because of his presumed inexperience and immaturity. In almost all states, persons who have not attained the age of twenty-one are considered minors, or infants.

However, a minor is liable for the reasonable value of necessaries furnished him at his request, if he is not already adequately supplied.¹ Necessaries are things such as food, lodging, clothing, medical attention, and education, that are essential and suitable to the minor and to his station in life. 

A gold watch might be a necessary for the son of a wealthy person, although it might not be for the son of a man of modest means. 

A minor may avoid his contract, even though he represented to the other party that he was of age when he entered into the contract. Also, he is not liable in tort for misrepresenting his age in most states where the question has arisen, the misrepresentation being regarded as a part of the contract. 

A minor may not avoid his marriage. Marriage is a status as well as a contract, and the interests of society require that this status be preserved. 

Even though a minor may avoid his contract, the contract is binding upon the other party. This is the law, also, in the case of contracts of insane persons and drunkards. § 2. Avoidance by minor.-A minor may avoid his executed contract any time during minority or a reasonable period after he becomes of age. After this time his non-action would be construed as ratification. In order to avoid, however, the minor must return the consideration to the other 

1 Strong v. Foote, p. 310. 41

CONTRACTS 

party, if he is still in possession of it. If the minor is not in possession of the consideration, irrespective of the reason, he is nevertheless permitted to avoid. 

A minor may avoid his executed contract relating to realty only during a reasonable time after he reaches majority. 

A minor may avoid his executory contract any time before or after he becomes of age, unless he has ratified such contract. 

Avoidance may be express, or it may be implied from conduct of the minor. § 3. Ratification by minor.-A minor may ratify his contract only after he reaches majority. Ratification may be express, or it may be implied from conduct or language of the minor. Examples: A minor accepting performance from the other party after the former reaches majority, or a minor failing to avoid an executed contract before the expiration of a reasonable time after he reaches majority, would be held to ratify the contract. 

§ 4. Liability of parent upon contract of minor child.-A 

parent is not liable upon the contract of his minor child unless the child is acting as agent for his parent. The parent is an utter stranger to the contract. However, a parent is liable upon a contract implied in law, or quasi contract, for necessaries supplied his minor child. 

§ 5. Liability of minor for torts.-A minor is liable for his torts. A tort is a wrong entitling the party injured thereby to recover damages. Examples of torts are negligence, assault and battery, conversion, slander, and libel. 

A parent is not liable for the tort of his minor child unless the parent has in some way contributed to the wrong. 

§ 6. Contracts of insane persons. An insane person may avoid his contract, except that he is liable for the value of necessaries furnished him. Of course, in avoiding the contract, he must return the consideration if he is in possession of it.

An insane person may avoid his contract any time until the expiration of a reasonable period after he becomes sane. 

Also, he may ratify such contract any time after he becomes sane.

VOIDABLE CONTRACTS 

43 A contract made by an insane person for whom a guardian or conservator has been appointed is void, not merely voidable, irrespective of the knowledge of the other party as to the appointment.

There are, of course, infinite varieties of insanity; but in using the term insane, we refer to a person who is unable to understand the nature and effect of a contemplated act. § 7. Contracts of drunkards.-A drunkard may avoid his contract, except that he is liable for the value of necessaries furnished him. The rules regarding insane persons are applicable also to contracts of drunkards.

By drunkard is meant a person so intoxicated that he is unable to understand the nature and effect of a contemplated act. In this respect the incapacity of drunkenness resembles that of insanity. 

§ 8. Contracts obtained by undue influence. A person may avoid a contract into which he has been induced to enter by undue influence. The reason is that a party induced to contract by reason of undue influence has not freely and voluntarily entered into the contract, as is necessary if a contract is to be binding.

Undue influence is any wrongful influence inducing a party to contract. The influence exerted by some persons occupying the positions of attorney, physician, spiritual adviser, and the like, will be scrutinized with particular care to determine whether it is undue. § 9. Contracts obtained by duress.-A person may avoid a contract into which he has been compelled to enter by duress. 

Such contract is not his voluntary act. 

Duress, according to the modern view, consists of threats, force, or wrongful influence, compelling a person to contract against his will. § 10. Innocent misrepresentation.-A person who has been induced to enter into a contract by reason of an innocent misrepresentation as to a material fact may avoid the contract. 

For example, 4 tells B that A's automobile is in first-class condition, and that he will sell it to B for $400. A does not know that the block of his car is cracked. B, relying upon

CONTRACTS 

the representation, purchases the car. B has the right to avoid the contract when he discovers that A's representation is untrue. 

The essential distinction between an innocent misrepresentation and a fraudulent misrepresentation is that in the latter case the person making the representation has knowledge of its falsity and intends to deceive the other party. 

Also, in fraud, the injured party has remedies in addition to the right to avoid the contract.

An innocent misrepresentation may also constitute a warranty by the seller of goods, in which event the buyer may have other remedies in addition to that of avoidance. This subject will be treated in the chapter on Sales. Fraud 

§ 11. Elements of fraud.-The elements of fraud are as follows: (1) false representation of material existing fact, (2) known to be false by the person making it, (3) made with the intent that it should be acted upon, (4) reasonably relied upon by the person to whom it is made, (5) to his damage. 

§ 12. False representation of material existing fact.- 

Ordinarily, a false representation is made in express words.

But a false representation may also be made by a statement of partial truth when a person is under a duty to disclose full information; and it may be made by active concealment of material facts for the purpose of preventing the other party from discovering them. 

Mere non-disclosure of facts is not fraud unless (1) the facts relate to some latent defect reasonably inaccessible to the other party; or (2) the party failing to make the disclosure occupies a relationship of trust and confidence to the other, as that of parent and child; or (3) the relationship is such that the one knows the other is relying upon him for correct facts, as the relationship of insurance company and applicant for insurance.

To avoid a sale on the ground of fraud on the part of the buyer as to payment, a seller must prove that the buyer has a

VOIDABLE CONTRACTS 

45 fixed intention and fraudulent purpose not to pay for the goods when he obtains them. 

Statements of opinion, judgment, estimate, and the like, are not fraud. These are not statements of facts; and, furthermore, the courts, recognizing that sellers will naturally tend to "puff their wares," allow them some latitude. Such statements are commonly referred to as "seller's talk.” 

As to these, the expression caveat emptor (let the buyer beware) is applicable.

Promises as to the future are not fraud. They are not statements of existing facts.

Misrepresentations as to law are not fraud. These are opinions as to the law, and are always understood as such. 

They may be tested by ordinary vigilance and attention. § 13. Knowledge of falsity of representation.-A person is deemed to know the falsity of his representation if he knows it is false; or if it relates to subject matter about which he can acquire knowledge; or if he makes it in such a manner as to imply that it is true when in fact he does not know whether it is true or false. § 14. Reasonable reliance. The injured party must have reasonably relied upon the representation, if he is to have a remedy for fraud. Reasonable reliance means that the representation was in fact a material inducement to his making the contract, and that a reasonable person in the position of the party to whom the representation was made would be so induced to contract. A person who undertakes to verify the facts misrepresented and to form a judgment of his own is held to rely upon his judgment rather than upon the misrepresentation; but a person may reasonably rely upon a misrepresentation even though he neglects to investigate its truth. § 15. Damage.-A person who has been defrauded must prove that he has been damaged, in order to recover for fraud. 

For example, a buyer who has been defrauded cannot recover if the goods purchased are worth what he paid for them. 

However, the damage may be other than monetary.

CONTRACTS § 16. Remedies for fraud. The injured party may elect any one of the following remedies: (1) He may avoid the contract; this act is commonly called rescission. In this event he must act as soon as he discovers the fraud, and must return or offer to return the consideration. Any acts of his that constitute ratification will deprive him of his right to avoid. (2) He may bring an action in tort for deceit (fraud), in which case he keeps the consideration received by him and seeks to recover damages for his injury. He may pursue this remedy until the Statute of Limitations has run. (3) He may set up the fraud as a defense in an action brought against him for recovery of the price; this is called recoupment. 

A person may not complain of fraud if he signs a contract expressly providing that no representation not contained in the contract shall be binding. § 17. Fraud in the execution of a contract.-Fraudulent representations as to the contract itself are referred to as fraud in the execution, as distinguished from fraud antecedent to the contract, which has just been discussed. 

Thus, fraud which induces a person to enter into a contract different in nature from that represented renders the contract void; for example, A induces B to sign a promissory note by a representation that the instrument is a power of attorney. 

Fraud which induces a person to enter into a contract the terms of which are misrepresented is merely voidable; for example, A fraudulently represents to B that the contract to purchase real estate, which B is signing, includes a certain parcel, whereas it does not. 

However, in the absence of fraudulent misrepresentations, a party cannot complain merely because he does not read or cannot understand the paper he signs. Mistake § 18. Mistake of one party only.-Mistake of only one party to a contract as to the subject matter, terms, or effect of a contract, which mistake is not known to the other party, does not affect the validity of a contract.2 For example, 2 Bostwick v. Mutual Life Insurance Co., p. 311.

VOIDABLE CONTRACTS 

47 A and B enter into a written contract providing that A is to construct a house for B, and B is to pay A the sum of $5,000 therefor. A mistakenly supposes that the amount set forth in the agreement is $7,000. A's mistake does not affect the validity of the contract.

However, if one party causes the mistake of the other, the contract will be voidable; but mere knowledge of one party that the other party is mistaken as to the quality or value of the subject matter does not affect the contract. 

A person may recover an overpayment of money which he has made under a mistake of fact. It is immaterial whether the mistake was mutual or solely his. It is sufficient that there has been a failure of consideration. § 19. Mutual mistake.—Mutual mistake as to any mate rial matter renders a contract void. Illustrations of material matters are the existence or identity of the subject matter, or the material terms of the contract. For example, if A contracts to sell B a parcel of land on Prospect Street, and B, without fault or negligence on his part, believes he is buying a parcel on another Prospect Street, no contract results. 

Also, if A buys from B a bar of base metal which both parties believe to be gold, no contract results.

But mutual mistake as to collateral matters does not affect the validity of the contract. By collateral matters is meant matters which are not conditions of the contract or which do not relate to its fundamental basis, although they may have some bearing or influence upon the agreement. For example, if A sells B a vase, the validity of the contract will not be affected by the mistaken belief of both that the vase is the workmanship of some celebrated artist; but if the contract were conditioned upon this fact, the contract would be void if this were not a fact.

A mistake by one party or both as to law does not affect the validity of the agreement. § 20. Reformation of written instruments.-A court in equity will correct a written instrument which, through mistake or oversight of both parties, does not conform to their intention.

CHAPTER V ILLEGAL CONTRACTS 

§ 1. In general. One of the elements essential to the creation of a contract is legal subject matter. The subject matter is illegal when it is so declared by law; when it violates, or has as its object the violation of, a statute or rule of common law; or when it is contrary to public policy. An illegal contract is unenforceable, and is generally void. The laws of the states are not uniform as to what contracts are illegal; this chapter will treat of those contracts most commonly held illegal in the various states. 

§ 2. Contracts violating law. Contracts the objects of which are the violation of any statute or rule of common law are void. Contracts for the commission of crimes or torts come within this classification. § 3. Sunday contracts. By statute in many states contracts entered into on Sunday are void. 

§ 4. Gaming contracts.-Gaming contracts are void in most states. A gaming contract is one in which one of the parties is to win, and the other is to lose, upon the happening of an uncertain event. In some states a person may recover money lost in gambling.

Contracts to purchase stocks, grain, and the like, where no delivery is made, are not gaming contracts if the parties intend an actual sale. But if the parties, not intending a sale, are to settle upon a difference, depending upon a rise or a fall of the market, the contract will be a gaming contract and will be void.

Insurance contracts are valid when the insured has an insurable interest. Illustrations of insurable interest are: the interest of a person in property owned by him or in which he has some other legal or equitable interest; the interest of a person in his own life; the interest of a creditor in the life of a 49

CONTRACTS 

debtor; the interests of married persons, parents and children, and partners in the lives one of the other. An insurance contract in which the insured does not have an insurable interest is a gaming contract and is unenforceable. 

5. Usurious contracts.-Usurious contracts are unen forceable to the extent provided by law in any particular state. 

A usurious contract is one providing for a rate of interest in excess of the maximum allowed by law. State laws vary considerably as to the maximum amount of interest that may be charged and as to the enforceability of usurious contracts. In some states, the lender may recover all except the excess interest; in others, only the principal; in still others, only a portion of the principal.

In most states pawnbrokers and professional lenders of small sums are permitted to charge a high rate of interest, because of the risk attending their loans.

The legal rate of interest in a state is to be distinguished from the maximum rate, the former being a rate upon debts due and upon loans on which interest is to be charged, but the rate of which is not fixed by the parties.¹ 

§ 6. Contracts in restraint of trade. A contract in general or unreasonable restraint of trade is void. For example, an agreement made by all the stores in a certain city that the X Store should be the only one to sell shoes would be void, since such a contract would result in a monopoly. 

Three Federal statutes have been enacted to prevent restraints of trade: the Sherman Anti-Trust Act, the Clayton

Act, and the Trade Commission Act. In brief, these statutes prohibit and punish certain combinations in the form of trust or otherwise, conspiracies in restraint of trade, monopolization of trade or of commerce, certain discriminations in price between different purchasers, certain acquisitions by one corporation of the stock of other corporations, certain "interlocking directorates," and unfair competition. 

§ 7. Valid contracts in restraint of trade.-Certain con tracts in restraint of trade are valid if reasonable. Agree- 

¹ Table showing Interest Rates and Usury Laws of the various states, p. 504.

ILLEGAL CONTRACTS 

51 ments that will generally be upheld are incidental provisions in some other contract.

Examples of such contracts are contracts of sale of a business wherein the seller agrees not to compete with the buyer, and contracts of employment wherein the employee agrees that upon termination of his employment he will not compete with his employer.

The reason for enforcing such agreements is the interest of society in protecting purchasers of the good will of a business, and in protecting employers against unfair competition of their former employees.

However, such agreements not to compete must be reasonable if they are to be upheld. What is a reasonable agreement depends, of course, upon the particular case presented. 

Ordinarily, such agreements are limited as to time or space, or both. Whether or not either or both limitations must be present, and whether the extent of the limitation is reasonable, will depend upon the case considered; but because of the hardship upon the party agreeing not to compete, such agreements will not be enforced beyond the point reasonably necessary to protect a buyer or an employer. 

For example, A, incidental to his contract of employment as a laundry driver in Chicago, agrees that upon the termination of his contract of employment he will never again engage in the laundry business anywhere. This agreement would not be enforced because it is unreasonable; but his agreement not to engage in the laundry business in Chicago for a year following termination of his employment would probably be enforced.

Again, suppose A, incidental to the sale of his drug store in Bangor, Maine, agrees that he will never again engage in the drug business anywhere. This agreement would be held unreasonable; but his agreement not to engage in that business again in Bangor would probably be enforced.

contracts may be contrary be contrary to public policy and opposed to the best interests of society. 

Contracts to influence public officials, fiduciaries, and those whose duties affect public interest are void. 

Contracts the objects of which are illicit cohabitation or restraint of marriage are void.

Contracts to compound a crime are void. For example, an agreement by a victim not to prosecute a criminal in consideration of reparation is unenforceable.

Stipulations in contracts limiting the liability for negligence of carriers, warehousemen, bailees for hire, and the like, are void. For example: A railroad transports goods under an agreement that it is not to be liable for any loss of, or damage to, the goods resulting from its negligence.

STATUTE OF FRAUDS § 1. In general. The Statute of Frauds is a statute, found in all states, which provides that certain kinds of contracts are not binding unless they are in writing and signed by the party to be charged, or his agent; or, in certain sales of personal property, unless there is a writing or some part performance.

The object of the Statute is to prevent fraud and perjured testimony in the proof of certain kinds of contracts, by requiring written evidence of the contract. The kinds of contracts enumerated in the Statute are those considered most likely to encourage attempts to establish a contract by fraud and false testimony.

CHAPTER VI 

The Statutes of Frauds in the various states are closely patterned upon sections of the "Statute of Frauds and 

Perjuries," enacted in England in 1676. 

§ 2. Text of typical statute.-I. "No action shall be brought: (1) to charge an executor or administrator, or an assignee in insolvency upon a special promise to answer damages out of his own estate; (2) to charge a person . . . to answer for the debt, default or misdoings of another; (3) upon an agreement made upon consideration of marriage; (4) upon a contract for the sale of lands or any interest in or concerning them; or (5) upon an agreement . . . not to be performed within one year from the making thereof; unless the promise, contract or agreement upon which such action is brought, or some memorandum or note thereof, is in writing and signed by the party to be charged therewith, or by some person thereunto by him lawfully authorized. The consideration. may be proved by any legal evidence. 

II. "A contract to sell or a sale of any goods or choses in action of the value of $500 or more shall not be enforceable by 51

STATUTE OF FRAUDS 

55 action unless the buyer shall accept part of the goods or choses in action. . . and actually receive the same, or give something in earnest . . or in part payment, or unless some note or memorandum in writing of the contract or sale be signed by the party to be charged or his agent in that behalf." 

The above Statute of Frauds is in force in Massachusetts. 

The statutes in other states are substantially the same. However, the amount relating to sales of personal property varies among the states.¹ 

It will be observed that the Statute does not declare void contracts which do not comply with it; such contracts are merely unenforceable. 

Also, a promise within the Statute, like any other promise, must be supported by consideration. § 3. Promise of executor.-Promises of executors, administrators, and assignees in insolvency to pay a debt of the estate from their own property are unenforceable unless they are in writing and signed. § 4. Promise to pay debt of another.-Promises to answer for the debt, default, or misdoings of another are unenforceable unless they are in writing and signed. For example, A owes 

B $100. C says to B, "If you will agree to refrain from bringing suit for two weeks, I will pay A's debt if he does not pay.' 

B agrees.

B cannot recover from C because C's promise is not made in writing. 

A promise is outside the Statute and enforceable though oral when it is an original promise made by a third party; or when it is a promise to pay the debt of another, resulting in the discharge of the principal debtor. In these cases the promise is not a promise to pay the debt of another if he does not himself pay. For example, C says to B, "Give A whatever groceries he needs. I will pay for them." This statement is an original promise by C and is not within the Statute. 

Again, A owes B $100. C says to B, "If you will release A from his debt, I will pay you the $100." B agrees to release 

A. The promise of C is his primary obligation, and is not 

¹ Table showing amounts of Statutes of Frauds in the various states, p. 509.

CONTRACTS 

within the Statute. This last situation, the substitution of a new debt for an existing one, is called a novation. 

§ 5. Agreements in consideration of marriage.—Agree ments in consideration of marriage are unenforceable unless they are in writing and signed. This rule refers to promises to pay money or to convey property in consideration of marriage. 

It does not refer to mutual promises to marry, which are binding though oral. 

§ 6. Contract for sale of land.-Contracts for the sale of land or for any interest in or concerning land are unenforceable unless they are in writing and signed. This provision applies to leases also, except that in most states leases for terms of not more than a specified period, usually one year, may be oral. The Statute applies also to contracts for rights of way and other easements, and to agreements to give or to enlarge a mortgage. The Statute does not apply to contracts for letting rooms.

Payments made in reliance upon an oral agreement within the Statute may be recovered. § 7. Agreement not to be performed within one year.- 

Agreements not to be performed within one year from their making are unenforceable unless they are in writing and signed. For example, A and B enter into an oral contract whereby A is to work for B for five years and B is to pay A $100 monthly. If, after five months, B were to discharge A without cause, A could not recover from B for breach of this contract. 

Contracts that may possibly be performed within one year are agreements to be performed within a year, although performance may probably take longer. For example, a contract by A to construct ten houses for B would be performable within a year, although A is likely to take two years for completion. A, by doubling his force, could complete the contract within a year. Again, A and B enter into a contract whereby A is to employ B permanently. This is an agreement to be performed within a year because A might die 

2 Derby v. Phelps, p. 313.

STATUTE OF FRAUDS 

57 within a year and, if he should, the contract would be completely performed. 

§ 8. Contract for sale of personal property.—Contracts for the sale of personal property for a price of $500 (the amount varies in states) or more are unenforceable unless they are in writing and signed, or unless the buyer receives part of the goods or pays part of the price. 

When the seller is to manufacture goods especially for the buyer and the goods are not suitable for sale to others in the ordinary course of the seller's business, the Statute does not apply. Such a contract is deemed a contract for labor and materials rather than a contract of sale. § 9. Sufficiency of writing.-Any kind of writing setting forth the names of the parties, the subject matter, and the material terms of the agreement, and signed by the party to be charged or his agent, will be sufficient. The consideration must be stated, unless the Statute in a particular state provides that it is unnecessary. Oral evidence may usually be introduced in court to explain ambiguous terms of the writing. 

The writing need not be confined to one paper. Frequently it is gathered from letters, telegrams, memoranda, and so forth, all of which refer to one contract. 

The signature of the party sought to be charged or of his agent is sufficient. Thus, cases arise in which one party is bound by the contract because he has signed a memorandum of it, while the other party is not bound because he has not signed.

An auctioneer is held an agent of both seller and buyer for the purpose of making and signing a memorandum within the 

Statute of Frauds. § 10. Other promises required to be in writing.-In many states the following are also unenforceable unless they are in writing and signed: (1) a promise by a bankrupt to pay a debt discharged by bankruptcy proceedings; (2) a promise to pay or an acknowledgment of debt barred by the Statute of Limitations; (3) an agreement to make a will or to give a legacy; (4) a representation concerning the character, credit, ability, and so forth, of another.

CHAPTER VII PARTIES AFFECTED BY CONTRACTS Joint Obligations 

§ 1. Joint obligations. A joint obligation arises when two or more persons make one promise. An example is a writing, "We promise to pay A $100 for his Buick car," signed by B and C.

Joint obligors must be sued together, or those sued will have a procedural defense of non-joinder.¹

A release of one joint obligor is a release of all. However, a covenant not to sue, or a qualified release of, one joint obligor does not discharge the others. 

§ 2. Several obligations.-A several obligation arises when two or more persons each make one promise. An example is a writing, "Each of us promises to pay A $100 for his Buick car," signed by B and C. 

Several obligors may be sued separately, and a release of one does not discharge the others. § 3. Joint and several obligations.-A joint and several obligation arises when two or more persons together and separately make one promise. An example is an agreement, "We and each of us promise to pay A $100 for his Buick car,' signed by B and C. 

Joint and several obligors may be sued together or separately, but a release of one is a release of all. § 4. Joint obligees. A release by one joint obligee discharges the rights of all. Joint obligees must sue jointly. 

Contracts for Benefit of Third Persons 

§ 5. Definition and law. A contract for the benefit of a third person is a contract under which a third party is directly 

1 City of Philadelphia v. Reeves and Cabot, p. 314. 59

CONTRACTS 

to benefit, but to which he is not a party; that is to say, the consideration moves from one party who is not to receive the benefit of the other party's promise. For example, A owns land upon which B holds a mortgage. A sells the land to C, who agrees with A to assume and pay B the amount of the mortgage as part of the purchase price of the land. B is a third party beneficiary of this contract between A and C. 

A third party beneficiary may sue upon the contract, by the weight of authority. In those states where he is not permitted to sue, many exceptions to the rule have been established; for example, the beneficiary of a life insurance policy is allowed to sue upon the contract of insurance. 

However, a third party beneficiary must be directly benefited by the contract if he is to have the right to sue. An incidental benefit will not suffice. Assignments § 6. In general.—An assignment of a contract is a transfer by one party to another, of the former's rights under a contract. For example, A loans B $100, which is to be repaid with interest a year from the date of the loan. A executes and delivers to C the following writing: "I hereby assign, transfer, and set over to C my right to receive $100 and interest from B. (Signed) A." The person who makes the assignment is called an assignor; the person to whom it is made, an assignee.

An assignment may be made orally or in writing and with or without consideration. 

§ 7. What may be assigned.-Ordinarily, a party may assign his rights under a contract. For example, A may assign to C the former's right to receive from B ten barrels of apples for which A has paid B. However, a party may not assign a right coupled with a liability; for example, if A, in the aforementioned example, is to receive the apples on credit, he cannot assign his right. Nor may a person assign rights involving a relationship of personal confidence. For example, A and B enter into a contract

PARTIES AFFECTED BY CONTRACTS 

61 whereby B is to work for A for a year at a stipulated salary. 

A may not assign to C his right to have B work for him for a year.

A party may not assign his duties under a contract. For example, B is under a contractual duty to work for A for a year. B may not assign this obligation to C. 

However, if duties do not involve personal services, a party may have them performed by another in his stead. 

For example, A and B enter into a contract whereby A is to sell B a new Buick car for a certain price. A may have C furnish and deliver the car for him. In this situation, of course, the assignor is still liable to B for performance of the contract, notwithstanding the assignment; but B would have no right to object to performance by the assignee. If the contract were for personal services, however, B could insist upon performance by A, the party with whom he contracted. 

Of course, in any case, if one party assents to the assignment of his contract by the other party to a third party, the assignment will be valid. In speaking of assignments in this section, we have referred only to assignments which are effective without the assent of the other party to the contract. § 8. Notice of assignment.-A party may perform his contract for the assignor until he is notified of an assignment by the assignee or by anyone else. After notice, he may perform only for the assignee. For example, A and B enter into a contract under which B is to pay A $100. A assigns his right to receive this sum to C, who does not notify B of the assignment. B may pay this sum to A; but if he pays it to 

A after notice of the assignment, he will still be liable to C for the amount of the payment.

If a party assigns his rights under a contract to two or more persons, the first assignee having no notice of prior assignments, who notifies the other contracting party of the assignment, prevails. 

§ 9. Rights of assignee.—An assignee acquires the rights of the assignor subject to all defenses which the other contracting party might raise against the assignor. For example, A assigns to C his claim for $100, arising under a contract with 1

CONTRACTS 

B. If A obtained this contract by fraud, B might raise the defense of fraud against C.

A transferee of a negotiable instrument who is a holder in due course is not subject to certain defenses which the obligor might have raised against the transferor. This point will be discussed further in Chapters IV and V of Negotiable Instruments. 

§ 10. Assignments by operation of law. Generally speaking, the rights and liabilities of a party pass, upon his death, to his executor or administrator, and, upon his bankruptcy, to his trustee in bankruptcy. Personal rights and liabilities, however, do not survive death and bankruptcy. For example, A owes B $100 under a contract performed by B. Upon 

B's death or bankruptcy, the right to collect this amount will pass to B's representative; but if B were bound by a contract to perform personal services for A, the contract would terminate upon B's death. 

Assignment by operation of law means an assignment which takes place upon the occurrence of an event which the law states shall cause an assignment.

CHAPTER VIII CONSTRUCTION AND PERFORMANCE § 1. Terms of contract are questions of fact.-The ques tion of what are the terms of a contract is a question of fact to be determined by the jury, or, if there is no jury, by the judge who is making findings of fact. For example, A sues 

B for breach of a contract by which B was to purchase an automobile. A delivered the automobile. A claims the contract price was $200; B contends that the price named by 

A was $100. Whether the price was $100 or $200 is a question of fact to be determined by a jury, or, if there is no jury, by a judge. The terms may appear expressly in conversations and writings of the parties; or they may be implied from the conduct of the parties and all the circumstances surrounding the transaction.

If certain terms of a contract are established, a further question may arise as to how the terms are to be construed. 

For example, A agrees to sell B his car for $400, and B agrees to buy it. A term of the contract is that the car is to be completely equipped." If A and B dispute as to what this term means, the court is called upon to construe the meaning. 66 

§ 2. Construction in accordance with intent.-A contract is construed in accordance with the expressed intent of the parties. This intent is discovered from the language used by the parties, if the agreement is entirely in writing. If the agreement is oral, or partly oral and partly written, the intent is gathered from what the parties have written, from what they have said, and from all the circumstances surrounding the transaction. 

§ 3. Rules of construction.-(1) The words of parties are construed in their ordinary meaning unless they are shown to have been given a different meaning by both parties. 64

CONSTRUCTION AND PERFORMANCE 

65 (2) A party is bound by the construction placed upon his words by the other party acting as a reasonable man. (3) The words will be construed most strongly against the party using them. (4) Written words prevail over printed words in case of conflict. (5) When a custom or usage is established, with knowledge of which both parties entered into a contract, the words will be considered as having been used in the sense such custom or usage attaches to them. § 4. Parol evidence rule. The parol evidence rule is that oral testimony may not be offered at a trial to alter or add to the terms of a written instrument. For example, A and B sign a written agreement providing that A is to sell B his horse for $80. B would not be permitted to testify at the trial that the parties had orally agreed, at the time the writing was executed, that the price was to be $50. The reason for the rule is that the written contract of the parties is the best evidence of their agreement, and to allow less trustworthy evidence to contradict it would afford an opportunity for fraud. However, oral testimony may be introduced to prove that the written agreement was never entered into; or that it was obtained by fraud, duress, or undue influence; or that there was mistake, illegality, and the like.

An incomplete written instrument may be completed by oral testimony as to terms orally agreed upon. For example, if A and B sign a written agreement stating merely that A agrees to sell his horse to B, A may offer oral testimony that the parties orally agreed upon a price of $50. 

Oral testimony of an agreement subsequent to the execution of the written agreement may be offered for the purpose of proving modification or rescission of the written agreement. 

The parol evidence rule excludes only oral testimony of agreements contemporaneous with or prior to the execution of the written agreement. 

§ 5. Conditions precedent.-A condition precedent is a term of a contract, generally an act, which must be performed by one party before the other party is obliged to perform his

CONTRACTS 

side of the contract. For example, A and B enter into a contract whereby A agrees to paint B's house, and B agrees to pay him therefor the sum of $100. The promise of A to paint B's house is a condition precedent, which must be performed before B can be held liable upon his promise. 

Whether a term of a contract is a condition precedent depends upon the intent of the parties, to be gathered from their words and surrounding circumstances. Implied terms, as well as express, may constitute conditions precedent. For example, in a contract whereby A is to sell B a car, it is impliedly a condition precedent to the liability of B that A should have title to the car he delivers to B. 

In building contracts providing that the contractor shall be entitled to payment for performance only upon presentment by a certain architect of a certificate setting forth satisfactory performance, the presentment of the certificate is held a condition precedent. But performance of the condition may be excused and the builder allowed to recover under the contract in certain cases, such as when the architect dies, becomes insane, or fraudulently or whimsically refuses to give the certificate.

Whether a term of a contract providing for performance at a certain time is a condition precedent depends upon whether the term is of great importance in the contract. 

Ordinarily, time is not considered a condition precedent.

However, in contracts for the manufacture or sale of marketable goods, time is apt to be considered a condition precedent. 

If the parties stipulate in the contract, or manifest an intent, that time shall be of the essence, it will be so held in construing the contract. § 6. Concurrent conditions. Concurrent conditions are terms of a contract which are to be performed by both parties at the same time. For example, A and B enter into a contract whereby A is to sell B his auto on Monday at three o'clock if B pays A $200 at that time. Here the delivery of the automobile and the payment of the price are acts which are to be performed simultaneously.

CONSTRUCTION AND PERFORMANCE 

67 Concurrent conditions are implied if the terms are such that they may be performed at the same time; also, if the time of performance is fixed at a definite time on one side, though not on the other.

A party may not recover for breach of the other party's concurrent condition unless he himself has performed or tendered performance on his side. § 7. Independent conditions.-Independent conditions are conditions which, while consideration one for the other, are to be performed without reference to each other. For example: 

A and B sign a lease which contains a covenant (promise) that A will make reasonable repairs during the period of the lease, and a covenant that B will pay a rental of $50 monthly in advance. 

A party who fails to perform his independent promise may nevertheless recover from the other party for breach of his independent promise; and the party sued may not claim, for the purpose of reducing damages, that the party suing also failed to perform his independent condition; to make this claim, the party sued must bring suit himself. 

Ordinarily, conditions are dependent, but when it appears from the sense of the contract, or from the times of performance, that performance on one side is not conditional upon performance on the other, the promises will be construed as independent.¹ § 8. Satisfaction of promisee.—A promise to be performed to the satisfaction of another party, which involves personal taste, feelings, or sensibilities, is not performed if the promisee is honestly dissatisfied. For example, A agrees with B to make a suit of clothes to B's satisfaction for a price of $30. 

A makes the suit, but B is honestly dissatisfied and returns the suit. A cannot recover upon the contract.

However, if the promise does not involve personal taste, feelings, or sensibilities, the promisor can recover if the promisee, as a reasonable man, should be satisfied with performance. An example is a contract to install a heating system to the buyer's satisfaction. 

¹ International Textbook Co. v. Martin, p. 316.

CONTRACTS 

§ 9. Payment. A debt must be paid in legal tender unless the creditor is willing to accept a substitute. If a creditor rejects a debtor's unconditional tender of payment in legal tender, the creditor may not recover interest for the period following the tender of payment, or the costs of suit. 

A debtor may direct that his payment be applied against one of several debts owed the creditor. In the absence of direction by the debtor, the creditor may apply the payment as he chooses.

Prima facie, in a few states, including Maine and Massachusetts, receipt by a creditor of a negotiable note or bill is considered payment, discharging the debt, but this rule is a mere presumption and may be overcome by evidence that the creditor did not intend to receive the instrument as payment. 

Excuses for Non-Performance 

§ 10. Importance.-A party whose failure to perform is excused is not liable in damages for breach of contract. 

Otherwise, he is liable.

Also, a party whose failure to perform is excused may sometimes recover from the other party for breach of contract. 

Ordinarily, a party who sues for breach of contract must prove that he has fully performed his side of the contract. § 11. Prevention.-Any act by one party, which prevents the other party from performing, excuses the latter's nonperformance. It may be said that it is an implied condition of a contract that one party shall do nothing to hinder or to obstruct performance by the other. § 12. Waiver.-Waiver by a party of his right to the other party's performance may excuse non-performance. For example, a party accepts a suit which he knows does not comply with the contract, and says nothing about the defects. 

He may be held to have waived his right to proper performance by the other party, and will himself be liable for the contract price.

Waiver is any conduct or language of a party indicating an intention not to enforce the provisions of a contract performed defectively, in part only, or belatedly by the other party.

CONSTRUCTION AND PERFORMANCE 

69 If a party desires to revive a condition of a contract which he has led the other party to believe was waived, he must give reasonable notice. 

§ 13. Impossibility.-Legal impossibility of performing a contract excuses non-performance. Certain types of legal impossibility will be discussed in the next section. However, the mere fact that performance becomes more difficult or burdensome than was expected does not constitute impossibility, excusing non-performance.¹ 

§ 14. Types of impossibility.-Death or illness of a promisor excuses non-performance of a contract for personal services, but not of a contract not requiring personal services. 

A change of law rendering performance illegal excuses non-performance.

The destruction of subject matter essential to the completion of a contract excuses non-performance-for example, A rents a theater to B and the theater burns before the night of performance; —but not if the subject matter is not essential to completion of the contract for example, if a builder contracts to construct a house and the house burns when it is half built, the builder must construct another house.

CHAPTER IX REMEDIES 

§ 1. Specific performance and injunction.-A court of equity may decree specific performance (performance in the specific manner agreed upon) when the law remedy (money damages) is inadequate. It is only in very exceptional cases that the law remedy of money damages is inadequate. 

Examples of contracts which courts of equity will specifically enforce are the following: (1) Contracts to sell land.

Money damages are inadequate because, since land possesses such qualities as location, neighborhood, soil, and so forth, the buyer cannot with money damages purchase another parcel of land like the one he has contracted to buy. (2) 

Contracts to sell personal property of rare or peculiar value, such as an old painting by a celebrated artist. Obviously, money damages would be an inadequate remedy for the seller's breach. However, contracts to sell such property as wheat, automobiles, and the like, which can be replaced, will not be specifically enforced.

A court of equity may enjoin a party not to break his contract when the law remedy for the breach is inadequate. A celebrated artist who has agreed to perform at a certain theater, and nowhere else, may be enjoined not to violate his contract by appearing at any other theater. A seller of a business who has agreed reasonably not to engage in that business may be restrained by injunction from violating his contract. However, a party will not be ordered to perform his contract for personal services and the like. Such injunction would require too much supervision by the court, and would also compel involuntary association. § 2. Replevin. The owner of goods wrongfully taken or withheld by another may recover such goods in an action of replevin. For example, A sells his automobile to B, who pays 71'

CONTRACTS 

A the price, but A refuses to deliver the automobile although title has passed to B. B may bring an action of replevin to obtain the car. If B prefers to receive money damages for 

A's wrong, instead of the car, B may bring an action in tort for conversion. § 3. Rescission.—A party may rescind a contract if the other party commits a material breach: that is, a breach going to the essence of the contract. However, the breach of subsidiary terms or of those for which compensation can be paid in money is not ground for rescission. 

A party may rescind if the other party commits a willful and deliberate breach. In such a case it is unimportant whether the breach is also material. 

A party may also rescind if he receives, prior to the time for performance, an unconditional notice from the other party of the latter's intention not to perform.

The right to rescind in the cases of infancy, fraud, mistake, and similar situations has already been considered. 

A right to rescind must be exercised promptly on discovery of the facts from which it arises, and the injured party must return or offer to return the consideration received by him under the contract. § 4. Damages.-A party may recover damages for any breach of contract by the other party. The object of damages is to place the injured party in as good a position as he would have been had the contract been carried out so far as money can put him in that position. 

The amount of damage, in tort as well as in contract, is whatever loss is the natural and proximate consequence of the breach, or was reasonably within the contemplation of the parties. A natural consequence of a breach is a loss which occurs in the ordinary course of events which might reasonably have been foreseen. A proximate consequence of a breach is a loss which is directly caused by the breach. 

For example, A contracts to construct for B a first-class refrigerator, in which B is to keep chickens for the market, and A is aware of this fact. A breaks his contract in that he builds a defective refrigerator. As a result of the defect

REMEDIES 

73 many of B's chickens spoil. B can recover as damage the difference between the value of a refrigerator built in accordance with the contract and the value of this defective refrigerator, and also the market value of the chickens lost. These are the natural and proximate consequences of the breach. 

An injured party cannot recover damage for a remote, speculative, or conjectural loss. Such loss would not be a natural consequence of the breach. Also, it is an elementary rule of the law of damages that the damage must be certain: that is, capable of reasonable ascertainment. 

§ 5. Mitigation of damage.—A party injured by a breach of contract must mitigate the damage; that is, he must reduce it as much as possible. For example, an employer breaks his contract by discharging an employee. The employee, although having a right to recover damages for breach of contract, must try to reduce the damage by making a reasonable effort to obtain similar work in the same locality. 

§ 6. Liquidated damages. When the contract stipulates the amount of damage to be recovered in the event of a breach, the injured party may recover only this amount. 

However, liquidated damages that are so large and out of proportion to the loss as to constitute a penalty for breaking the contract, or a forfeiture, will be disregarded, and damages will be determined by the court as if there were no agreement. § 7. Recovery for part performance. A party performing his contract substantially and in good faith may recover in quasi contract for his part performance.¹ He may not recover upon the contract, because he has not fully performed it; but he may recover in quasi contract, because justice requires that under the circumstances a party should pay for the benefit he has received. This theory of recovery is sometimes called recovery in quantum meruit (as much as he deserves), the law implying a promise on the part of a party to pay the other party as much as he deserves. 

A party failing willfully to complete his contract is entitled to recover nothing, generally speaking. 

¹ Manitowoc Steam Boiler Works v. Manitowoc Glue Co., p. 320.

CONTRACTS 

§ 8. Anticipatory breach.-An anticipatory breach is a repudiation by one party, prior to the time for performance, of his obligation under the contract. The injured party, by the great weight of authority, may elect to sue for damages at once upon an anticipatory breach of a contract by the other party. If he does not elect to act upon the anticipatory breach, the performance of the contract is not affected by the breach. The doctrine of anticipatory breach is not recognized in a few states, including Massachusetts. 

§ 9. Interference with contract.—An injured party may recover damages in tort from a person who, with notice of an existing contract, wrongfully procures a breach of it. An injunction in equity may be obtained against one who attempts or threatens wrongfully to procure such breach.

Also, it may be held actionable for one who knows that persons are negotiating to contract with the injured party, or that they habitually contract with him, wrongfully to procure their refusal to contract.

CHAPTER X DISCHARGE OF CONTRACTS § 1. Discharge by performance.—A contract is discharged by full performance of its terms.

§ 2. Discharge by agreement.-A contract may be dis charged by mutual agreement to terminate it. This agreement may be oral or in writing. The release of one party is consideration for the release of the other. However, if one party has fully performed his side of the contract, his release of the other party, in order to be binding, must be supported by some consideration other than a promise to release. 

A contract may be discharged by merger. Merger occurs when a contract is modified or altered by a subsequent agreement, the old contract merging with the new.

A contract may be discharged by a novation, which extinguishes an existing agreement and substitutes a new one in its place; for example, C promises to pay A's debt to B in consideration of B's promise to release A. 

§ 3. Discharge by accord and satisfaction.-A contract may be discharged by an accord and satisfaction. An accord is an agreement whereby a party is to perform in some way other than that stipulated in the contract. Satisfaction is performance of the new agreement. For example, A has contracted to sell B his horse for $100. A and B agree that A may deliver his Buick car instead of the horse. A delivers the car and B pays the price. The original contract is now discharged.

An accord alone does not discharge a contract, for the reason that the parties do not intend to discharge the original contract until the accord is performed (satisfied). 

§ 4. Discharge by material alteration.-A written contract will be discharged by an intentional, material alteration made 76

DISCHARGE OF CONTRACTS 

77 without the consent of the parties.

This point will be con sidered further in Chapter VII of Negotiable Instruments. 

§ 5. Discharge by operation of law. The discharge in bankruptcy of an obligor, or the running of the Statute of Limitations upon a claim, may discharge the right to sue upon a contract. Technically, the obligation is not affected by bankruptcy or by the running of the Statute of Limitations; simply, the courts will not allow suit to enforce the claim, if either defense is affirmatively raised.

AGENCY

AGENCY CHAPTER I CREATION OF AGENCY 

§ 1. Definition of an agent.-An agent is one authorized to act in behalf of another. The person in whose behalf he acts is called the principal. 

The chief distinction between the relationships of principal and agent and master and servant is that an agent generally represents his principal in contracts with third parties, while a servant generally performs personal services and labor for his master. For example, a chauffeur would be considered a servant while he was driving his employer's car, and an agent while purchasing supplies for his employer. However, it is unimportant to distinguish between the relationships, because, in general, the principles governing them are the same. The term agent will be used hereafter in referring to one who is an agent or a servant. § 2. Distinction between agent and independent contractor. An independent contractor is one who is not subject to the direction and control of his employer as to the details of his employment, whereas an agent is so subject. An independent contractor undertakes to accomplish a certain result, usually for a gross sum, and the choice of means and methods is left to him.¹ For example, X enters into a contract with C whereby C is to construct a house for X, in accordance with certain plans and specifications, for $5,000. C is an independent contractor. However, if X employed A to make such repairs on his house as he may designate and in the manner directed, at a price of $1 an hour, A would be an agent. 

¹ Lawrence v. Shipman, p. 323. 81

AGENCY 

The reason it is important to determine in a particular case whether a person is an agent or an independent contractor is that an employer is liable upon the contracts and torts of his agent, entered into or committed within the scope of the agent's employment, but not upon those of an independent contractor, generally speaking. 

§ 3. Capacity to be principal and agent.-Any person competent to act himself may be a principal. Thus, while a minor may appoint an agent, the contract of agency, as well as the contract entered into by the agent with a third party, would be voidable at the election of the minor. 

Any person may be an agent, irrespective of his competency to perform the act for himself. Thus a minor may be an agent, and his contract in behalf of his principal with a third party would be binding on both the principal and the third party. The reason for this rule is that the principal and the agent are regarded as one person, the agent being considered merely an extension of the principal. 

§ 4. What may be performed through an agent. The general rule is that a person may perform through an agent anything which he may do himself. However, there are many acts which by law, by public policy, or for other reasons may not be performed through an agent. For example, a citizen may not vote through an agent at a public election; a person may not perform his contract for personal services through an agent; a person may not make oath through an agent, since the object of the oath is to search the conscience of the person making it; trustees, public officers, and the like may not delegate duties involving discretion; a person may not appoint an agent to perform an illegal act. § 5. Form of appointment. Generally speaking, the appointment of an agent may be made orally or in writing, expressly or impliedly,2 with or without consideration. An instrument authorizing a person to act as agent is known as a power of attorney.3 

2 Hill v. Morey, p. 325. 

3 Form of Power of Attorney, p. 487.

CREATION OF AGENCY 

83 An agent appointed to execute an instrument under seal must be authorized under seal. This requirement is sometimes expressed as follows: The authority of the agent must be of equal dignity with the instrument to be executed by him.

Generally, the agency relationship will not arise without a principal's authorizing an agent to act for him. Exceptions to this rule are agency by necessity, by estoppel, and by ratification. 

§ 6. Agency by necessity.-A wife without adequate means herself is an agent by necessity for her husband, in purchasing necessaries with which he has wrongfully failed to supply her. This is an agency implied by law. The assent of the husband to such purchase is immaterial. Of course, if the wife is already adequately supplied with necessaries, or if she has adequate means of her own, or if she is living apart from her husband through fault of her own, such authority is not implied.

A notice by a husband to third parties not to extend credit to his wife does not exempt the husband from liability for necessaries properly supplied to her, although the notice might terminate an agency implied in fact of the wife to bind her husband's credit.

Similarly, a minor child may be an agent by necessity to bind his parent for necessaries with which the parent has failed to supply him. § 7. Agency by estoppel.-A person may be estopped to deny that another is his agent, although in fact he is not. For example, P and X meet T on the street. P says to T: "X is my agent in purchasing cars for me. He may see you in that connection." Later, X purchases a car from T in the name of P. If T sued P for the price of the car, P would be estopped from denying, that is to say, prevented from denying in court, that X was his agent, whether or not he was in fact. 

The doctrine of estoppel is also encountered in other branches of the law. Briefly, estoppel is a bar raised by law preventing a person from denying in court a certain fact, in consequence of his previous statements or conduct. The

AGENCY 

elements of estoppel are generally the following: (1) A representation of a certain fact, (2) made by one party to induce action by another, (3) reasonably relied upon by the latter, (4) to his damage. 

§ 8. Agency by ratification.—A person acting for another without authority becomes an agent, upon ratification of his act by the other. The ratification relates back to the time of the act, curing the absence of original authority. 

Ratification may be made expressly; or it may be implied from language or conduct, as, for example, when a person receives the benefit of an unauthorized act, or brings a suit based upon an unauthorized act, or, knowing about an unauthorized act, remains silent beyond a reasonable length of time. Ratification need not be communicated to the third party.

Ratification of any part of an unauthorized act is ratification of the entire act, and may not be withdrawn when once made. 

§ 9. Essentials of ratification.-(1) Ratification is not binding unless it is made with full knowledge of all material facts. (2) The agent must have acted as an agent; that is, he must have disclosed to the third party that he was acting as an agent for the ratifier. (3) The ratifier must have been in existence, and competent to act, at the time of the unauthorized act. For example, a corporation may not ratify a contract made in its behalf before its incorporation, although it may be liable upon an implied contract if it accepts the benefits of an unauthorized contract. Of course, a corporation will be bound by a new contract embodying the terms of a contract made prior to its incorporation. (4) In many states the ratification must be in the form required for the original authorization. In these states an unauthorized contract under seal could not be ratified except by a sealed instrument.

CHAPTER II PRINCIPAL AND AGENT Duties of Principal 

§ 1. To compensate.-A principal is under a duty to compensate his agent in accordance with the contract of agency. 

If there is no express contract for compensation, a principal may nevertheless be bound by an implied contract if he knew the agent rendered services with the expectation of payment. 

When relatives perform services, one for the other, it is ordinarily presumed that the services are gratuitous, but this presumption may be overcome by evidence to the contrary. 

§ 2. Compensation in event of termination by agent.-A 

principal is not obliged to compensate an agent who wrongfully terminates a contract which is entire; but if the contract is divisible, the principal is obliged to compensate for such parts as the agent has performed. For example, A contracts to work for P for a year at a salary of $3,000. After working two months, A quits without justification. P is not obliged to pay A anything, and may recover from him for breach of contract. However, if the contract provided that A was to receive $250 a month, A could recover for his services during the two months he had worked, although he would be liable to a suit by P for breach of contract. 

§ 3. Compensation of real estate brokers.-A real estate broker is entitled to his fee when he brings to his client a purchaser ready, willing, and able to buy upon the terms outlined by his client. If the sale is not consummated through fault of the client, the broker is nevertheless entitled to his fee. 

However, if the client has not stated the terms upon which he will sell, but has merely asked the broker to find a purchaser, 86

PRINCIPAL AND AGENT 

87 the broker will not be entitled to his fee unless the sale is consummated. § 4. To reimburse and to indemnify.—A principal is under a duty to reimburse his agent for expenditures properly made in the course of the agency.

Also, a principal is under a duty to indemnify his agent against losses and liabilities incurred in good faith in the course of the agency.¹ For example, P instructs A to drive a certain car to a garage. A, thinking the car is P's, drives the car to the garage. In fact, the car belongs to X, who recovers $200 in a suit against A for conversion of the car. A has a right to be indemnified by P against this loss. § 5. To compensate for personal injuries. Under certain circumstances, an employer is under a duty to compensate his employee for personal injuries sustained in the course of employment. This duty is governed in many states by two statutes, the details of which vary among the states. 

Briefly, these statutes are as follows: 

(1) Employers' Liability Acts. These Acts generally give most employees, injured in the course of their employment, the same right to recover from their employers that persons not employees would have. That is, if an employee, while exercising due care, is injured as a result of the negligence of the employer or his agents, the employee can generally recover. 

Prior to these Acts, an employer might have prevented recovery by the employee, by showing that the injuries were caused by the negligence of a coemployee (known as the fellow-servant rule) or that risk of the injuries had been assumed by the employee when he undertook employment. 

(2) Workmen's Compensation Acts. These Acts gener ally make provision for employers' insuring their employees against injúries, the insurance company to pay the injured employee stipulated sums, irrespective of whether the employer is negligent or the employee contributorily negligent. 

This compensation is received by the employee in lieu of any sum he might recover in a suit against his employer. Gener- 

¹ Moore v. Appleton, p. 326. ·

AGENCY 

ally, it is not compulsory that employers carry workmen's compensation insurance, nor that employees accept it in lieu of reserving their rights to sue their employers, but an employer who does not carry it, or an employee who does not accept its benefits, is penalized in suits brought by employees. 

Duties of Agent 

§ 6. To obey instructions. An agent is under a duty to obey instructions within the scope of his employment. His failure to follow instructions not only constitutes a breach of contract, but also renders him liable for any loss resulting therefrom. The latter rule applies also in the case of gratuitous agents. Although they are not obliged to perform, because of lack of consideration, if they do perform, they are liable for any loss resulting from failure to follow instructions. 

Of course, an agent may disobey an instruction to perform an illegal or immoral act. And in the event of an emergency, an agent may depart from instructions. § 7. To use ordinary care.—An agent is under a duty to use at least ordinary care in the performance of his duties: that is, the care of an ordinary person in his position. The failure to use such care is negligence. An agent is liable to his principal for any loss caused the principal by the former's negligence in performing his duties. For example, if A, a taxi driver for P, negligently runs into T, and if T recovers from P damages in the amount of $200, A is liable to P for this loss. § 8. To be subordinate.-An agent has a duty to be subordinate. Disrespectful words or conduct of an agent, amounting to insubordination, justifies a principal to terminate the agency relationship. § 9. To be loyal.-—An agent has a duty to be loyal and to exercise utmost good faith in performing his contract of agency.

An agent may not sell his own property to the principal, nor buy for himself property of the principal, without the full knowledge and consent of the principal. 

An agent may not represent parties with conflicting interests unless his double employment is known and assented to

PRINCIPAL AND AGENT 

89 by both parties;2 nor may he represent any interest conflicting with that of his principal, without the principal's assent. It is immaterial whether the principal is in fact harmed by his agent's serving conflicting interests. The wrong lies in the agent's creating an opportunity for taking advantage of the principal, which opportunity, presumptively, the agent will act upon for his own mercenary interest. 

An agent may not make a personal profit from his agency other than the compensation paid him by his principal. If he does, the principal may require him to account for the profit. 

Also, an agent may not use secret processes or other confidential information, acquired in the course of his employment, in competition with his principal, either before or after termination of the employment. An injunction may be secured in a court of equity against an agent violating this duty. 

An agent who fails to disclose to his principal material facts discovered by him in the course of his agency violates his duty of loyalty. § 10. To perform personally.-Generally, an agent must perform his duties personally. He may not delegate them to others. For example, a person employed to conduct a symphony orchestra may not delegate his work to another. 

The reason is that an agent is selected by the principal because of the confidence and trust reposed in him and because of his personal qualifications, and the principal would not receive that for which he had contracted if the agent were allowed to employ a substitute.

Nevertheless, an agent may delegate to another ministerial and mechanical duties: that is, duties not involving discretion.

Thus, if an agent were employed to prepare a promissory note, he could have another, to whom he would dictate its contents, write it.

Also, an agent may delegate his duties when he is expressly authorized by his principal to do so; or impliedly authorized, 2 Quinn v. Burton, p. 327.

AGENCY 

as, for example, when it is customary, or when it is necessary from the nature of the agency. The following is an illustration of the last situation: H, the holder of a note, deposits this note with the X Bank for collection in another state. The 

X Bank may, of course, send the note for collection to Y Bank, located in the same state that the drawee is located. 

§ 11. Liability of agent appointing subagent.-When the agent is authorized to appoint a subagent, he incurs no liability to the principal for the subagent's performance unless the agent has been negligent in selecting the subagent; but when the agent, without authority and for his own account, selects a subagent to assist him, the subagent is the agent's agent, and the agent is responsible to the principal for the subagent's performance.

Also, when the agent is authorized to appoint a subagent, the relationship between the principal and subagent is that of principal and agent, accompanied by the usual rights and liabilities; that is, the subagent is entitled to be compensated by the principal and is responsible to the principal for his performance; the principal is liable to third parties upon contracts and torts of the subagent within the scope of the latter's authority.

Termination of Agency § 12. By terms of original agreement.-An agency termi nates upon expiration of the period stated in the contract of agency, or upon accomplishment of the object for which the agency was created.

If the parties continue the agency relationship, without a new agreement, beyond the period specified, a contract for a further period of the same duration, embodying the terms of the original contract, will be implied by the courts. § 13. By act of the parties. The parties may terminate an agency contract, as any other contract, by mutual agreement. 

Also, either party generally has the power to terminate the relationship at any time, but if he terminates it without right —that is, in violation of the contract of agency—he is liable in damages to the other party for the breach. Of course, a

PRINCIPAL AND AGENT 

91 material breach by one party, such as insubordination or failure of the agent to obey instructions, justifies termination by the other party.

When an agency is created for an indefinite period, either party has the right to terminate it upon reasonable notice. In the case of contracts of employment, reasonable notice is generally considered to be notice for a period equal to the period for which compensation is paid. Thus, an employee working for no particular period and receiving his pay weekly, would be entitled to a week's notice of termination by the employer; similarly, his employer would be entitled to receive a week's notice of termination by the employee. § 14. Agency coupled with an interest.—A principal has not the power to terminate an agency coupled with an interest. 

An agency is coupled with an interest when the agent has some interest or estate in the subject matter of the agency, not merely in the agency itself. For example, P owes A $100. 

P delivers his car to A, instructing A to sell it and to apply the proceeds against the debt. P cannot terminate this agency because of A's interest in the subject matter. 

A mere statement by the principal that his appointment is irrevocable does not prevent his revoking the agency, although he may have to answer in damages if he does revoke. § 15. By operation of law.-Death, insanity, or bankruptcy of either party terminates the agency, except one coupled with an interest, by operation of law. Bankruptcy has this effect only when it operates upon the subject matter of the agency.
