CHAPTER III PRINCIPAL, AGENT, AND THIRD PARTY Contracts § 1. Liability of principal upon contracts.-A principal is liable to a third party upon contracts entered into by the agent within the scope of his authority. 

The question of what acts of the agent are within the scope of his authority is frequently most difficult to answer. Third parties are generally bound at their peril to ascertain not only the fact of agency but also the extent of authority.¹ The authority of an agent may consist of one or more of the following kinds: express, implied, and apparent. 

No particular difficulty is encountered in determining whether an agent has express authority. It is simply a question of fact whether or not the principal has by his language or conduct authorized his agent to perform a certain act. 

Whether or not an agent has implied or apparent authority depends upon many factors, which will be considered separately. 

§ 2. Implied authority.—An agent has implied authority to do what is customary or what is reasonably convenient and necessary in order to carry out his express authority. Thus, an agent expressly authorized to sell flour would have implied authority to warrant that the flour is sweet and sound if it is customary for agents to give such warranties. Also, an agent expressly authorized merely to sell an automobile would have implied authority to determine such incidental matters as to whom to sell it and the price to be charged. 

1 Law v. Stokes, p. 329.

Also, an emergency may confer implied authority upon an agent to perform an act. Thus, in case of a train wreck, 93

AGENCY 

the conductor might have implied authority to summon a doctor, for whose services the railroad would be liable. 

Manifestly, the implied powers of a general agent, one authorized to transact all of his principal's business of a particular kind, would be wider than those of a special agent, one authorized to transact only a particular piece of business. 

§ 3. Implied authority in particular cases.-Ordinarily, an agent does not have implied authority to bind his principal, by making or indorsing negotiable paper; nor to borrow money in the name of his principal; nor to extend credit in sales; nor to purchase on credit.

An agent does not have implied authority to sell property of his principal merely because it is in his possession, unless he is a factor (selling agent in possession of goods); nor, if authorized to sell, to receive payment unless he is in possession of the goods or unless it is customary for the agent to collect the price of the goods he sells. Thus, ordinarily, a traveling salesman would not have implied authority to collect the price of goods he sells. § 4. Apparent authority. An agent has apparent authority to bind his principal when (1) a principal so represents to the damage of a third party reasonably relying thereon (estoppel) or (2) when an incidental power of an agent is restricted by the principal without the knowledge of the third party. The first situation, estoppel, has been treated in 

Chapter I on Creation of Agency. 

The following is an example of the second situation: A is a salesman for the P Cigar Company. He is assigned to a particular territory, but is instructed not to accept an order under any circumstances from a certain retail store in his territory. Contrary to instructions, A contracts in the name of the P Cigar Company to sell a certain quantity of cigars to this retailer, who has no knowledge that A was forbidden to sell to him. The contract is binding upon the P Cigar 

Company. Primarily, A was an agent to sell and was so held out by his principal. Determining the persons to whom sales will be made is an implied or incidental power which rests apparently with the agent, so far as the third party

PRINCIPAL, AGENT, AND THIRD PARTY 95 

knows. A restriction upon this apparent power is not binding upon the third party. The rule is sometimes stated as follows: The third party is not bound by secret limitations upon the authority of the agent. In other words, if a principal holds out his agent as having a certain general authority, a third party may assume that the agent has those powers that such an agent customarily or usually has. He is not bound to inquire whether incidental matters relating to the exercise of the authority have been restricted by the principal. 

In the above illustration, if the agent had no express authority to sell, the principal would not be bound by his contract with the retailer, even though the agent represented to the retailer that he had such power. A principal is not bound by unauthorized assertions of an agent that he has authority, when in fact he has none. 

Disclosed or Undisclosed Principals § 5. Simple contracts.—A principal is liable and may sue upon simple contracts of his authorized agent, generally speaking, whether the principal is disclosed or undisclosed. 

The reason is that the principal is the motive force, whether he is disclosed or undisclosed.

A principal is said to be undisclosed when the agent does not disclose to the third party the existence and identity of his principal. By simple contract is meant oral or written contracts other than sealed or negotiable instruments. 

For example, A says to T: "I will sell you this car for $400," or, "In behalf of P, I will sell you this car for $400.”

T replies, "I accept." In either case P is liable if A is acting with authority.

An agent of a disclosed principal is not liable and may not sue the third party upon a contract unless the agent has personally made himself a party to the contract; but the agent of an undisclosed principal is so liable and may so sue, since the third party has entered into the contract on the strength of the agent's credit. 

For example, A says to T, “In behalf of P, I will sell you this car for $400." T replies, "I accept your offer." Here,

AGENCY 

A is not liable since he has disclosed his principal, nor may he sue the third party if the latter fails to perform; but if A had said to T: "In behalf of P, I will sell you this car for $400. 

You can treat me as the party liable, and you can make payment to me personally," A would be liable and might sue, although he has disclosed his principal, because he has made himself a party to the contract. Also, if A says to T, “I will sell you this car for $400," A is liable to and may sue T, since he has not disclosed his principal and T is entering into the contract on the strength of A's credit. § 6. Exceptions to liabilities and rights of undisclosed principal. An undisclosed principal is not liable and may not sue upon a contract of his agent to render personal services. 

The reason is that the third party has entered into the contract because of his confidence in the agent, and has a right not to have some other person, the undisclosed principal, thrust into the place of the agent. For example, if A, authorized agent for P, says to T, "I will decorate your new house for $200," and T replies, "I accept," P is not liable and may not sue upon this contract. 

An undisclosed principal, paying his agent for the benefit of the third party in good faith and before disclosure, is not liable to the third party; and, similarly, a third party, paying the agent of an undisclosed principal before disclosure, is not liable to the principal.

In a suit by an undisclosed principal, the third party may set off any claim he may have established in a suit brought by the agent. For example, A owes T $100. A, acting for 

P, says to T, "I will sell you this boat for $200." T replies, "I accept." If P sues T for breach of contract, T may set off against the claim of P his claim of $100 against A. § 7. Sealed and negotiable instruments. A principal is not liable and may not sue upon a sealed or negotiable instrument executed by his agent unless the former's name appears thereon as a party to the instrument. An agent is liable and may sue upon a sealed or negotiable instrument on which his name appears as a party. Thus, the sealed or negotiable instrument executed by an agent must be distinguished from his simple contract.

PRINCIPAL, AGENT, AND THIRD PARTY 97 

A 

For example, a negotiable instrument is signed “A.” is liable upon this instrument because his name appears as a party upon it; but P would not be liable because his name does not appear on it. A signature "P by A" or "A for P" binds

P, but not A, since A indicates that he is signing merely in a representative capacity and not as a party. However, A is bound if his name is followed by mere words of description, such as "A, agent," without disclosure of the name of the principal. The party upon this instrument is A alone. 

The reason that the only person bound on a sealed or negotiable instrument is the one who appears upon the face thereof to be a party is that the parol evidence rule forbids introduction of oral testimony to alter the clear terms of the instrument. Thus, if A alone signs such instrument, oral evidence is not admissible to show that A was acting for P, and that P is the real party in interest. However, the parol evidence rule is not invoked in the case of simple written contracts, and parol evidence may therefore be introduced in these cases to show that A was acting for P. § 8. Election by third party.-A third party having a right of action against either the principal or the agent must elect (choose) which one he will hold. For example, suppose both P and A are liable to T as a result of A's not disclosing his principal at the time of the dealings. T may not hold both P and 

A; he must elect which one he will hold. 

A third party is held to have made an election when he recovers judgment against either the principal or the agent, although in some states less than this procedure will constitute an election. It is sometimes said that while a third party may have two modes of recovery, he has but one right of action, and when he recovers judgment, his right of action has merged in the judgment, thus exhausting his remedy. 

Of course, a third party is not held to have made an election if he recovers judgment against the agent, without knowledge of the identity of the principal. For example, A says to T, "I will sell you this radio for $50." T says, "All right." A fails to perform, and T recovers judgment against 

A, not knowing that A was acting as agent. Despite the

AGENCY 

unsatisfied judgment against A, T may sue P, upon learning the latter's identity.

Torts 

§ 9. Liability for agent's torts.-A principal is liable for the torts committed by his agent while the latter is acting within the scope of his employment. For example, A, agent for P, while driving P's laundry truck, negligently runs into and injures T. T may recover from P damages for his injuries. One reason for this rule is the concept that the principal and the agent are one person; it is the principal, through his agent, who commits the wrong. Also, a principal will be more careful in selecting his agents if he is subjected to liability for their wrongs. 

A test for determining whether a wrong of an agent is within the scope of his employment is whether the agent is acting, partly at least, to achieve his principal's purpose when he commits the wrong.2 If he is, it is immaterial that the wrong is committed willfully, or in violation of the principal's instructions, or partly for the benefit of the agent. For example, if a taxicab driver, an agent, willfully runs into the car of a competitor in order to reach a passenger before his competitor, the principal will be liable; it would make no difference that the principal had expressly instructed his agent never to damage the property of competitors, or that the agent's reason for running into the other cab was in part animosity towards the other driver.

However, a principal is not liable for the torts of his agent, committed in an independent enterprise of the agent's, popularly referred to as a "frolic of his own." For example, if 

A, chauffeur for P, drives to town to see a friend, and on the way negligently runs into T, P is not liable. 

An agent is always liable to a third party for his torts, irrespective of whether his principal is also liable. If both are liable, their liability is generally several; that is, they must be sued separately. 

2 Garretzen v. Duenckel, p. 332.

PRINCIPAL, AGENT, AND THIRD PARTY 

99 § 10. Knowledge of and notice to agent binds principal.- 

A principal is bound by the knowledge of or any notice to his agent in respect to a transaction in which the agent is acting for his principal. This rule has been expressed by the statement that the principal is bound if the agent is "an agent to know," for the reason that the principal and the agent are regarded as one person.

However, if the agent is acting fraudulently, or is under a duty to someone else not to disclose his knowledge, the principal is not bound by the knowledge of or notice to his agent. 

§ 11. Notice of revocation of agency. A principal revok ing an agency is liable to a third party relying upon continuation of the agency if the principal does not give the third party notice of the revocation. Actual notice must be given to those who have extended credit prior to the revocation; and general public notice, such as a newspaper advertisement, must be given to all others. § 12. Implied warranties of authority and of existing, competent principal.—An agent is held impliedly to warrant to a third party that he is acting with authority and for an existing and competent principal. If it develops that in fact any one of these warranties is not true, the agent is liable in damages to the third party for breach of warranty. For example, A says to T, "In behalf of P, I will sell you this furniture for $100." T says, "All right." If in fact P had not given A authority to sell his furniture, or if there were no such person as P, or if P were a minor and avoided the contract, T might sue A for breach of warranty. 

However, if the third party knows or is in as good a position as the agent to know that the warranty is not true, he may not recover for breach of warranty.

SALES

SALES CHAPTER I  § 1. Uniform Sales Act.-The Uniform Sales Act¹ is a code embodying principles relating to sales of personal property. 

It was prepared by a commission for the purpose of codifying in one act the sound, leading principles relating to sales in the various states and of rendering the law of sales uniform in the various states by adoption of the Act by state legislatures. 

The Act has been adopted, sometimes with minor changes, in a large number of the states. 

In those states where the Act has been enacted as a statute, the provisions of the Act naturally repeal any prior cases or statutes which are in conflict. However, the decisions rendered by the courts, prior and subsequent to the adoption of the Act, are useful and essential in construing provisions of the Act, and in establishing the law upon points on which the 

Act is silent.

This treatment of the law of sales is based upon the Act when it is applicable. This does not mean that the law herein set forth is necessarily in conflict with the laws of states which have not adopted the Act, since the Act is merely a codification of general principles of the law of sales. 

Since a sale is a contract, the general law of contracts will govern transactions of sales as to aspects not expressly treated in the Sales Act. Consequently, many of the principles treated in the chapters on contracts are applicable also in these chapters on sales. 

1 Text of Uniform Sales Act, p. 401. 

103

SALES Formation of the Contract 

§ 2. Definitions.-A sale is an agreement whereby the seller transfers to the buyer for a consideration, called the price, the property in goods (title). 

A contract to sell is a contract whereby the seller agrees to transfer to the buyer, at some future time, for a consideration, called the price, the property in goods. 

Thus, the distinction between a sale and a contract to sell is that in the former, property in goods passes at once; while in the latter, the seller merely agrees to transfer property sometime in the future.

A bill of sale is a written agreement under seal, by which one person transfers to another his title or interest in personal property.2 § 3. Sale distinguished from gift.-A gift is a transfer, without consideration, of the property in goods. Both a sale and a gift have the effect of vesting ownership in another. 

A promise, or a a mere intention, to make a gift is unenforceable.

The principal requisites of a valid gift are (1) present intention to make a gift and (2) delivery of the property by the donor to the donee. Constructive delivery will suffice in some cases; for example, A makes a gift of his automobile to B, delivering only the key. Also, delivery may be made by delivery of a written instrument evidencing the gift, without manual delivery of the property; for example, A makes a gift of his automobile to B, delivering only a deed in which A recites that he transfers his automobile to B. 

§ 4. Statute of Frauds.-A contract to sell or a sale, involving a sum of $500 or more, is not enforceable unless (1) the buyer accepts part of the goods, or (2) makes a part payment, or (3) unless some memorandum in writing is made and signed by the party to be charged or his agent. 

2 Form of Bill of Sale, p. 488. 

³ Amount varies in states. Table showing the amounts in the various states, p. 509.

This section of the Statute of Frauds has been treated in detail under the subject of Contracts. 

Subject Matter of Contract 

§ 5. Existing and future goods.-There may be a sale only of property which is in existence and which is owned by the seller, but a person may contract to sell property to be acquired in the future (called future goods) or even property the acquisition of which depends upon a contingency. For example, S may sell his car to B; but if the car has not been manufactured, or if it is now owned by T, from whom S merely expects to acquire it, S may enter into a contract to sell it. § 6. Sale of undivided share.-A person owning an undivided share in property may sell this share. If he does so, the purchaser of his share becomes an owner in common with the owners of the remaining shares. For example, S, T, and X have an equal interest in an automobile. S may sell his undivided one-third interest to B. § 7. Fungible goods.-A person may sell an undivided share of a specific mass of fungible goods, though the sale is of a definite number, weight, or measure of the goods, and though the weight, number, or measure of the goods in the mass is undetermined. By this type of sale the buyer becomes owner in common of such a share of the mass as the number, weight, or measure bought bears to the number, weight, or measure of the mass. For example, For example, S owns 1,000 bushels of wheat.

He sells to B 200 bushels of this wheat for $125 and B pays the price. Although B's 200 bushels have not been separated from the mass, he owns an undivided one fifth of the mass, in common with S. Of course, if the parties had intended a contract to sell instead of a sale, B would not have acquired an undivided interest in the mass. 

Fungible goods are goods, such as grain, coal, wine, and the like, any unit of which from its nature or usage is treated as the equivalent of any other unit. 

4 O'Keefe v. Leistikow, p. 335.

SALES 

§ 8. Destruction of goods sold. A purported sale of specific goods which have wholly perished at the time of the sale without the knowledge of the seller is void. If the goods have perished in part only, or have merely deteriorated in quality, the buyer may at his option: (1) avoid the sale; (2) if the contract is indivisible, as in the sale of a car, pay the full price; (3) if the contract is divisible, as in the sale of 

500 bushels of wheat at 65 cents a bushel, pay for such part as is not destroyed.

A contract to sell specific goods which wholly perish, without the fault of the parties, after the time of the contract but before the transfer of the risk to the buyer, is thereby avoided. In the event that the goods perish in part only, or merely deteriorate in value, the buyer has the options stated in the preceding paragraph.

Warranties § 9. Express warranty.-An express warranty is any affirmation of fact or any promise by the seller relating to the goods, the natural tendency of which is to induce the buyer to purchase, and which is relied upon by the buyer. For example, S says to B: "This stone is a genuine diamond. 

I will sell it to you for $100." B says, "I accept." The statement that the stone is a diamond is an express warranty. 

If B discovers later that the stone is of paste, he may sue S for breach of warranty.

However, statements as to the value of the goods or statements of opinion only are not construed as warranties. 

Examples of such statements are the following: "This car is worth $1,000, but I will sell it to you for $300," or "In my opinion, this car is in A-number-1 condition." It is recognized that sellers will "puff their wares" (this term is sometimes called sellers' talk), and a buyer may not reasonably rely upon such talk. Indeed, when a seller talks in this way, caveat emptor let the buyer beware.

Also, an affirmation of fact relating to a visible defect is not a warranty, when the buyer inspects the goods. In such a case, the buyer would not reasonably rely upon the affirmation.

§ 10. Oral warranties in written contracts. Generally, when the contract of sale is in writing, testimony as to oral warranties may not be introduced at a trial. It will be recalled that the parol evidence rule, explained in Contracts, forbids the introduction of oral evidence to alter or to add to the terms of a written instrument. Consequently, when a sale is induced by oral representations and the contract is reduced to writing, the buyer should make sure that the written contract includes all representation made by the seller.

Many times the form of contract furnished the buyer by the seller contains a stipulation something like the following: "No representation, statement, or agreement not herein contained shall be binding upon the seller." If a buyer signs a contract including this provision, he will be bound by it and will have no remedy for oral warranties or fraudulent .statements inducing the sale, but not set forth in the written contract. 

§ 11. Implied warranties.-An implied warranty is a war ranty a seller does not state, but is held by law to make to a buyer under certain circumstances. The various types of implied warranties are treated in the following sections. 

These warranties are not implied when the parties express a contrary intention. 

§ 12. Implied warranties of title.-A seller impliedly war rants to a buyer that (1) he has the right to sell the goods; (2) the buyer will enjoy quiet possession against lawful claims; (3) the goods are free from incumbrances not known to the buyer. 

§ 13. Implied warranty in sale by description. In a sale of goods by description, there is an implied warranty that the goods correspond with the description; and when purchased from a seller dealing in goods of that description, that the goods are of merchantable quality. For example, if B orders from S, and S sells to B, "prime quality winter oil," S impliedly warrants that the oil he delivers is prime quality winter oil; and if he is a dealer in this kind of oil, that the oil is merchantable, that is, fit for sale and free from defects. 

§ 14. Implied warranties in sale by sample.—In a sale by sample, there is an implied warranty that the goods will

SALES 

correspond with the sample; and if the seller is a dealer in goods of that kind, that the goods are merchantable. § 15. Implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose. -When the buyer, relying upon the skill or judgment of the seller, expressly or impliedly makes known to the seller the particular purpose for which the goods are required, there is an implied warranty that the goods are fit for such purpose. 

For example, B tells S that he wants a heater adequate to heat his house and gives S a complete description of his house, relying upon S to furnish a suitable heater. If the heater supplied by S is not adequate to heat the house, B may recover from S for breach of an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.

Also, an implied warranty of quality or fitness may be annexed by usage of trade; but there is no such implied warranty in the sale of an article under its patent or trade name, although the sale may be accompanied by an express warranty.

If the buyer examines the goods, there is no implied warranty as regards defects which such examination ought to have revealed.

A dealer upon whose skill and judgment a buyer relies in purchasing food impliedly warrants that the food is wholesome, that is, fit for consumption. A restaurant is held to make this warranty to guests. Also, it is made by dealers selling canned goods. 

§ 16. No other implied warranties of quality. Except for the implied warranties enumerated in preceding sections, there is no implied warranty of quality or fitness for a particular purpose in a sale. For example, if S, not a dealer or manufacturer, sells his car to B, B cannot claim breach of an implied warranty if the car is not in condition to operate. In cases like this, the doctrine of caveat emptor applies. 

§ 17. Extent of warranties.-Ordinarily, a warranty does not extend beyond the buyer; that is, a third party injured by reason of a breach of warranty may not sue the seller. 

5 Friend v. Childs Dining Hall Co., p. 336.

The reason is that a warranty is part of a contract of sale, and since a third person is not a party to the contract, he has no rights under it. For example, S sells B a horse, stating that the horse is sound. B, in turn, sells the horse to X, who discovers that the horse is afflicted with a disease. X cannot sue 

S for breach of warranty.

However, in certain cases a manufacturer or seller may be liable in tort to a remote consumer: (1) When he is negligent in the preparation of food for human consumption. Thus, a concern manufacturing canned peas might be liable to an ultimate consumer injured by a foreign substance in the peas. (2) When he is negligent in the preparation of an article inherently dangerous to human life or health, such as poison or an explosive. Thus, in one case, in which S sold B laudanum as tincture of rhubarb and B administered it to X, it was held that X could recover from S. (3) When the seller knows about the defect. 

By the weight of authority, a seller is not liable to an ultimate consumer in the sale of an article which is not inherently dangerous but becomes so by reason of negligence in its manufacture, as in the case of an automobile manufactured with a defective spoke. 

§ 18. Remedies for breach of warranty.-A buyer may: 

(1) Keep the goods and set up against the seller the breach of warranty in diminution of the price; this procedure is called recoupment. (2) Keep the goods and sue the seller for damages for breach of warranty. The measure of damages is the difference between the actual value of the article sold and its value as warranted, and any other damage resulting directly and naturally from the breach. (3) Refuse to accept the goods and sue for damages for breach of warranty. (4) Rescind the sale. In the event of rescission, the buyer must notify the seller, within a reasonable time, of his election to rescind and must return the goods in substantially as good a condition as he obtained them.

CHAPTER II  

§ 1. Importance of determining who has title. The question of who has title is important for the following reasons: (1) The person holding title ordinarily bears the risk of This is the general rule; but parties may by agreement shift the risk of loss to a party not holding title. loss. (2) If a debtor has title to property, a creditor of his may attach or levy execution upon the property. (3) Only the person holding title to goods may convey the title to another. 

Transfer as Between Seller and Buyer 

§ 2. Intention determines transfer.-Title passes to the buyer when the parties intend that it shall pass. Thus, if S and B agree that title to a car B is purchasing from S shall pass on the following Monday, title will pass on that day in accordance with their agreement. In a cash sale, the parties do not intend that title shall pass until payment of the price, even though the buyer in some manner acquires possession of the goods before paying the price. 

In ascertaining the intention of the parties, the courts consider the terms of the contract, the conduct of the parties, usages of trade, and the circumstances of the case. 

Five rules are set forth in the Sales Act for determining when title passes to the buyer, and these rules govern when the parties have not manifested a different intention. These rules are stated and discussed in the following sections. 

§ 3. Specific goods. (Rule 1.)-Title passes at once in an unconditional contract to sell specific goods in a deliverable 

1 Cook & Laurie Contracting Co. v. Bell, p. 340. 112

state. For example, S says to B, "I will sell this car to you for $400." B replies, "All right." Title passes to B at the time of the contract.

It is immaterial in any case whether the time of payment or the time of delivery, or both, is postponed. 

§ 4. Goods to be put in deliverable state. (Rule 2.)— 

When the seller is to do something to put specific goods in a deliverable state, title does not pass until the work is done.2 

Thus, if B agreed to purchase from S a suit which S was to alter, title would not pass until the alterations were completed. 

§ 5. Sales on trial. (Rule 3.)-In a sale on trial or approval, title passes to the buyer when he signifies his acceptance; but if he retains the goods beyond the period agreed upon or beyond a reasonable time, without giving notice of rejection, title passes to him upon the expiration of such time.

In a "sale and return," title passes to the buyer at once, but he may revest title in the seller by returning the goods within the period agreed upon, or, if no period is agreed upon, within a reasonable time. 

§ 6. Unascertained goods. (Rule 4.)—In a contract.to sell unascertained goods, title passes when goods of the description ordered are unconditionally appropriated to the contract by one party with the assent, express or implied, of the other. For example, B places with S an order for a new Buick car at a certain price. Later S notifies B that the car has reached S's shop and B says that he will call for his car in a few days. This statement would amount to implied assent by B to the appropriation by S, and title would pass at that time.

When the seller delivers goods to the buyer, or to a carrier for transmission to the buyer, the seller is generally presumed unconditionally to have appropriated the goods to the contract, except as provided to the contrary in Rule 5. 

Thus, ordinarily, title will pass to the buyer upon delivery of the goods to the carrier. The mere fact that the goods are 

2 Joyce et al. v. Adams et al., p. 340.

SALES 

sent C.O.D. (cash on delivery) will not prevent title from passing upon delivery to the carrier. A C.O.D. shipment does not affect the passing of title. § 7. Delivery to buyer or carrier. (Rule 5.)-If the seller is required by the contract to deliver the goods to the buyer or at a particular place, or if he is to pay the cost of transportation to the buyer, title does not pass until this has been done. 

For example, a contract provides, "The seller is to deliver the said goods to the buyer at his store in New York," or "The seller is to pay all freight charges upon said goods." In either case, title will not pass until the goods are delivered to the buyer. Again, if the seller agrees to deliver the goods "F.O.B. Detroit" (meaning that the seller is to deliver the goods free on board in Detroit, without expense to the buyer for packing, transportation, and so forth), title does not pass until delivery in Detroit.

A C.I.F. contract would come within Rule 4 rather than within Rule 5, and title would pass when the goods were delivered to the carrier. A C.I.F. contract is one the price of which includes cost, insurance, and freight to the destination. In reality, the buyer is paying insurance and freight, but the three items are lumped so as to enable the parties to make a complete settlement at the shipping point. 

Thus, it appears from Rules 4 and 5 that if the buyer is to pay freight, title passes when the goods are delivered to the carrier; if the seller is to pay freight, title passes when the goods are delivered by the carrier to the buyer. The reason for this rule is that the carrier is acting as the agent for the person whose duty it is to pay him. If the buyer is paying freight, he receives delivery of the goods when they are delivered to him through his agent, the carrier. 

§ 8. Bills of lading and warehouse receipts.-Bills of lading and warehouse receipts are documents issued by carriers and warehousemen, reciting the receipt of goods for carriage or storage and the terms and conditions thereof. They may be non-negotiable, in which case they are called straight bills and receipts; or they may be negotiable, in which case they are called order bills and receipts. For example, if a bill of

lading recites that the carrier is to deliver the goods to the buyer, it is called a straight bill of lading; but if it provides that the carrier is to deliver to the order of the buyer, it is an order bill and is negotiable.

These instruments are called documents of title. They are the emblems or evidences of title to goods in the possession of a carrier or warehouseman. Consequently, the person to whom delivery is to be made under the terms of the instrument or his indorsee, if the instrument is negotiable-is regarded as the owner of the goods. 

However, when a seller reserves title for security by the form of the bill of lading and, but for the form, title would have passed to the buyer, the risk of loss rests with the buyer. The reason is that the buyer is the real, beneficial owner of the goods. This is an exception to the general rule that risk of loss follows title.

A seller may reserve title for security by the form of a bill of lading: (1) by designating himself or an agent as consignee; (2) by retaining a bill of lading in which the buyer is consignee; (3) by sending to the buyer a draft attached to a bill of lading in which the buyer is consignee. 

An example of the rule stated in the preceding paragraphs follows: B, in New York, contracts with S, in Detroit, to purchase certain merchandise to be sent to B F.O.B. Detroit. 

In order that B may not obtain the merchandise without paying for it, S designates himself as consignee in the bill of lading. If the goods are destroyed in transit, B bears the loss because S is retaining title only for security; B is the real, beneficial owner; but for the form of the bill of lading, title would have passed to B, since he is paying cost of transportation.

Conditional Sales 

§ 9. Definition.-A conditional sale is one in which title does not pass to the buyer until the occurrence of a specified condition, usually payment of the price. The object of such 3 

3 Form of Conditional Sale Agreement, p. 489,

SALES 

sale is to secure to the seller his price, by preventing the buyer from becoming complete owner of the goods sold until he has paid for them. Without some such security, the buyer could do as he wished with the goods and the seller would have no remedy except that of suing for the price. § 10. Distinguished from other transactions.-A so-called installment sale is not a conditional sale unless the parties agree that title is not to pass until payment of the last installment.

A lease of goods under which the lessee is to pay installments of rent, with the option of purchasing the goods by paying a slight amount in addition to the installments, is generally regarded as a conditional sale; but if the rental is a reasonable price for the use of the goods, the lease will not be so regarded.

A chattel mortgage is a transfer, by the owner of goods, of title to them; the mortgage is absolute in form, but subject to the condition that if the amount and the interest are paid and other terms performed, the transfer is void. Sometimes sellers employ this device to secure payment of the price of goods, selling them outright to the buyer, the buyer simultaneously executing a chattel mortgage to the seller, to secure a balance of the price. In most states, chattel mortgages are not valid as to third parties unless the mortgages are recorded; that is, in the absence of a record, a mortgagor in possession of the goods can sell them, free of the mortgage, to another. 

When a mortgagor defaults upon his mortgage, the mortgagee may foreclose as provided either in the mortgage or by statute. § 11. Recording of conditional sales. In some states, all conditional sales must be recorded or they will not be valid as against innocent third parties—that is, those without notice of the conditional sale; in other states, only certain types of conditional sale need be recorded; while in still others, there is no requirement as to recording. 

In cases in which recording is not required, a conditional buyer may not convey title to another, since he has none; but if he is a factor, that is, an agent intrusted with possession 

4 Forms of Chattel Mortgage and Chattel Mortgage Note, p. 491, 493.

of the goods, with authority to sell them, he is permitted by Factors' Acts to make a valid sale to a purchaser in good faith. 

In the latter case, it may be said that the seller, having clothed the buyer with apparent power to sell, is estopped to deny that the latter did not have such power. 

In cases in which recording is required, and the seller fails to record a sale, the conditional buyer may sell the property to a purchaser in good faith. Since the seller has failed, by not recording the sale, to give others notice of his title, and has intrusted the buyer with possession, the seller is prevented from asserting his title as against innocent third parties. § 12. Rights of conditional seller.-Upon a default by the buyer, the seller in a conditional sale may elect to pursue either of the following remedies: (1) Sue for the price. In this event, title to the goods vests in the buyer if the seller recovers judgment for the price. (2) Reclaim the goods; this procedure is called repossession, rescission of the contract, or foreclosure. The seller may retake the goods himself; but if he does not do so peaceably, he may render himself liable for such crimes and torts as assault and battery and breach of the peace. It is therefore safer for him to recover possession by an action of replevin.

Repossession cuts off all rights of the buyer, and the seller is permitted to retain all payments made by the buyer, in the absence of an agreement or a statute providing to the contrary. 

Many states have statutes regulating the foreclosure and the rights of parties thereunder. Some of these statutes, in event of repossession, provide for notice of a period during which the buyer may redeem; and for resale of the goods by the seller if the buyer has paid more than a certain percentage of the price, with payment to the buyer of any surplus realized.

Also, the rights of the parties are governed by the contract into which they enter. Unfortunately, many conditional sellers induce buyers to sign very harsh and oppressive agreements. § 13. Rights of conditional buyer.—A conditional buyer is entitled to the possession and beneficial use of the property so

SALES 

long as he is not in default. Since he is the beneficial owner, the seller retaining title for security only, he must bear the risk of loss. This is another exception to the general rule that risk of loss follows title. 

A buyer may assign to another whatever interest he has under a conditional sale, unless he is prohibited from doing so by the contract. Of course, he remains liable upon the contract even though he transfers his rights under it. 

Other Transfers of Title 

§ 14. General rule in sales by person not the owner.-The general rule is that a person selling goods which he does not own, or selling them without authority, can convey no title to a third person, however innocent, unless the owner is precluded by his conduct from denying the seller's authority. 

Thus, a thief cannot convey good title to a purchaser for value without notice. This rule is subject to the exceptions considered in the following sections. 

§ 15. By one having voidable title.-A purchaser for value without notice from one having voidable title acquires good title. For example, S, by fraudulent representations, induces B to sell S his automobile. Then S, before B rescinds the sale, sells the car for a fair price to X, who has no notice of the defect in S's title. X acquires good title. § 16. By seller continuing in possession of property sold.- 

A purchaser for value without notice from a seller continuing in possession of property sold acquires good title. Since the buyer has made it possible for the seller to deceive the third party, he is deemed in law expressly to have authorized the sale. This rule is another application of the principle of estoppel.

In many states, retention of possession by a seller is primafacie evidence of fraud. Thus, if S sells his automobile to B, but continues in possession of it, creditors of S may be able to attach and levy upon the automobile, notwithstanding the sale to B. § 17. By factors.-A purchaser for value without notice from a factor or other agent entrusted with possession of

goods or bills of lading acquires good title. Factors' Acts in the various states provide that the factor shall be deemed the true owner, in order that such sales may be valid. This doctrine is based upon estoppel. § 18. Sales of goods in bulk.-In some states, a dealer may not make a bulk sale of his stock in trade unless he complies with a statute requiring him, among other things, to give notice of the sale to creditors. § 19. Fraudulent conveyances.-A creditor may have set aside a conveyance of property made by a debtor with the intent of defrauding creditors. The remedy ordinarily pursued by a creditor is that of filing a bill in equity to reach and apply the property so conveyed. If the equity court adjudges the conveyance fraudulent, it will decree that the property be applied in satisfaction of the claim of the creditor, notwithstanding the conveyance. Another remedy of the creditor is to attach the property or seize it upon execution, as though no conveyance had been made. Of course, the creditor pursuing this remedy would have to be able to prove the conveyance was fraudulent, or he would be liable in damages to the grantee of the debtor for conversion. 

The question of whether a debtor has conveyed his property with the intent of defrauding creditors is one of fact, to be determined from all the circumstances surrounding the transaction. Circumstances commonly constituting evidence of fraud are: inadequacy of consideration; transfers in anticipation of or pending a suit; secrecy or haste; concealment of or failure to record a conveyance; insolvency and deep indebtedness of the debtor; retention of possession by the debtor; relationship of the parties; transfer to a person having no apparent use for the property. 

If a debtor conveys his property without consideration, the conveyance will ordinarily be considered fraudulent insofar as it affects creditors whose claims existed at the time of the conveyance. But a conveyance supported by consideration of the love and affection of the debtor for his child or his wife is not ordinarily fraudulent. However, if the debtor at the 

5 Peter Bent Brigham Hospital v. McClure and Another, p. 342.

SALES 

time of such conveyance is insolvent and deeply indebted, these circumstances constitute strong presumptive evidence of fraud.

CHAPTER III PERFORMANCE AND REMEDIES § 1. Law of contracts governs.-The rights and liabilities of the parties with respect to performance is governed largely by the general law of contracts. Only a few general points will be considered in connection with performance of contracts of sale. § 2. Delivery and payment as concurrent conditions. 

Unless otherwise agreed, delivery of the goods and payment of the price are concurrent conditions; that is to say, the seller must be ready and willing to give possession in exchange for the price, and the buyer must be ready and willing to pay the price in exchange for possession.. § 3. Right of buyer to examine goods. The buyer is not deemed to have accepted the goods unless and until he has a reasonable opportunity to examine them for the purpose of ascertaining whether they are in conformity with the contract. 

If goods are sent C.O.D., the buyer does not have the right to examine them before payment of the price unless there is an agreement that he may do so. § 4. Acceptance not a bar to an action for damages.—A buyer may sue for breach of contract or warranty, notwithstanding his acceptance, provided that he gives the seller notice of the breach within a reasonable time after he knows or ought to know of the breach. § 5. Buyer not bound to return goods wrongly delivered. -A buyer is not bound to accept goods wrongly delivered. 

If he refuses to accept them, having the right so to do, he is not bound to return them to the seller, but it is sufficient if he notifies the seller that he refuses to accept them. § 6. Buyer refusing to accept delivery.-A buyer refusing, without right, to accept delivery is liable to the seller for any 122

PERFORMANCE AND REMEDIES 

123 loss occasioned by such refusal, and also for a reasonable charge for the care and custody of the goods by the seller. 

Remedies of Seller 

§ 7. Unpaid seller's lien.-An unpaid seller in possession of the goods has a lien upon them—the right to retain them for the price even though title may have passed, (1) if credit was not agreed upon, or (2) if the term of credit has expired, or (3) if the buyer becomes insolvent. 

However, such unpaid seller loses his lien if he parts with his possession. § 8. Stoppage in transitu.—An unpaid seller may stop the goods in transit, that is, while they are in the possession of the transportation agency, if the buyer is insolvent. This right may be exercised by the seller's giving notice of his claim to the transportation agency. The goods are no longer considered in transit when they have been delivered by the carrier to the buyer or are held by the carrier as agent for the buyer. § 9. Resale by unpaid seller.-An unpaid seller having a lien upon the goods may resell them if the buyer has been in default an unreasonable time in payment of the price. He need not give the buyer notice of his intention to resell, nor is he liable to the buyer for any profit he makes on the resale. 

If he sustains a loss, he may recover damages for the loss from the buyer. § 10. Rescission by unpaid seller.-An unpaid seller having a lien upon the goods may rescind the transfer of title if the buyer has been in default an unreasonable time in payment of the price, and may also recover damages for breach of contract.

In order to rescind, the seller must give notice to the buyer or manifest his intention by some other overt act. § 11. Action by seller for price.-The seller may maintain an action against the buyer for the price if, title having passed, the buyer neglects or refuses to pay the price according to the terms of the contract, or if goods the buyer refuses to accept cannot be readily resold for a reasonable price.

SALES § 12. Action for damages for non-acceptance of goods.- 

The seller may maintain an action for damages for nonacceptance of goods if the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to accept them. Ordinarily, the measure of damages is the difference between the contract price and the market value of the goods. § 13. Rescission of contract of sale. A seller may totally rescind the contract if the buyer has repudiated it, or has manifested his inability to perform his obligations thereunder, or has committed a material breach thereof. 

Remedies of the Buyer § 14. Action of replevin or for conversion. If the seller wrongfully neglects or refuses to deliver goods, title to which has passed to the buyer, the buyer may obtain the goods by an action of replevin or may maintain an action in tort for conversion of the goods. § 15. Action for breach of contract.-If the seller wrongfully neglects or refuses to deliver the goods, the buyer may maintain an action for damages for non-delivery. Ordinarily, the measure of damages is the difference between the contract price and the market price of the goods.

BAILMENTS CHAPTER I IN GENERAL 

§ 1. Definition.-A bailment is a transaction in which an owner delivers to another personal property to be returned to the owner or disposed of in accordance with some agreement. The owner is called a bailor; the person receiving the property, a bailee. The essentials of a bailment are: (1) title remains in the bailor; (2) possession passes to the bailee; (3) possession is to return to the bailor or to whomever he designates. For example, E rents a car from B. 

A proprietor of a restaurant has been held not to be a bailee of a coat hung upon a wall by a guest, since there is no delivery of possession.

A consignment is a bailment. Ordinarily, it is a transaction in which the owner of goods delivers them to a factor for the purpose of sale by the latter. 

§ 2. Distinction between bailment and sale. A trans action is a bailment and not a sale whenever the identical property or another form of it is to be returned to its owner. 

For example, if B delivers to E a barrel of apples to be crushed into cider and the cider given to B, this transaction is a bailment; but if B is to receive in exchange for his apples the cider from some other apples, the transaction is a sale. 

The importance of determining whether a transaction is a bailment or a sale is that if it is a bailment (1) the bailee may not sell the property; (2) his creditors may not attach or levy execution upon it; (3) the risk of loss would ordinarily fall upon the bailor, since he holds title. In a sale, the opposite is true in each case. 

§ 3. Types of bailments.-Bailments are generally classi fied as one of the following: (1) bailment for the benefit of the 129

BAILMENTS 

bailor, also called a gratuitous bailment; (2) bailment for the benefit of the bailee; (3) bailment for the mutual benefit of the bailor and the bailee. For example, if B asks E, as a favor, to deliver his car to a certain garage, this would be a bailment for the benefit of the bailor; if E asks B if he may borrow his car to attend a school dance, it would be a bailment for the benefit of the bailee; if E rents B's car, it would be a bailment for mutual benefit. 

§ 4. Liability of bailor to bailee injured by defects in property. In bailments for the benefit of the bailor or for mutual benefit, the bailor is liable to the bailee injured by defects in the property, about which the bailor knew or reasonably ought to have known and notice of which was not given to the bailee. For example, B rents a car to E. Assume that B knows the steering gear is defective or that he has had trouble with the gear but has not examined it. He does not notify E of the defect and as a result E drives the car into a tree. E may recover damages from B.

However, in a bailment for the benefit of the bailee, the bailor is liable to the bailee only for defects about which he knows and notice of which he has not given to the bailee. 

§ 5. Liability of bailee for loss of or damage to property.- 

Ordinarily, the bailee is not liable to the bailor for loss of or damage to the property unless the bailee has failed to exercise a proper degree of care with respect to it. The degrees of care are as follows: (1) In a bailment for the benefit of the bailor, the bailee is liable if he fails to exercise slight care; that is, only if he is grossly negligent.¹ (2) In a bailment for the benefit of the bailee, the bailee is liable if he fails to exercise great care; that is, if he is even slightly negligent. (3) In a bailment for mutual benefit, the bailee is liable if he fails to exercise ordinary care; that is, if he is guilty of ordinary negligence.

What is slight, great, or ordinary care, or gross, slight, or ordinary negligence, is a question of fact, depending upon all the circumstances of the particular case. Slight care in 

¹ Spooner v. Mattoon, p. 345.

IN GENERAL 

131 holding a book as a favor for the owner would be less care as compared with slight care in holding a pearl necklace as a favor for the owner. Ordinary care is the care an ordinary person exercises towards his own property under similar circumstances. 

§ 6. Limitation of liability by contract.-An ordinary bailee may limit his liability for loss to the bailment, subject to the following limitations: (1) The contract must not be in violation of law or of public policy. (2) It must not exempt the bailee from liability for fraud or for negligence. (3) The terms of the contract must be clear. 

§ 7. Liability of bailee for violating contract terms.—A 

bailee intentionally violating the terms of the contract is liable for any loss of or damage to the property during such time, irrespective of his degree of care. This rule is based on the theory that the bailee is guilty of conversion during the time he is using the property contrary to agreement. For example, B delivers his boat to E to be stored for the winter in E's boathouse. E transfers the boat to X's storehouse, which burns. E is liable for the loss.

Also, a bailee is liable in conversion if he delivers the property to an unauthorized person or refuses to redeliver to the bailor upon demand. The bailee is estopped to deny that the bailor has title, since possession by the bailee was acquired by virtue of the title of the bailor.

Liens 

§ 8. In general.—A lien in bailments is the right of the bailee in certain cases to hold the property as security for his charge or for some other debt of the bailor. A bailee does not have a lien upon the property unless it is conferred by common law, by statute, or by agreement of the parties. 

A bailee is guilty of conversion if he withholds property, claiming a lien without right; or if, having a lien, he claims an excessive amount. In the latter case, the bailor, to recover for conversion, must tender the correct or a reasonable amount.

BAILMENTS 

A bailee having a lien loses it if he voluntarily parts with possession of the property. § 9. Particular liens. By common law, a bailee bestowing labor or material upon the property of another has a lien upon it for an agreed or a reasonable charge; also, common carriers and warehousemen have a lien upon property intrusted to them, and innkeepers upon the baggage of their guests. 

By statute, liens are commonly given to boarding-house keepers upon the baggage of their guests and to proprietors of public garages upon automobiles stored with them. 

The lien of the bailee is enforced by the sale of the property subject to the lien. Statutes of states vary as to how long the bailee must wait before selling the property, what kind of notice he must give the bailor, and whether or not he must first obtain an order of court to sell the property. Pledges § 10. In general.-A pledge is a bailment of property as security for a debt. The lien of the pledgee does not arise until he acquires possession of the property.

Property commonly pledged as security for a debt includes certificates of stock, bonds, bank books, negotiable instruments, bills of lading, warehouse receipts, and articles accepted by pawnshops. Other articles of personal property, such as automobiles and the rolling stock of a railroad, when used as security, are more commonly the subject matter of a chattel mortgage, because, in a mortgage, possession of the property need not be delivered to the mortgagee. 

A further distinction between a pledge and a mortgage is that a pledgee merely has a lien upon the property, whereas in many states the mortgagee has title to the property, subject to its revesting in the mortgagor upon his compliance with the terms of the mortgage. 

§ 11. Rights of parties under pledge agreement.—The rights of the parties in a pledge are governed primarily by the agreement, which is usually set forth in a promissory note called a collateral note.2 The terms of a pledge agreement

133 made with such professional pledgees as banks, pawnshops, and the like, are ordinarily extremely onerous upon the pledgor. He is required in such agreements to contract away most of the rights he possesses by common law. For example, such a pledgee usually reserves the right to hold the pledged property as security for any other debt owed him by the pledgor; to repledge the property; to sell the property any time he feels himself insecure; to repay himself for all expenses incurred in connection with such sale; to sell the property at a public or private sale with or without notice and with the privilege of purchasing it himself. § 12. Rights of parties at common law. In the absence of an agreement, the pledgee is entitled to retain as additional security any natural increase in the pledged property; he may not retain the property as security for any other debt of the pledgor; he may not repledge the property without also assigning the debt secured; he may sell the property only upon a default by the pledgor; he must sell in good faith at a public sale, give notice of the sale to the pledgor, and may not purchase himself without the consent of the pledgor. 3 

Innkeepers § 13. Liability of innkeeper for property of guest.-By common law, an innkeeper is liable, irrespective of his negligence or care, for loss of or damages to the property of guests, unless such damage is caused by an act of God or by the fault of the guest. In other words, the innkeeper is an insurer of all property of the guest.

However, this absolute liability of an innkeeper is modified in various ways by statute in most of the states. For example, statutes commonly provide that when loss occurs through fire, the innkeeper is liable only if he has been negligent; that his liability for other losses is limited to a certain amount, as $500; that if he notifies guests in the manner provided by statute, he is not liable for loss of money and valuables not delivered to him for safekeeping. An innkeeper may be defined as one who keeps an inn or a public house in which lodging and entertainment are provided for travelers. 

Because of the nature of the business, an innkeeper, unlike a boarding-house keeper, must provide accommodations for all persons of good conduct who have the means of payment.

CHAPTER II COMMON CARRIERS 

§ 1. Definition.—A common carrier is one who undertakes, for the public generally, to transport goods or passengers from place to place for hire.¹ Examples of common carriers are railroad, steamboat, express, electric-car, and bus companies. 

A private carrier is one who undertakes to transport only in a particular case, not making it his vocation nor holding himself out to the public as ready to act for all who desire his services. § 2. Duty to transport.-A common carrier is under a duty to transport such goods or persons as he is accustomed to carry for all who seek his services and tender reasonable compensation for such service. However, he may limit his business to the transportation of a particular kind of property, such as small packages, furniture, and passengers; and he may reject property which is not within such limitation. 

A common carrier may not discriminate as to service or rates, between persons who are similarly situated, with respect to distance and the kind of goods offered for carriage. 

The Interstate Commerce Act, regulating commerce between the states, imposes certain restrictions upon common carriers who transport between the states and to foreign countries. In brief, this Act prohibits discrimination by common carriers as to service or rates; and provides that rates shall be reasonable, and proportionate for long and short distances, and that the schedule of rates shall be published and filed with the Interstate Commerce Commission. 

Also, in most of the states there are statutes which closely regulate intrastate transportation. 

1 Jackson Architectural Iron Works v. Hurlbut, p. 348. 

136

COMMON CARRIERS 

137 

Common Carriers of Goods § 3. Liability for safe carriage. Subject to five excep tions, a common carrier is liable as an insurer for the safe carriage and delivery of goods; that is to say, he is absolutely liable for any loss, irrespective of whether or not the loss is caused by his negligence. For example, if a thief steals a shipment from a freight car without negligence on the part of railroad employees, the railroad is liable for the loss. The exceptions to this extreme liability of common carriers are losses caused by the following: (1) An act of God, such as lightning or a tornado. Fire would not be an act of God unless it was caused by lightning. (2) The action of an alien enemy; that is, any country at war with the United States. (3) An order of public authority; for example, when a sheriff under legal process attaches or levies upon goods. (4) The inherent nature or natural propensities of the goods; for instance, when a cow dies a natural death while being transported. (5) Neglect of the shipper; for example, when a shipper has failed to pack the shipment properly. 

In many states, the relationship of common carrier terminates and that of warehouseman begins when the goods have been unloaded from the car and placed in the freight house. 

§ 4. Limitation of liability by contract.-A common carrier may, by agreement with the shipper, limit his liability for losses, except those caused by his negligence or bad faith. It is contrary to public policy to allow a common carrier to limit his. liability for negligence or bad faith. For example, a railroad and a shipper enter into a contract whereby the railroad is not to be liable for damage caused "by fire occurring from any cause whatsoever." This stipulation is invalid, since it would cover fires caused by the negligence of the railroad. But a stipulation that the 

2 Mobile & Ohio Ry. Co. v. Weiner, p. 349.

BAILMENTS 

"railroad is not to be liable for fires arising from accidental causes" would be upheld and would release the common carrier from its extreme liability. 

Also, a common carrier may by contract limit his liability to a valuation upon which he has agreed with the shipper at the time of receipt of the goods. The reason for this rule is that the rate may be based upon the valuation of the goods and it would be unjust for the carrier to incur a liability greater than that for which he had been paid. Common carriers may contract that if no valuation is given, they shall not be liable in excess of a certain amount, such as $50. Such a contract will be upheld. 

§ 5. Liability for injuries to passengers.-A common carrier is liable for injuries to passengers caused by his failure to exercise the highest degree of care consistent with the mode of transportation and its practical operation. For example, if a motorman were to start a car while a passenger was in the act of leaving it, this act might be held failure on the part of the company to exercise the highest degree of care, and the company would be liable for the injuries sustained by the passenger.

The carrier's duty of exercising the highest degree of care applies not only to the operation of vehicles, but also to the providing of safe and suitable vehicles for carriage. Thus, if a passenger suffers from exposure because the temperature in a car is 24 degrees during December, the carrier is liable; also, he would be liable for injuries to a passenger, caused by a drunkard or another offensive person whose misconduct might have been anticipated or guarded against. 

However, a passenger who rides on the platform of a vehicle when there is room inside may be prevented by his contributory negligence from recovering for his injuries.

A common carrier may refuse to carry passengers when the vehicle is crowded. He may refuse to carry, and may eject, persons, such as drunkards, notorious criminals, and persons infected with a contagious disease, who are a nuisance or a menace to the other passengers. He may also prescribe reasonable rules as to smoking, showing of tickets, and so forth.

COMMON CARRIERS 

139 

§ 6. Liability for baggage of passenger.-A common carrier is absolutely liable for loss of or damage to personal baggage of a passenger delivered to it, except in the five situations stated in Section 3. By baggage is meant such sums of money and articles of personal necessity, convenience, and comfort as travelers are accustomed to carry under the circumstances. It would not include such articles as bed linen, articles of household furniture, and large sums of money. As to property not coming within the classification of personal baggage, the carrier is liable only if loss or damage is caused by his negligence.

A carrier is not liable for any loss of or damage to baggage which a passenger retains in his possession. 

§ 7. Limitation of liability by contract.-A common carrier may not by contract limit his liability for injuries to passengers. Such a contract would be against public policy. But such an agreement will be upheld if in consideration of it the passenger is carried gratuitously; for example, when an employee is given a pass on which is a stipulation against liability for injuries; and also when passengers are allowed to ride on a part of the car other than where they are customarily carried, as the front platform of an electric car on which is posted a notice that persons riding there do so at their own risk.

A carrier may make reasonable limitations upon his liability for loss of a passenger's baggage, provided that these limitations are brought to the passenger's attention: for instance, when a carrier calls the passenger's attention to a rule that his liability for baggage is limited to $50. A mere stipulation on the ticket, if the passenger's attention is not called to it, would not be sufficient.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS CHAPTER I IN GENERAL § 1. The Negotiable Instruments Law. The Negotiable 

Instruments Law¹ is an act embodying sound and leading principles relating to negotiable instruments. It was drawn for the purpose of making the law of negotiable instruments uniform in the various states by adoption of the act by state legislatures. The act has been adopted in all states. 

This treatment of negotiable instruments is based upon the act when its provisions are applicable. However, case law is still essential for the purpose of construing provisions of the act and applying law to points upon which the act is silent. § 2. Definition.-A negotiable instrument is one under which the rights are transferred by indorsement and delivery (order paper) or by delivery alone (bearer paper), vesting the legal title in the transferee.

The term negotiable means transferable quality: the capacity to pass from one person to another. It is because of this quality that negotiable instruments are commonly used as a substitute for money. § 3. Negotiable instruments distinguished from other contracts. A negotiable instrument is a written contract, but it differs from ordinary contracts in that its language must conform to the strict requirements of the Negotiable Instruments Law; also, this Law governs the rights and liabilities of parties to the instrument and the method of delivering and transferring it.

Negotiable instruments, unlike ordinary contracts, are subjected to special rules-the Negotiable Instruments 

¹ Text of Negotiable Instruments Law, p. 429. 143

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

Law-because of the important use of such instruments in the commercial world as a substitute for money. 

To say that an instrument is non-negotiable does not mean that it is invalid. It may be a perfectly good contract, but if it is non-negotiable, it will not be governed by the Negotiable Instruments Law, nor will the holders of it have the privileges and advantages conferred by the act upon holders of negotiable instruments. For example, the holder of a negotiable instrument is presumed to have given consideration for the instrument, and he is therefore not obliged, in suing the maker, to prove that he gave consideration, but the holder of a non-negotiable instrument or other simple contract claim must prove consideration at the outset of the case. § 4. Distinction between negotiation and assignment.- 

The essential distinction between negotiation of negotiable instruments and assignment of ordinary contract claims is as follows: An assignee of an ordinary contract claim takes the claim subject to all defenses which the obligor might raise against the assignor; but the transferee of a negotiable instrument who is a holder in due course, acquires the instrument, free of certain defenses, such as payment, failure of consideration, improper delivery, and the like, which the obligor might have raised against the transferor. For example, let us suppose that an obligor upon a contract has a defense that he has paid the claim. He may raise this defense against the other contracting party, or against the assignee if the claim is assigned. However, if the contract were represented by a negotiable instrument, he could not raise the defense against the transferee of the payee if such transferee were a holder in due course.

The ability of a transferee of a negotiable instrument who is a holder in due course, to gain a position superior to that of the transferor is one of the most important characteristics of negotiable paper. It is this feature which in large part makes such paper attractive to purchasers and enables it to circulate as a substitute for money.

IN GENERAL 

145 

Types of Negotiable Instruments PROMISSORY NOTES § 5. Definition.-The Negotiable Instruments Law defines a negotiable promissory note as "an unconditional promise in writing made by one person to another, signed by the maker, engaging to pay on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time, a sum certain in money to order or to bearer." § 6. Kinds of promissory notes.-A simple promissory note² is one for which no security is given. 

A collateral note³ is one secured by a pledge of personal property; that is, the holder of the note receives and retains personal property, such as stocks and bonds, as security for the payment of the note.

A chattel mortgage note is one secured by the conveyance of some legal or equitable right in personal property to the holder of the note.

A real estate mortgage note is one secured by the conveyance of title to real estate to the holder. 

A conditional sale note is given as part of the purchase price of property sold upon a conditional sale. It usually recites that title to the property sold is to remain in the seller until payment of the note, and that the seller may repossess the goods if the buyer defaults upon the note. 

A judgment note is one containing a provision authorizing the holder or any attorney to enter an appearance in court for the maker and to agree to the entry of a judgment against him for the sum named, upon a default in payment of the note. 

§ 7. Special forms of promissory notes.-A certificate of deposit is an instrument, issued by a bank to a depositor, reciting a deposit of a sum of money, payable to order on demand or at a fixed time. Such a certificate is negotiable. 

A bond is a promissory note, under seal, issued by a corporation. It is generally negotiable in form, although in some cases the language upon the face of the instrument destroys

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

negotiability in that it imposes a condition upon the promise. 

A registered bond is one transferable only upon the books of the company, interest being paid to the registered holder. 

Coupon bonds are payable to bearer; these bonds have coupons attached, which represent the interest due from time to time, also payable to bearer.

BILLS OF EXCHANGE § 8. Definition.-A bill of exchange is an unconditional order in writing, addressed by one person to another, signed by the person giving it, requiring the person to whom it is addressed to pay on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time a sum certain in money to order or to bearer.¹

The parties to a bill of exchange are the drawer, the drawee, and the payee. If the drawee accepts the bill, he is known as an acceptor.

Thus, a promissory note is a promise by one person to pay another, whereas a bill of exchange is an order by one person to another to pay a third person, the payee. However, if a bill of exchange is accepted by the drawee, his position is analogous to that of the maker of a promissory note.

A drawee accepts a bill of exchange by writing across the face of the bill as follows: "Accepted, New York, June 1, 

1933. John Doe." A check which has been accepted by the drawee bank is called a certified check. 5 

§ 9. Special forms of bills of exchange.—A check is a bill of exchange drawn upon a bank, payable on demand. A cashier's check is one issued by a bank and signed by its cashier.

A bank draft is a bill of exchange drawn by one bank upon another, payable upon demand. The term draft is a common name for a bill of exchange.

A sight draft is a bill of exchange payable at sight: that is, on presentment to the drawee. A time draft is a draft payable at a designated future time, as thirty days after sight. 

4 Form of Bill of Exchange, p. 496. 

5 Form of Check, p. 496.

IN GENERAL 

147 A foreign bill of exchange is a bill drawn in one state and payable in another. An inland bill is one drawn and payable in the same state.

A trade acceptance is a time bill of exchange, drawn by the seller of merchandise on the buyer for the purchase price of goods, specifying the time and place of payment, and accepted by the buyer. The object of the trade acceptance is to allow the buyer a certain period in which to pay the price, and at the same time to give the seller an instrument of credit. The seller usually either discounts a trade acceptance at a bank or uses it to secure a loan. It is very common for buyers to pay for goods by means of trade acceptances. 

A banker's acceptance is a bill of exchange accepted by a bank. Banks commonly accept bills of exchange in behalf of clients who are purchasers of goods, receiving as security for the liabilities that they incur bills of lading, warehouse receipts, bank deposits, and the like. Naturally, a bill accepted by a bank is more attractive to sellers of goods than one accepted by the buyer, since, in the former case, there is more likelihood of payment of the bill. 

§ 10. Instruments not governed by Negotiable Instru ments Law. A number of instruments, like bills of lading, warehouse receipts, and certificates of stock, may be transferable by indorsement and delivery, or by delivery, but such instruments are not governed by the Negotiable Instruments Law because their language is not within the definitions of a negotiable promissory note or a bill of exchange.

Consequently, such instruments will not be considered in connection with negotiable instruments.
