CHAPTER II FORMATION OF NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

§ 1. In general. An instrument must contain all the elements specified in the definitions of a negotiable promissory note or a bill of exchange if it is to be a negotiable instrument. 

The language of the instrument need not necessarily follow the express language of the act, but it must clearly indicate an intention to conform to its requirements.

The object of this chapter is to discuss the elements of negotiable instruments with a view to determining what they mean and how they must or may be expressed. 

In the consideration of the elements of a negotiable instrument, it should be constantly borne in mind that negotiable instruments are commonly used as a substitute for money and that one of the objects of the Negotiable Instruments Law is so to regulate the language of negotiable instruments that such instruments will be attractive to prospective purchasers and will circulate freely as a substitute for money. 

Therefore, to determine whether the language of a particular instrument impairs negotiability, an excellent test is: Does the language impair marketability; that is, does the language make the instrument less attractive to prospective purchasers? 

§ 2. Writing and signature.-An instrument to be nego tiable must be in writing and signed. However, no particular form of writing or signature is required. Both the body of the instrument and the signature may be printed, stamped, or written.

Any mark or designation used as a substitute for a name binds the person using it. The signature may be affixed by a duly authorized agent. 

§ 3. Promise or order. To be a negotiable promissory note, an instrument must contain a promise; to be a negotiable bill of exchange, an instrument must contain an order. 149

NECOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

However, the words promise or order need not be used, provided that the language imports a promise or order. 

For example, the words "I will pay" import a promise, but not the words "I hope to pay" or "I owe you," which are merely an acknowledgment of indebtedness. 

The words "I command you to pay" import an order, but not "I authorize you to pay," or "I request you to pay." 

Mere words of civility, such as "Please pay," do not impair the force of an order. § 4. Unconditional promise or order.-An instrument to be negotiable must contain an unconditional promise or order. 

For example, "I promise to pay X $500 if he paints my house" could not constitute a negotiable promissory note.

Such an instrument would not be readily marketable, because the promise might not have to be carried out. Even performance of the condition does not cure the defect, since negotiability is determined solely by what appears on the face of the instrument.

A statement of the transaction which gives rise to the instrument does not affect negotiability. For example, at the bottom of a note in the ordinary form are the words: "The price for painting my house." But additional language destroys negotiability if it is construed as imposing a condition upon the promise or order, such as the language in a conditional sale note: "Title to remain in the seller until payment of this note.' This language imposes a condition, because if the seller elects to repossess the property, the buyer does not have to carry out his promise to pay the price. 

A mere indication of the fund out of which the drawee is to reimburse himself does not impair negotiability, such as: "Pay to the order of P $25. You may reimburse yourself from the estate of my father." But an order or promise to pay out of a particular fund destroys negotiability, since the promise or order is conditioned upon existence of the fund, such as: "Pay to the order of P $25 from the estate of my father." § 5. Payable in money. An instrument to be negotiable must be payable in money. An instrument reading: "I

FORMATION OF NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 151 

promise to pay 100 bushels of wheat "would not be negotiable. However, an instrument giving the holder an election to require something in lieu of payment of money is negotiable, as: "I promise to pay to the order of P $50 or, at the election of the holder hereof, 100 bushels of wheat." Such an election promotes marketability.

Money is construed to mean any currency circulating at par with legal tender. The designation of a particular kind of current money does not impair negotiability. 

§ 6. A sum certain.—An instrument to be negotiable must provide for payment of a sum certain in money. "I promise to pay to the order of P all that I can " could not constitute language of a negotiable note.

However, the sum is not uncertain merely because it is to be paid (1) with interest; (2) by stated installments, with a provision that upon default the whole shall become due; (3) with exchange, at a fixed or current rate; or (4) with costs of collection or an attorney's fee. Provisions of this kind aid the marketability of the instrument. § 7. Payable on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time. To be negotiable, an instrument must be payable on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time.¹ 

An instrument reading: "I promise to pay to the order of P when John Smith is elected president " would not be • • • negotiable.

An instrument is payable on demand (1) when it is so stated, or when it is payable at sight or on presentation; (2) when no time of payment is expressed; or (3) when the instrument is overdue. 

¹ Woodbury, Williams & English v. Roberts, p. 351.

An instrument is payable at a determinable future time when it is payable (1) at a fixed period after date or sight; (2) on or before a determinable future time specified therein, such as: "In or within three years I promise to pay... or: "I promise to pay to the order of P three years after date. or upon default at the election of the holder hereof • • د.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

(instruments containing language hastening the time of payment are called accelerable instruments); (3) on the occurrence of a specified event certain to happen, though the time of happening is uncertain, such as: "when my sister dies . . ."; but "when my sister marries " could not constitute language of a negotiable instrument because the event is not certain to happen. It is a mere contingency, and even the occurrence of the event does not cure the defect. § 8. Payable to order or to bearer. An instrument to be negotiable must be payable to order or to bearer; any words expressing such intention will be sufficient, such as: "This instrument to be negotiable."

An instrument is also held bearer paper (1) when it is payable to the order of a fictitious or non-existing person and such fact was known to the person making it so payable; (2) when the name of the payee does not purport to be the name of any person, as an instrument payable to "Cash"; (3) when the only or last indorsement is an indorsement in blank. 

An instrument may be made payable also to the order of two or more payees jointly; or to one or some of several payees. 

§ 9. Language not affecting negotiability.—The negotiable character of an instrument is not affected by any provisions which (1) authorize the sale of collateral securities in the event of default; (2) authorize a confession of judgment, as in the case of a judgment note; (3) waive the benefit of any law intended for the protection of the obligor. It will be observed that provisions of this kind aid rather than impair the marketability of the instrument. 

§ 10. Matters not affecting negotiability. The negotiable character of an instrument is not affected by the fact that (1) it is not dated (nor does antedating or postdating of an instrument affect its validity); (2) it does not specify that value has been given; (3) it does not specify the place where it is drawn or is payable; or (4) it bears a seal. 

§ 11. Rules of construction.-The following rules are applied in the construction of ambiguous language used in a negotiable instrument: 

---

FORMATION OF NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 153 

(1) When the sum is expressed in words and figures, the words govern. (2) Interest, if provided for, runs from the date of issue, if no date is stated. (3) An undated instrument is considered to be dated as of the date of issue. (4) Writing prevails over print in case of conflict. (5) If the holder has any doubt as to whether an instrument is a note or a bill, he may treat it as either. (6) A signature so placed that it is doubtful in what capacity the person signed, is deemed an indorsement. (7) Two or more persons signing "I promise to pay" are jointly and severally liable. 

§ 12. Completing an incomplete instrument. The holder of an incomplete instrument has prima-facie authority to complete such instrument; that is, it is presumed that he has such authority. For example, H is the holder of a note on which there is no date. Prima facie, he has the authority of the maker to insert the date. Prima facie means on the first appearance; presumably. Prima-facie evidence is evidence sufficient to establish a fact in court, which, if not rebutted or contradicted, will remain sufficient. Consequently, a holder having prima-facie authority to complete an instrument, in suing upon the instrument, would not have to prove in the first instance that he acted in accordance with authority. 

A holder in due course of an instrument completed and negotiated to him acquires a valid instrument, irrespective of whether it was completed in accordance with authority. 

§ 13. Liability of agent.-An authorized agent signing a negotiable instrument is not liable if he discloses the name of his principal. For example, a signature reads: "P Manufacturing Company, by A, Treasurer." But the mere addition of words to the agent's name describing him as agent, without disclosing the name of his principal, does not relieve the agent of personal liability, as the signature, "A, Treasurer." § 14. Liability of minors and corporations. A minor has the same right to avoid his signature upon a negotiable instrument that he has to avoid any other contract. A corporation

NEGOTIABLE INSTRÜMENTS 

whose signature appears upon a negotiable instrument in excess of the authority conferred upon it in its charter is not liable upon the instrument.

Nevertheless, the indorsement of a negotiable instrument by a minor or by a corporation in excess of authority passes title to the transferee.

CHAPTER III CONSIDERATION AND DELIVERY 

Consideration § 1. Consideration is essential.-Consideration is just as essential to the formation of a negotiable instrument as it is to the formation of any contract. The consideration required for negotiable instruments is defined in the Negotiable Instruments Law to be any consideration sufficient to support a simple contract. In addition, an antecedent, or preëxisting, debt constitutes consideration for negotiable instruments. 

For example, M owes P $100. M gives P his promissory note in payment of his debt. If P sued M upon the note, M could not set up the defense of absence of consideration. 

His debt of $100 is sufficient consideration to support the note. 

The term value is commonly used in place of the word consideration in connection with negotiable instruments. 

Value is an abbreviation for valuable consideration. 

A holder is deemed a holder for value if value has at any time been given for the instrument. For example, P delivers his automobile to M as consideration for M's note in the amount of $300. P then negotiates the instrument to H as a gift. H would be a holder for value. 

An accommodation party is one signing an instrument without receiving value therefor and for the purpose of lending his name to some other person. He is liable to a holder despite the fact that he has not received consideration. 

§ 2. Presumption of consideration.-When a negotiable instrument is held by an ordinary holder (one who is not a holder in due course), it is presumed to have been issued for consideration, and parties thereon are presumed to have received value until the contrary is proved. For example, H is an ordinary holder of a negotiable promissory note.

In 156

CONSIDERATION AND DELIVERY 

157 suing the maker, he does not have to prove that the maker received consideration; this is presumed, and if M is to prevail on the ground of absence or failure of consideration, he must introduce evidence rebutting the presumption. This presumption of consideration is one of the advantages not enjoyed by the holder of non-negotiable paper. Such a holder has the burden of proving consideration in the first instance, as in the case of any contract. 

When a negotiable instrument is held by a holder in due course, the presumption of consideration is conclusive; that is, the party sued may not introduce evidence rebutting the presumption. For example, H is a holder in due course of a negotiable promissory note. He sues the maker, M. M may not set up as a defense the absence or failure of consideration. 

Delivery § 3. Delivery is essential.—A negotiable instrument is incomplete and revocable until delivery for the purpose of giving effect thereto.¹ For example, M makes a promissory note payable to the order of P. P acquires no rights upon the instrument until it is delivered to him by M or his agent. 

This is true of all contracts upon negotiable instruments. An indorsee would acquire no rights by means of an indorsement to him unless the instrument were delivered to him. 

§ 4. Presumption of delivery.—When a negotiable instru ment is held by an ordinary holder, valid delivery is presumed until the contrary is proved. For example, H is the holder of a negotiable instrument. In suing M, the maker, H does not have to prove in the first instance that M delivered the instrument. This is presumed, and M has the burden of proving the absence of delivery. Here again a privilege is conferred upon holders of negotiable instruments. 

When a negotiable instrument is held by a holder in due course, the presumption of valid delivery is conclusive; that is, it may not be rebutted by the obligor. 

1 Burson v. Huntington, p. 352.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

However, even a holder in due course acquires no rights upon an incomplete, undelivered instrument which is completed and negotiated to him. No valid instrument is created when these defects concur. But if the obligor were negligent in the care of such an instrument—that is, if he left it in a public place he might be prevented from setting up these defects as a defense in a suit brought by a holder in due course.

CHAPTER IV ACCEPTANCE, NEGOTIATION, HOLDERS IN DUE COURSE Acceptance § 1. Definition.-The acceptance of a bill is the significa tion by the drawee of his assent to the order of the drawer, as when the drawee writes across the face of the bill, "Accepted, June 1, 1933, John Smith."

The acceptance must be in writing and must be signed by the drawee. A holder may require that the acceptance be written on the bill. If this request is refused, he may treat the instrument as dishonored.

An acceptance written upon a separate sheet of paper binds the acceptor only in favor of a person to whom it is shown and who acquires the paper for value in reliance thereon.

An unconditional promise to accept is deemed an acceptance in favor of persons acquiring the paper for value in reliance thereon. 

§ 2. Implied acceptance. The drawee is allowed twenty four hours after presentment to decide whether he will accept the bill. He is deemed to have accepted it if, within such time, he refuses to return the bill or if he destroys it. § 3. General and qualified acceptances.-A general acceptance is assent without qualification to the order of the drawer. 

A qualified acceptance is one which imposes some qualification upon the acceptance, as the condition that the drawer reimburse the drawee; or an acceptance to pay only a part of the bill.

The holder may refuse to take a qualified acceptance and may treat the instrument as dishonored by non-acceptance. 159

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

If he takes a qualified acceptance, the drawer and indorsers are discharged unless they consent thereto. 

§ 4. Acceptance of checks (certification).—The certifica tion of a check by the drawee bank is equivalent to an acceptance, and renders the bank liable; but prior to certification, the bank is not liable upon the check to the holder. 

Certification of a check at the request of the holder discharges the drawer and indorsers, for if the holder had received payment instead of certification, the instrument would have been discharged. But certification at the request of the drawer does not affect the secondary liability of the drawer and indorsers. § 5. Acceptance; payment for honor.-Acceptance for honor is the acceptance of a bill by a person not a party thereto for the honor of a party liable thereon, made when the bill has been protested but is not overdue. This is also called "acceptance for honor supra protest." Thus, an acceptor for honor is one who intervenes with the consent of the holder and who volunteers to assume the position of the drawee.

Payment for honor is the payment of a bill by a person not a party thereto for the honor of a party liable thereon, made when the bill has been protested for non-payment. Negotiation 

§ 6. Kinds of negotiation.-A negotiable instrument may be negotiated by delivery or by indorsement and delivery. If paper is payable to bearer, it is negotiated by delivery alone; if payable to order, it is negotiated by the indorsement of the holder, completed by delivery. § 7. Indorsements in general.—An indorsement must be written upon the instrument itself or upon paper attached thereto.

When the name of the payee or indorsee is wrongly described or is misspelled, he may sign his name as described in the instrument, adding, if he thinks fit, his proper signature.

A transferee of unindorsed order paper has such title as

NEGOTIATION 

161 his transferor and, in addition, the right to have the indorsement of the transferor.

A holder reacquiring an instrument may further negotiate it, but he may not enforce payment against any intervening party to whom he was liable. 

A drawee has no right to require a holder presenting a bill for payment to indorse such a bill. Surrender for payment is not negotiation.¹ Since the bill directs the drawee to pay to the bearer or to the order of the payee, the drawee is under a duty to the drawer to pay the bill without imposing a condition of indorsement. The failure to comply with the order because of absence of an indorsement by the holder is a violation of this duty; but since the drawee is under no duty to the holder to comply with the order, the holder has no remedy against a drawee who refuses to pay without the holder's indorsement. However, it is common for the drawee to insist upon the indorsement of the holder as a receipt for payment, and this practice serves the useful purpose, for both the drawee and the drawer, of identifying the person to whom payment has been made and creating a receipt for the payment. § 8. Kinds of indorsement.-A blank indorsement is accomplished merely by writing the name of the indorser on the back of the instrument, such as "John Smith." An instrument indorsed in blank is payable to bearer, and may be negotiated by delivery. The holder of an instrument may convert a blank indorsement into a special one by writing above the name of the indorser: "Pay to the order of Henry Brown."

A special indorsement is one which specifies a particular indorsee, as: "Pay to the order of M. (Signed) T." Of course, the indorsement of M is then necessary to further negotiation. 

A qualified indorsement is one which qualifies or limits liability of the indorser by adding the words "Without 

¹ National Bank of Commerce of Lincoln v. Farmers' & Merchants' Bank of 

Lincoln, p. 353.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

recourse. (Signed) T." As will be pointed out later, even a qualified indorser has certain liabilities growing out of his indorsement.

A conditional indorsement is one which imposes a condition upon the negotiation, such as: "Pay to the order of M if he paints my barn. (Signed) T."

A restrictive indorsement is one which in some way restricts further negotiation of the instrument, such as: "Pay to M only. (Signed) T," or: "Pay to M for collection only. (Signed) T," or: "Pay to M, attorney for B. (Signed)

T." 

Holders in Due Course § 9. Holders in general. There are two classes of holders of negotiable instruments: (1) holders in due course, namely, those who comply with certain requirements; (2) ordinary holders, those who fail to meet the requirements of a holder in due course. 

Any holder acquires all the rights upon the instrument possessed by his transferor, as does any assignee under an assignment. But a holder in due course may acquire rights superior to those of his transferor; that is to say, he may rise higher in that he is not subject to personal defenses when suing the obligor, whereas the transferor may have been. 

For example, P is the payee of a note made by M. The note is paid by M before maturity, but M fails to take up the note. 

If P, or any ordinary holder to whom P negotiates the instrument, sues M to enforce payment a second time, M may set up the defense of payment. But if H, a holder in due course, sues, M may not raise this defense. Of course, if M has no defenses, it is immaterial whether or not the holder suing him is a holder in due course.

The superior rights conferred upon a holder in due course constitute one of the reasons why negotiable paper circulates as a substitute for money. A person acquiring such paper knows that the obligation it represents is separate from the transaction giving rise to it.

HOLDERS IN DUE COURSE 

163 § 10. Requirements of a holder in due course.-A holder in due course is a holder who has acquired paper (1) complete and regular upon its face, (2) before it is overdue, (3) in good faith and for value, (4) without notice of any infirmity in the paper or defect in the title of his transferor. 

A payee may be a holder in due course if he satisfies these requirements. However, he is not so likely to be one as a transferee if there are defenses, such as payment, fraud, and the like, because as an immediate party he has knowledge of them. 

§ 11. Paper complete and regular upon its face. A holder acquiring paper not complete and regular upon its face does not satisfy the requirements of a holder in due course.2 For example, let us suppose a note reads: "I promise to pay to the order of $100... The absence of the name of the payee would make the paper incomplete and irregular. 99 § 12. Before paper is overdue.—A holder acquiring overdue paper does not satisfy a requirement of a holder in due course. The reason is that an instrument circulating after maturity arouses suspicion as to why it has not been paid. 

The inference is that there must be some defense available to the obligor.

An instrument maturing on a fixed date is, of course, overdue after that date.

Demand paper is overdue an unreasonable length of time after issue. What is a reasonable length of time is a question of fact, depending upon the nature of the instrument, usages of trade or business, and the facts of the particular case. 

Ordinarily, a reasonable time in the case of demand notes is about sixty days; in the case of checks, the day following the date of issue. § 13. In good faith and for value.—A holder acquiring paper not in good faith and for value does not satisfy the requirements of a holder in due course. Thus, if a transferee of a note knew when acquiring it that the maker had paid the note, he would not acquire it in good faith and could not be a holder in due course. 

2 In re Philpott's Estate, p. 353.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

A transferee must himself give value in order to qualify as a holder in due course. He is not aided by the provision in the 

Negotiable Instruments Law stating that a holder is deemed a holder for value if value has at any time been given for the instrument. This provision relates generally to the necessity of negotiable instruments being supported by consideration, and merely enables a holder who has not himself given value to sue an obligor upon the instrument, provided that some party prior to the holder gave value. Value, we have seen in 

Chapter III, Section 1, is any consideration sufficient to support a simple contract-an antecedent, or preëxisting, debt also constituting value. § 14. Without notice of any infirmity or defect.-A holder acquiring paper with notice of any infirmity in it or of any defect in the title of his transferor does not satisfy the requirements of a holder in due course.

Notice of an infirmity or a defect is stated in the Law to be actual knowledge, or knowledge of such facts that the taking of the instrument amounts to bad faith. But mere knowledge of suspicious circumstances, doubts as to genuineness of title, gross negligence, and the like, are not necessarily sufficient to amount to bad faith, disqualifying a purchaser from being a holder in due course.

For example, H, acquiring paper which he knew his transferor had stolen, could not be a holder in due course; nor if he knew that his transferor could not have come into possession of the note without finding or stealing it, since taking the instrument with this knowledge would amount to bad faith. § 15. Transferee of holder in due course.-A transferee of a holder in due course acquires all the rights of a holder in due course, although he may not satisfy the requirements of one. The reason is clear. Since even in an assignment the assignee acquires all the rights of his assignor, the transferee of a holder in due course should rise as high as his transferor.

Of course, this would not be so if such transferee were a party to any fraud or illegality affecting the instrument.

CHAPTER V DEFENSES OF PRIMARY PARTIES AGAINST HOLDERS § 1. In general.-Primary parties are makers of promis sory notes and acceptors of bills of exchange. They are so called because they are the first or principal obligors upon the instrument, as compared with indorsers and drawers, whose liability is secondary in nature. 

The maker and the acceptor may be able to raise various defenses against a holder suing to enforce payment of the instrument. Their defenses may be divided into two classes: (1) Personal defenses. These are defenses not inherent in the instrument but arising out of the dealings between the parties. They may be raised against any holder except a holder in due course. (2) Real defenses; also called absolute defenses. These are defenses inherent in the instrument. They may be raised against any holder, including a holder in due course. 

§ 2. Kinds of personal defenses.-Personal defenses may be classified as follows: 

(1) Payment before maturity. This defense arises when the maker or acceptor neglects to require surrender of the instrument and it is further negotiated. Payment at or after maturity discharges the instrument. (2) Counterclaims, as when the maker of a note claims that the payee is indebted to him in a certain sum. (3) Absence or failure of consideration, as when the maker claims that the note was a gift. 

Fraud antecedent to the note or bill,¹ as when the payee makes fraudulent representations about a car in payment for which the maker gives his note. 1 Mueller v. Buch, p. 355. 166

DEFENSES OF PRIMARY PARTIES 

167 (5) Duress, as when the payee compels the maker, under threat, to sign a note. (6) Non-delivery or improper delivery, as when M makes a note and it reaches the payee without authorization by M. (7) Illegality, as when the maker gives a note to the payee, a public official, to influence his decision regarding a public matter. But if the contract upon the instrument is declared void by statute, as in the case of wagering and usurious contracts, illegality will be a real defense. 

§ 3. Kinds of real defenses.-Real defenses may be classified as follows: 

(1) Fraud in the execution, as when the payee induces the maker to sign a negotiable instrument, and the maker is unaware that he is signing such an instrument. (2) Forgery, or absence of authority, as when the payee forges the drawer's name to a check. But a maker or an acceptor may be precluded from raising the defense of forgery or absence of authority if he leaves a stamp of his signature where anyone can have easy access to it. (3) Material alteration; except that a holder in due course can enforce the instrument according to its original tenor. 

For example, the payee changes the sum of a note from $100 to $800. He can recover nothing on the note, but if he negotiates it to H, a holder in due course, H can recover $100.

A material alteration is any change in the date, the sum, the time or place of payment, the number or relation of the parties, the medium of currency; or any alteration in the legal effect of the instrument. (4) Incapacity, as when the maker of a note is a minor, an insane person, a corporation acting outside the powers granted it by its charter, or a drunkard. (5) Non-delivery of an uncompleted instrument, as when the maker signs a note in blank and locks it in his safe, from which it is stolen and negotiated. But if the maker were negligent-for example, if he left the note in a public placehe would be precluded from setting up this defense.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

(6) Illegality, as when the contract upon the instrument is declared void by statute.

CHAPTER VI OBLIGATIONS OF THE PARTIES Primary Parties § 1. Maker of note.—The maker of a note by making it engages that he will pay it according to its tenor and admits the existence of the payee and his then capacity to indorse. 

§ 2. Acceptor of bill.—The acceptor of a bill by accepting it engages that he will pay according to the tenor of his acceptance, and admits (1) the existence of the drawer, the genuineness of his signature, and his capacity and authority to draw the instrument; and (2) the existence of the payee and his then capacity to indorse. 

Prior to acceptance, a drawee is not liable upon the bill to the holder, but if the drawee refuses to accept or pay the bill, he may be liable to the drawer in damages for breach of contract.

Secondary Parties § 3. Drawer of bill.-The drawer admits the existence of the payee and his then capacity to indorse, and engages that (1) if the instrument is duly presented, (2) if it is dishonored, and (3) if due notice of the dishonor is given, he will pay the holder or any indorser compelled to pay it. 

However, the drawer of a check is not discharged by the non-performance of these three conditions. He is discharged only by and to the extent of a loss caused by a failure to present the check within a reasonable time. A reasonable time within which to present a check is generally the day of issue or the day thereafter. If the parties live in different places, this time would be extended to include the mailing time. For example, let us suppose that the drawer, the holder, and the drawee bank are in the same city. On 169

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

Monday, the drawer issues the check to the holder. The holder presents it for payment on Thursday, only to find that the bank closed on Wednesday. If the drawer receives only fifty cents on the dollar from the bank, the holder can recover only fifty cents on the dollar in a suit against the drawer. § 4. Warranties of indorsers.-Indorsers may be classified as qualified and unqualified. A qualified indorser is one indorsing without recourse. He warrants that: (1) The instrument is genuine and in all respects what it purports to be. (2) He has good title to it. (3) All prior parties had capacity to contract. (4) He has no knowledge of any fact impairing the validity of the instrument or rendering it valueless. 

A transferor by delivery makes the same warranties as the qualified indorser.

Unqualified indorsers warrant the first three of the above and that the instrument is genuine at the time of the indorsement.

It will be noted that an indorser seeking to limit his liability by indorsing "without recourse" does not escape all liability upon the instrument; he is held to make the above warranties notwithstanding his indorsement.¹ The only effect of his qualified indorsement is that of relieving him of the conditional liability, discussed in the next section. 

It is not surprising that indorsers and transferors by delivery are held to make these warranties. In the discussion on sales, it was found that sellers of personal property make implied warranties concerning property sold, as the implied warranty that the seller has title to the goods. Also, sellers of real estate are held to warrant certain things, the kind of warranties depending upon whether the deed is a quitclaim or a warranty deed. In a warranty deed, the seller of real estate warrants, among other things, that he has a fee-simple title to the premises and the right and power to convey them. 

¹ Palmer v. Courtney, p. 355.

OBLIGATIONS OF THE PARTIES 

171 

§ 5. Conditional liability of unqualified indorsers.—An unqualified indorser engages that (1) if the instrument is duly presented, (2) if it is dishonored, and (3) if due notice of the dishonor is given, he will pay the holder or any subsequent indorser compelled to pay it. 

What constitutes due presentment, dishonor, and due notice will be discussed in subsequent sections. 

§ 6. Order of liability among indorsers.-Prima facie, indorsers are liable to one another only in the order they indorse, but they may agree otherwise. For example, A, B, and C are indorsers in that order upon a note held by H. If H recovers from C, C may recover from B, B from A, and A from the maker. But if H recovers from B, B may not recover from C unless C has agreed to be liable to B. 

A holder may sue any one or all of the indorsers, as well as the maker or acceptor, if he has performed the three conditions. His suit against one of these parties does not prevent him from bringing suit against the others. 

Presentment, Dishonor, and Notice 

§ 7. In general. An indorser or drawer, it has been stated, is discharged from his conditional liability unless (1) the instrument has been duly presented, (2) it has been dishonored, and (3) due notice of the dishonor has been given. 

Consequently, a holder must perform these conditions if he wishes to preserve his rights against secondary parties.² If performance of the conditions is excused or waived, the holder may hold the secondary parties, notwithstanding non-performance. Of course, performance of these conditions is not necessary to charge parties primarily liable. 

PRESENTMENT § 8. Time of presentment for payment. An instrument maturing on a fixed date must be presented on that date. 

Demand notes must be presented within a reasonable time after issue. What constitutes a reasonable time varies 

2 Worley v. Johnson, p. 356.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS. 

with the circumstances surrounding the particular case. 

In one case sixty days was held a reasonable time to present the demand note therein considered.

Demand bills of exchange must be presented within a reasonable time after the last negotiation. A reasonable time might be days or weeks, depending upon all the circumstances. 

Delay in presentment is excused when the delay is caused by circumstances beyond the control of the holder and when it is not imputable to his fault. § 9. Manner of presentment for payment.-Presentment must be made by the holder or his agent to the person primarily liable, or, if he is absent or inaccessible, to anyone found at the proper place of presentment.

The instrument must be presented at a reasonable hour, on a business day, and at the proper place. The proper place is the place designated in the instrument, or the address of the party as therein specified; if neither specification is made, the instrument must be presented at the place of business or residence of the party who is to make payment, or wherever he can be found.

The holder must exhibit the instrument to the party to whom presentment is made; and upon payment the instrument must be delivered to such party. § 10. When presentment for payment is not required.- 

Presentment for payment is not required under the following circumstances: (1) When the drawer has no right to expect or require the drawee or acceptor to pay. For example, one person draws a bill of exchange upon another when he knows that the latter has no money with which to pay the bill. (2) When an instrument is made or accepted for the accommodation of the indorser. (3) When, after reasonable diligence, proper presentment cannot be made. (4) When the drawee is a fictitious person. (5) When the secondary party has waived presentment, as when an indorsement reads, "Waiving demand and notice."

OBLIGATIONS OF THE PARTIES 

173 

§ 11. Presentment of bill for acceptance. A bill of exchange must be presented for acceptance (1) when it is payable after sight or when it is necessary to fix maturity, as "thirty days after sight"; (2) when it so stipulates; (3) when it is payable elsewhere than at the residence or place of business of the drawee.

Except in these cases, the holder of a bill is not obligated to present it for acceptance in order to hold secondary parties. 

He need present it only for payment. 

Even when they are not required to do so, holders generally present bills for acceptance to strengthen the value of the paper by having the promise of the acceptor, and to acquire an immediate right of recourse against secondary parties in the event of non-acceptance.

A holder has an immediate right of recourse against secondary parties when acceptance is refused. It is immaterial whether or not presentment for acceptance is required. 

Indeed, the holder must treat the bill as dishonored by nonacceptance and give notice to secondary parties, or he will lose his right of recourse.

DISHONOR § 12. Definition.-Dishonor is the refusal of a party to pay a note or a bill or to accept a bill duly presented.

NOTICE OF DISHONOR § 13. Time notice must be given.-Notice of dishonor must be given before the end of the business day following the day of dishonor, if the holder and the secondary party reside in the same place. If they reside in different places, notice by mail must be posted the day following the date of dishonor. 

Notice properly addressed and mailed is held sufficient, even if it miscarries in the mail. 

Delay in giving notice is excused when the delay is caused by circumstances beyond the control of the holder and is not imputable to his fault. § 14. Kind of notice.-Notice of dishonor may be given orally or in writing. No particular form is required. 

3 Form of Notice of Dishonor, p. 497. 

3

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

Notice may be given to the secondary party or his agent by the holder, or his agent, or an indorser liable to the holder. 

Notice must be sent to any address of the party specified on the instrument; or if none is specified, to his residence, to his place of business, or to the place where he is sojourning. § 15. Notice by indorser notified of dishonor. An indorser notified of dishonor has the same time for giving notice to prior parties that the holder has after dishonor. Thus, if the second of three indorsers of a note receives notice of dishonor on Monday, he must give notice to the first indorser by Tuesday, if both live in the same place. 

The failure of an indorser notified of dishonor to give notice to a prior party deprives him of a right of recourse unless the holder has already given notice to the prior party. 

Notice by the holder inures to the benefit of all other indorsers having a right of recourse. § 16. When notice is not required.-Notice is not required when it has been waived, as in the case of an indorsement reading "Waiving demand and notice," and when, after reasonable diligence, notice cannot be given. 

Notice of dishonor need not be given the drawer when: (1) The drawer and drawee are the same person. (2) The drawee is a fictitious person or one having no capacity to contract. (3) The drawer is the person to whom the instrument is presented for payment. (4) The drawer has no right to expect that the drawee or acceptor will honor the instrument. (5) The drawer has countermanded payment. 

Notice of dishonor need not be given an indorser when: (1) The drawee is a fictitious person or a person having no capacity to contract and the indorser had knowledge of this fact when he indorsed the instrument. (2) The indorser is the person to whom the instrument is presented for payment. (3) The instrument was made or accepted for the accommodation of the indorser.

OBLIGATIONS OF THE PARTIES 

175 Protest 

§ 17. When required.-Foreign bills of exchange must be protested for non-acceptance or non-payment, or else the drawer and indorsers will be discharged. It is not necessary to protest inland bills and notes, but they are often protested for the purpose of furnishing evidence of due presentment, dishonor, and due notice. 

§ 18. Description of protest.—A protest is a formal state ment in writing made by a notary public or other respectable resident in the presence of two witnesses-at the request of the holder, stating that payment or acceptance was demanded and refused, and the reason for the protest, if any; that the instrument is therefore protested against all parties and they will be held responsible for all loss or damage arising from the dishonor; and that notice has been sent to certain parties. 

The formalities with which a protest must comply are set forth in Section 153 of the Negotiable Instruments Law. 

The protest must be made on the day of dishonor unless the delay is excused.

CHAPTER VII DISCHARGE OF NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS § 1. Discharge of instrument itself. A negotiable instru ment may be discharged in any one of the following ways: (1) Payment in due course by or for the principal debtor.

Payment by a secondary party does not discharge the instrument; such party is remitted to his former rights and may again negotiate the instrument. (2) Payment in due course by a party accommodated: that is, a party for whom the instrument was made or accepted. (3) Intentional cancellation by the holder, such as the burning or the tearing up of the instrument. (4) Any other act discharging a simple contract for the payment of money, such as accord and satisfaction, novation, bankruptcy, running of the Statute of Limitations. (5) The principal debtor's becoming the holder of the instrument in his own right at or after maturity. (6) Renunciation in writing by the holder at or after maturity; or orally if accompanied by delivery of the instrument. § 2. Discharge of secondary parties.-A secondary party may be discharged in any one of the following ways: (1) Discharge of the instrument. (2) Intentional cancellation of his signature by the holder. (3) Discharge of a prior party. (4) Valid tender of payment made by a prior party. (5) Release of the principal debtor, unless the holder's right of recourse against the secondary party is expressly reserved. (6) Binding agreement of the holder to extend the time of payment, unless made with the assent of the secondary party, or unless a right of recourse against him is expressly reserved.¹ 

¹ Adams v. Ferguson, p. 358. 177

PARTNERSHIPS

PARTNERSHIPS CHAPTER I IN GENERAL § 1. Types of business organizations.-Business is con ducted generally by one of the following types of organizations: (1) sole proprietorship; (2) partnership; (3) corporation.

A sole proprietorship is a business organization owned and carried on by one person. The owner may employ others to assist him in his business, but such persons occupy the position of employees only; they are agents or servants. Commonly, a sole proprietor does business under some name other than his own. For example, John Smith may do business under the style of "Frigid Beverages of Dallas."

A partnership is a business association owned and carried on by two or more persons. Important characteristics of a partnership are the following: (1) Death of a partner dissolves the firm. (2) A partnership is not an entity, except in certain limited respects; it is a relationship. (3) A partner's private assets may be seized by firm creditors.

A joint stock company is a firm, the capital of which is divided into numerous transferable shares. Generally, a joint stock company comprises more persons and uses greater capital than an ordinary partnership. Also, its name does not generally disclose the names of its members as does the ordinary partnership. 

A corporation is a legal entity created by the state. 

Important characteristics of a corporation are the following: (1) Death of a stockholder does not affect corporate existence. 181

PARTNERSHIPS 

(2) A corporation is an entity in the eyes of the law. It can hold title to property, sue, and be sued in its own name. (3) Stockholders are not generally liable upon debts of the corporation.

Further on in the text, we shall deal more fully with corporations. 

§ 2. Uniform Partnership Act. The Uniform Partnership 

Act¹ is an act embodying certain elementary principles of law relating to partnerships. It has been enacted as a statute by the legislatures of many states, but not so widely as the 

Uniform Sales Act and the Negotiable Instruments Law. 

As in the case of these two latter acts, common-law cases are still essential in states adopting the Uniform Partnership Act for the purpose of construing provisions of the Act and applying law to points as to which the Act is silent. 

This treatment of partnerships is based upon the Act when it is applicable. This fact does not impair the value of the text in states which have not as yet adopted the Act, since the Act was drawn for the purpose of codifying sound, leading principles relating to partnerships In many states, there has also been enacted as a statute, the Uniform Limited Partnership Act, which embodies principles of law relating to limited partnerships. 

§ 3. Kinds of partnership.- 

General and limited. A general partnership is usually one in which the liability of all partners to firm creditors is unlimited. A limited partnership is one in which the liability of one or more of the partners to firm creditors is limited in amount. Limited partnerships will be more fully treated.later in this chapter.

Trading and non-trading. A trading partnership is one engaged primarily in buying and selling commodities, such as a partnership conducting a meat market. A non-trading partnership is one engaged primarily in producing commodities or in rendering service, such as a partnership of accountants. 'Text of Uniform Partnership Act, p. 457.

IN GENERAL 

183 § 4. Kinds of partners. A general partner is one whose liability for firm debts is unlimited. 

A special partner is one whose liability for firm debts is limited to a certain amount. He is also called a limited partner.

An ostensible partner is one who is represented to others as a partner, whether or not he is in fact a partner. 

An active partner is one who takes an active part in the conduct of the firm's business.

A silent or dormant partner is one who is not known by third persons to be a partner. His position corresponds to that of an undisclosed principal.

A secret partner is one whose membership in the firm is concealed. He has all the liabilities of any other general partner.

A nominal partner is one who appears to be a partner, but who in fact has no real interest in the firm. 

§ 5. Articles of copartnership.-Articles of copartnership is the name of a written instrument embodying the terms of the partnership agreement. Such instruments usually con tain provisions relating to the following matters: (1) names of the partners; (2) name of the partnership; (3) nature of business; (4) duration of partnership, (5) place of business; (6) amounts and manner of contributions of partners; (7) interests of partners; their shares in profits and losses; (8) duties of partners; (9) time for accounting; how much, if any, each partner may draw; (10) keeping of partnership books; (11) salary of partners, if any; (12) matters relating to retirement of partners and to dissolution; (13) method of settling disputes; and so forth. 2 Third parties are not bound by provisions in the articles of copartnership, of which provisions they have no knowledge. 

The articles of copartnership, like any other contract, may be modified by any subsequent agreement of the parties; but the articles govern the rights and liabilities of partners among themselves while these articles are in force. 

2 Form of Articles of Copartnership, p. 497.

PARTNERSHIPS 

Under the Statute of Frauds a valid partnership may be created and conducted without articles of copartnership unless the contract is not to be performed within one year. 

However, it is prudent for partners to reduce their partnership agreement to writing in order that the terms of the agreement may be definitely understood by the parties. § 6. Definition of a partnership.-A partnership is an association of two or more persons to carry on as coöwners a business for profit.

Whether or not persons are partners depends upon whether their association contains the elements set forth in this definition. This, of course, is a question of fact, to be determined by the jury or the court from the circumstances surrounding the association. It is immaterial whether or not persons call or regard themselves partners. What they say and what they do in the light of the definition is of chief importance.

However, a real partnership cannot exist without an agreement, express or implied, between the parties. 

Tests of Partnership 

§ 7. Effect of sharing profits.-Receipt of a share in the profits of a business is prima-facie evidence that the person is a partner. For example, A and B operate a restaurant. B receives at the end of each week 25 per cent of the profits. 

This evidence, standing alone, is sufficient to warrant the court in holding that A and B are partners. However, a prima-facie case can always be overcome by evidence to the contrary. If B, sued as a partner by a creditor of the business, introduces evidence showing that he is not a partner, the burden rests upon the creditor to introduce further evidence proving a partnership.

However, the sharing of profits is not prima-facie evidence of a partnership if the profits are received in payment of a debt, as wages or rent, annuity to the widow or representative of a deceased partner, interest on a loan,³ or consideration for the sale of business or other property. 

³ Meehan v. Valentine, p. 361.

IN GENERAL 

185 A mere sharing of gross returns does not of itself establish a partnership. § 8. Effect of coöwnership. The various kinds of coöwnership, such as joint tenancies, tenancies in common, tenancies by the entirety, and so forth, do not of themselves establish partnerships, whether or not the coöwners share the profits arising from the use of the property. For example, a father devises a house and land to his two sons as tenants in common. The two sons rent the property and divide the profits. This act alone is not sufficient to make the sons partners with respect to the property. 

§ 9. Effect of agency relationship. The mere relationship of principal and agent between two persons obviously is not evidence that they are partners. Yet partners occupy the relationship of principal and agent. A partner while acting within the scope of the partnership business is the agent of the firm and every partner. § 10. Non-profit organizations.-Organizations not having for their object the making of a financial profit are not partnerships. This is obvious from the definition. Thus, a fraternity, a political association, a charitable group, or the like, would not be partnerships.

In organizations which are not partnerships, a member is not liable for the acts of officers or of other members unless it can be proved that he authorized such acts, expressly or impliedly. But a partner is liable for the acts of any one of the other partners if it can be proved that a partnership exists and that the acts are performed apparently to carry on the partnership business. 

§ 11. Partnership by estoppel.-A person representing another to be a partner, or consenting to another's representing him as a partner, is estopped to deny partnership. 

He is liable to a person who has extended credit on the faith of such representation. Thus, the two elements of partnership by estoppel are (1) representation of partnership; (2) reliance by the third party to his damage. For example, A says to C, "B is a partner in my automobile sales concern." 

In fact, B is not a partner, but an employee. B purchases a

PARTNERSHIPS 

car from C, charging it to the concern. A is liable to C precisely as though B were a partner. Limited Partnerships¹ § 12. Definition.-A limited partnership is one having one or more general partners and one or more limited partners. 

To state it another way, a limited partnership is one in which the liability of one or more of the partners, but not of all, is limited to the amount of capital contributed at the time of organization. A limited partner is not otherwise bound by partnership obligations. 

§ 13. Requirements for formation. In order to form a limited partnership, the partners must sign, swear to, and file in a designated place, such as the registry of deeds or the office of the secretary of state, a certificate setting forth such information as the name of the partnership, the character of the business, the location, the term of partnership, the names of the general and the limited partners, the contribution to be made by each limited partner, the share of profits of each limited partner, and so forth. 

If any subsequent changes are made in the partnership, the certificate must be amended to reflect such changes. § 14. When limited partner is liable as a general partner. -A limited partner is liable as a general partner if his name appears in the partnership name, and the creditor does not know that he is a limited partner; but not if his name is also the name of a general partner or if his name had been in the firm name prior to the formation of the limited partnership. 

Also, a limited partner is liable as a general partner if he takes part in the control of the business.

CHAPTER II PARTNERSHIP PROPERTY § 1. Partnership capital.-Partnership capital consists of the total amount of property contributed to the partnership by the partners. It may consist of money, personal or real property, or even services, although ordinarily services are not regarded as capital.

The proportion that each partner contributes to firm capital is determined by the agreement between the partners. 

It is not unusual for one partner to contribute all the capital, say $20,000, and for another, who is of limited means but of exceptional ability, to contribute merely his services. 

§ 2. Partnership property.-Partnership property consists of the total property owned by the firm, however acquired, including capital contributed by the partners. 

The mere use of property by a partnership does not necessarily constitute it firm property, since a partner may own the property individually and merely lend the use of it to the firm. The test of whether property is firm property is whether the partners intend that it shall so be. 

The good will of a firm is part of its property. Surviving partners must account to representatives of a deceased partner for the good will of the firm, together with other assets. 

§ 3. Title to partnership property. Title to personal prop erty may be acquired and held in the firm name, or in the names of one or more of the partners; and, similarly, title to real estate may be so acquired and held under the Uniform Partnership Act. Allowing a partnership to acquire title to real property in the firm name is recognition of the partnership as an entity in this respect. 

Property Rights of a Partner 

§ 4. Extent of partner's property rights. The property rights of a partner are (1) his rights in specific partnership 188

PARTNERSHIP PROPERTY 

189 property, (2) his interest in the partnership, and (3) his right to participate in the management. § 5. Nature of partner's right in specific partnership property.—A partner is a coöwner with his partners of specific partnership property, holding as a tenant in partnership. 

A partner has an equal right with his partners to use specific partnership property for partnership purposes, but not for other purposes without the consent of his partners. 

A partner may not assign his right in specific partnership property unless all partners join in the assignment.¹ 

A partner's right in specific partnership property is not subject to attachment by his individual creditors. In other words, individual creditors may not attach firm property in a suit against a partner; but they may reach and apply his interest in the firm as described in Section 8, below. 

On the death of a partner his right in specific partnership property vests in the surviving partners for partnership purposes. Of course, they must account to representatives of the deceased partner.

A partner's right in specific partnership property is not subject to dower, curtesy, or allowances to widows. 

6. Nature of partner's interest in partnership. A partner's interest in a partnership is his share of profits and surplus, and is regarded as personal property. Thus, if a partner dies, his interest, like his personal property, passes to his executor or administrator, rather than to his heirs at law, even though the partnership property consists entirely of real estate. § 7. Assignment of a partner's interest.-A conveyance by a partner of his interest does not of itself dissolve a partnership. Prior to the Uniform Partnership Act, such conveyance would dissolve the partnership. 

The assignee is entitled merely to receive the profits to which the assigning partner would otherwise be entitled; in case of dissolution, he is entitled to receive his assignor's interest, together with an accounting from the date of the last 

¹ Spencer v. Spencer, p. 363.

PARTNERSHIPS 

accounting. He is not entitled to interfere in the management, to inspect the books, or to require any information or any accounting during continuance of the partnership. § 8. Right of creditor of partner to charge his interest.— 

A creditor holding a judgment against a partner may petition the court to charge the interest of the partner with payment of the unsatisfied amount of such judgment. The court may appoint a receiver to collect the partner's share of profits and may also order a sale of the partner's interest to satisfy the judgment. In the event of a sale, the partnership is not dissolved. The purchaser at the sale occupies the position of any other assignee of the partner.

CHAPTER III RELATIONS OF PARTNERS TO ONE ANOTHER § 1. Agreement governs.-The relations of partners to one another are governed by the partnership agreement. 

The rules set forth in the sections that follow apply in cases in which partners have not made any agreement to the contrary. § 2. Rights of contribution and indemnity.—A partner has a right of contribution against his partners for any payments made by him, whether by way of capital or advances. 

If he makes any payment or advance beyond the capital agreed upon, he is entitled to interest from the date of such payment or advance. Also, he is entitled to receive interest on the capital contributed by him from the date when repayment should be made.

A partner has a right to be indemnified by the partnership for payments made and personal liabilities reasonably incurred by him in the ordinary and proper conduct of the business. 

For example, A, B, and C are partners engaged in the purchase and sale of second-hand cars. A purchases a car which he reasonably believes belongs to T. In fact, T stole the car from X. X brings a suit for conversion against A and recovers judgment in the amount of $500. A has a right to be indemnified against this liability by the partnership. § 3. Right to share in profits and surplus; losses.—In the absence of agreement, a partner has the right to share equally in the profits and surplus remaining after all liabilities, including those to partners, are satisfied. However, the share in profits is generally regulated by the partnership agreement. 

A partner must contribute towards losses sustained by the partnership according to his share in the profits. The mere fact that one partner has contributed more capital than another does not affect his share in losses or in profits, unless the partners have agreed to the contrary. 191

PARTNERSHIPS 

§ 4. Right in management.-All partners have equal rights in the management and conduct of the partnership business. 

Any differences as to ordinary matters connected with the partnership business, such as the institution of suit in the partnership name, may be decided by a majority of the partners; but any act violating the agreement, such as changing a business from an automobile sales concern to a repair business, requires the consent of all partners.

No person may become a member of a partnership without the consent of all the partners. The reason is that the relationship of partners is personal and confidential. § 5. Right to inspect books and to information.-A partner has the right to have access to and to inspect the books of the partnership. These books must be kept at the principal place of business, unless the partners agree otherwise. 

Also, a partner has the right to demand true and full information as to all matters affecting the partnership. § 6. Right to an accounting.-A partner has a right to a formal accounting as to partnership affairs (1) if he is wrongly excluded from partnership affairs, (2) if the right exists under the agreement, (3) if a partner has derived profit without the consent of his partners, (4) whenever it is just and reasonable, or (5) upon the dissolution of the firm. 

A partner holds, as trustee for the partnership, any profits derived by him without the consent of his partners, and he must account for them. For example, a partner receiving a fee without the knowledge of his partners' is regarded as holding the fee in trust for the partnership and must account for it. § 7. No right to remuneration.-A partner is not entitled to remuneration for acting in the partnership business, in the absence of agreement,¹ even though one partner devotes considerably more time to partnership affairs than another. 

But, quite commonly, partners will agree that salaries shall be paid to them.

A surviving partner is entitled to reasonable compensation for his services in winding up the partnership affairs. 

1 Cole v. Cole, p. 364.

RELATIONS OF PARTNERS TO ONE ANOTHER 193 § 8. Continuation of business. If partners continue the business beyond a fixed term or after the undertaking agreed upon, without a new agreement, their rights and duties nevertheless remain the same so far as is consistent with a partnership at will. § 9. Fiduciary relationship of partners.-Partners occupy a fiduciary relationship to each other: that is, one of confidence and trust, as in the case of principal and agent, trustee and beneficiary, director and corporation. In consequence, a partner may not compete with the firm; nor may he take any secret advantage of the firm; nor may he serve any interest conflicting with that of the firm. § 10. Suits by partners.-Suits by a partner against his partners, when he desires an accounting or other relief, must be brought in a court of equity; they may not be brought in law courts.

CHAPTER IV RELATIONS OF PARTNERS TO PERSONS DEALING WITH THE PARTNERSHIP § 1. Powers of partner in general. The powers of a partner are governed substantially by the law of principal and agent. 

As between the partners themselves, the powers of a partner depend upon the partnership agreement, just as the powers of an agent depend upon his agreement with his principal, as between themselves. For example, A and B are law partners. A purchases a set of Rhode Island Reports, charging them to the firm. Whether or not A has power to do this, as between him and B, depends upon their agreement. 

If A has power under the partnership agreement to purchase such books as the firm needs, he might be held to have power to make this purchase.

From the standpoint of third persons, the power of a partner to bind the partnership depends upon whether the partner has authority, express, implied, or apparent,¹ just as the power of an agent to bind the principal in dealing with a third party depends upon whether the agent has express, implied, or apparent authority. Every partner is an agent of the partnership for the purpose of its business. 

§ 2. Liability of partnership; general rules.—A partner ship is bound by any act of a partner performed apparently for the carrying on of the partnership business in the usual way, unless the person dealing with a partner knows that he is acting without authority. For example, A and B are partners in the furniture business. A purchases 100 desks from X on credit, in the firm name, without consulting his partner.

The partnership is bound by this contract, since it was made 

¹ Hoskinson et al. v. Eliot et al., p. 365. 194

RELATIONS OF PARTNERS TO OTHERS 

195 apparently for the carrying on of the partnership business in the usual way. But if X knew that A was making the contract without the authority of B, the partnership would not be bound.

A partnership is not bound by an unauthorized act of a partner not performed apparently for the carrying on of the partnership business in the usual way. Thus, in the preceding illustration, the partnership would not be bound if A, without authority, purchased a touring car.

Of course, it is a question of fact in every case whether an act is performed "apparently for the carrying on of the partnership business in the usual way." The question depends upon such circumstances as the nature of the partnership business, its size, the kind of contract made, and so forth.

In a trading partnership, a partner is generally held to have implied power to borrow money on the credit of the firm and to bind the firm by executing negotiable paper; but not in a non-trading firm. The reason for this difference is that in trading firms the borrowing of money and the execution of negotiable paper are usual transactions. 

A partnership is not bound by acts of a partner whose authority has been restricted if the third party has knowledge of the restriction. § 3. Acts requiring authority of all partners.-A partner does not have power to do any one of the following unless authorized by all the partners: (1) Make an assignment for the benefit of creditors. (2) Dispose of the good will of the business. (3) Do anything that would make it impossible to carry on the ordinary business of the partnership. (4) Confess a judgment. (5) Submit a partnership claim or liability to arbitration. § 4. Admissions of and notice to partner. A partner's admission concerning partnership affairs, made within the 

2 Wagner v. Simmons & Co., p. 368.

PARTNERSHIPS 

scope of his authority, may be used in court as evidence against the partnership. 

Notice to a partner of any matter relating to partnership affairs is notice to the partnership. 

Knowledge of a partner who acts in a particular matter or who should reasonably communicate such knowledge to the acting partner is knowledge of the partnership, unless the partner has been guilty of or has consented to fraud. 

§ 5. Estoppel and ratification. As in the relationship of principal and agent, the partnership is bound by an unauthorized act of a partner if it is estopped to deny the absence of authority or if it has ratified the unauthorized act. The elements of estoppel and ratification have been discussed in the law of agency. 

§ 6. Liability for torts. A partnership is bound by the wrongful act or omission of any partner acting with authority or in the ordinary course of the business. Of course, the partner committing the tort is also liable, as is any person who commits a wrong; we have seen heretofore that agents, even minors, insane persons, and the like, are all liable for their torts. § 7. Nature of partner's liability. Upon contracts, all partners are liable jointly only. In consequence, a release of one partner is a release of all. All partners must be sued together, but after a creditor has obtained a joint judgment against all the partners, he may satisfy such judgment by levying execution against the individual property of any or all of them.

Upon torts, all partners are jointly and severally liable. 

This means that the partners may be sued separately or together; a release of one partner is a release of all. 

A partner will be jointly and severally liable upon a partnership contract if he enters into a separate obligation to perform it. 

§ 8. Liability of incoming partner. An incoming partner is liable upon all existing obligations of the partnership, except that the liability must be satisfied only out of partnership property.

CHAPTER V DISSOLUTION 

§ 1. In general.-Dissolution is the change in the relation of the partners, caused by any partner's ceasing to be a member of the firm. 

On dissolution, the partnership is not terminated, but continues until the winding up of partnership affairs is completed. 

§ 2. Causes of dissolution.-Dissolution is caused in any one of the following ways: (1) Without violation of partnership agreement, (a) By the expiration of the term or completion of the undertaking agreed upon; (b) By the will of any partner, if it is a partnership at will; (c) By mutual agreement; (d) By the expulsion of a partner as provided for in the agreement. (2) In violation of a partnership agreement, by the will of a partner at any time. (3) By an event rendering partnership business unlawful. (4) By the death of any partner. (5) By the bankruptcy of any partner or of the partnership. (6) By a decree of a court of equity, which will be given upon application of a partner whenever: (a) A partner is declared a lunatic in any judicial proceeding or is shown to be of unsound mind; (b) A partner becomes incapable in any way of performing his part of the partnership contract; (c) A partner is guilty of such conduct as tends to affect prejudicially the carrying on of the business; 198

DISSOLUTION 

199 (d) A partner willfully or persistently breaks the partnership agreement, or otherwise so conducts himself that it is not reasonably practicable to carry on the business in partnership with him; (e) The business of the partnership can be carried on only at a loss¹; (f) Other circumstances render a dissolution equi table. 

§ 3. Effect of dissolution on authority of partner.-Gen erally speaking, dissolution terminates all authority of a partner, except so far as may be necessary to wind up the partnership affairs or to complete unfinished transactions. 

However, a partner incurring a liability after dissolution, caused by the act, bankruptcy, or death of a partner, has a right of contribution from his partners if he did not know of such dissolution. § 4. Liability of partnership to third party upon new contract after dissolution.-A partnership is not liable to third parties upon a new contract after a dissolution caused by bankruptcy of a partner or by an event rendering the partnership business illegal.

But the partnership is liable upon a new contract after dissolution, caused in any other way, to a third party who has not received proper notice of the dissolution. In the case of former creditors of the firm, proper notice is actual notice or knowledge of the dissolution. In the case of parties knowing of the firm, but who have not extended credit, notice may be given by an advertisement in a newpaper in the community where the business was carried on. These rules also apply when a partner withdraws or retires from the business.2 

He should protect himself by giving proper notice to third parties that he has withdrawn. 

§ 5. Continuation of business after dissolution caused wrongfully. The partners, other than the one responsible, may continue the business after a dissolution caused wrong- 

¹ Seighortner v. Weissenborn, p. 368. 

2 Prentiss v. Sinclair, p. 369.

PARTNERSHIPS 

fully by one of the partners. In order to do this, they must pay the partner causing the dissolution the value of his interest in the partnership, not considering the good will, less damages for his wrong in causing the breach; and must indemnify him against present or future partnership liabilities.

When dissolution is not caused wrongfully, all partners have the right that the partnership property be applied to discharge its liabilities, and the surplus applied to pay in cash the net amount owing to the partners. 

§ 6. Effect of dissolution by death.-Upon dissolution by death, the surviving partner acquires title to the partnership property. The executor or administrator of the deceased partner does not have title; he has only the right to have the partnership affairs wound up and settlement made with the estate.

Firm creditors may sue either the surviving partner or the estate of the deceased partner. The estate is liable for partnership debts, subject to the prior payment of the separate debts of the deceased partner.

Quite commonly, a partnership transacts business after the death of a partner very much as it did before his death; the surviving partners settle with the executor or administrator of the deceased partner, and continue the business. 

In law, the partnership of the survivors is a new one, although creditors of the old firm are also creditors of the new firm. 

§ 7. Continuation of business after death or retirement of partner. When a partner dies or retires and the business is continued without settlement, the retired partner or representative of the deceased partner, unless otherwise agreed, may have the value of his interest ascertained and shall receive as an ordinary creditor an amount equal to the value of his share, with interest; or at his option, he may have, in lieu of interest, the profits attributable to the use of his right in the property of the dissolved partnership. 

In this event, creditors of the dissolved partnership have priority in claims against the partnership as against the separate creditors of the retired or deceased partner, or as

DISSOLUTION 

201 against the claims of the retired partner or representative of the deceased partner. § 8. Order for distributing firm assets. The liabilities of a partnership, in order of payment, rank as follows: (1) firm debts; (2) advances of partners; (3) capital of partners; (4) profits of partners. § 9. Marshaling assets of insolvent firm.-When both the firm and the partners are insolvent, a court of equity may acquire jurisdiction over the assets of both for the purpose of determining the order of payment to firm and individual creditors. This is called marshaling the assets. The rules are as follows: 

(1) Individual creditors have priority over firm creditors against individual assets. (a) Except that firm creditors share equally with individual creditors when there are no firm assets or no living solvent partner. (2) Firm creditors have priority over individual creditors against firm assets.
