CORPORATIONS CHAPTER I IN GENERAL. 

§ 1. Foreword.-Much of the practical law relating to corporations is statute law, and naturally is not uniform in the states. Unfortunately, there is no uniform act relating to corporations, comparable to the Sales Act and the Negotiable Instruments Law. An effort will be made, when the law is embodied in conflicting statutes, to present the law most widely in force in the various states. § 2. Definition. A corporation is a legal entity (person) created by or under the authority of the laws of a state or a nation, existing separate and distinct from the members who compose it.

The following attributes of a corporation are suggested by this definition: (1) A corporation is a person in the eyes of the law. In the language of Chief Justice Marshall, of the United States Supreme Court, it is "an artificial being, intangible, invisible, and existing only in contemplation of law." Whenever the word person is used in law, it is deemed to apply to corporations as well as to natural persons, unless the context clearly restricts the meaning to the latter. (2) A corporation is a franchise; that is to say, a special privilege is conferred by government upon the members who compose the corporation. The franchise is expressed or evidenced by a document known as a charter. (3) A corporation is legally separate and distinct from the members who compose it. It may sue and be sued by its 

¹ People's Pleasure Park Co. (Inc.) and Others v. Rohleder, p. 371. 205

CORPORATIONS 

members. It may enter into contracts with them. Property owned by the corporation is not owned by its members. 

The conception of a corporation as an entity distinct from its members is called the corporate fiction. The fiction is adopted to enable corporations to transact business more efficiently. In occasional cases, the courts disregard the fiction for the purpose of achieving justice and recognize the corporation and its members as being one and the same. For example, a debtor conveyed all his property, with the intent to defraud creditors, to a corporation in which he owned practically all the stock. The court, disregarding the fiction, held that the debtor and his corporation were substantially the same, and set aside the conveyance. § 3. Distinctions between a corporation and a partnership. The principal distinctions between a corporation and a partnership are as follows: (1) A corporation is created by the state; a partnership is created merely by an agreement between the parties. (2) A corporation has only those powers conferred upon it by the state; a partnership has unlimited powers. (3) A corporation is a legal entity-a person; a partnership is a group of persons for most purposes a relationship. (4) A corporation's existence is perpetual unless expressly limited; a partnership's existence may be terminated by such events as the death of a partner, the express will of a partner, and so forth. (5) The members of a corporation are not liable for its debts, in the absence of statute; the members of a partnership are personally liable for its debts. (6) A corporation is managed by its duly appointed officers and agents; a partnership is managed, ordinarily, by all the partners. (7) A corporation is subject to strict supervision of the state, as the requirement that it file annually statements of its condition; a partnership is not subject to state supervision, generally speaking. (8) A member of a corporation may transfer his interest in it with little difficulty, since it is usually represented by a

IN GENERAL 

207 transferable certificate of stock. A member of a partnership is likely to experience more difficulty in transferring his interest because of the personal liability for firm debts incurred by a transferee of a partner. 

§ 4. Advantages and disadvantages of incorporation.— 

From the foregoing discussion and the sections that follow, it appears that the principal advantages of a corporation as contrasted with a partnership or a single proprietorship, are the following: (1) status of legal entity, distinct from its members; (2) limited liability of its members; (3) perpetual existence; (4) transferability of interests of its members; (5) larger capital, as a result of the division of ownership into as many shares as are desired; (6) management by duly appointed officers and agents.

The principal disadvantages of a corporation are the following: (1) limitation of its powers to those conferred by law; (2) strict supervision by the state, entailing reports of corporate affairs; (3) fees of state for incorporation and necessity of filing reports and papers; (4) necessity of conducting meetings and performing corporate acts in compliance with by-laws and state statutes.

Types of Corporations 

§ 5. Classification as to purpose.-Corporations may be broadly classified as follows:

Public corporations. These are created for governmental purposes. They are in effect agents of the state in the administration of civil government, generally within a particular subdivision of the state, and are usually vested with subordinate and local powers of legislation. Examples of public corporations are counties, cities, towns, and school districts. 

Private corporations. These are created by private individuals for private purposes, as distinguished from governmental purposes. In this class is the wide variety of types of corporations not organized for purposes of government. The term "quasi public" is sometimes applied to private corporations, such as railroads, electric light and gas companies, and

CORPORATIONS 

the like, which contribute to the comfort, convenience, or welfare of the general public. Such corporations are more correctly called public service corporations. Private corporations may be divided into the following types: (1) Stock corporations. In these, membership is represented by ownership of shares of stock. Such corporations are organized for the purpose of financial profit. Examples of stock corporations are the 

United States Steel Corporation, Montgomery Ward 

& Co. This text primarily treats of the law relating to corporations of this class. (2) Non-stock corporations. In these, membership is not regulated by ownership of shares of stock, but by compliance with the conditions set forth in the by-laws. The conditions for membership vary widely, as would be expected. Non-stock corporations are organized for such purposes as the following: charity, as a hospital; education, as a college; pleasure or fellowship, as a school fraternity; mutual assistance, as mutual benefit societies; and so forth. 

Certain professional men, such as doctors and lawyers, are not allowed to incorporate, for the reason that it is contrary to public policy for corporations to conduct their practices. § 6. De jure and de facto corporations.-A de jure (“of right") corporation is one organized in compliance with law. 

This is the usual type of corporation. 

A de facto ("in fact") corporation is one organized in good faith, operating as a corporation, but without full compliance with the law. For example, let us suppose a state statute requires that incorporators shall state in organization papers the principal place of business of the corporation. A, B, and 

C organize a corporation in good faith under this statute, but omit to specify the principal place of business, and the state through oversight issues a charter to the corporation. The business functions as a corporation, and is called a de facto corporation.

IN GENERAL 

209 The legality of a de facto corporation may be questioned only by the state, which may possibly dissolve it because of its failure to comply with the law. But no one else may challenge the defects in the organization of a de facto corporation-neither the corporation itself nor third parties dealing with it. § 7. Corporations sole and aggregate.—A corporation sole is one composed of a single member and his successors in office. It is created by some governments to give a legal capacity to a person, as that of perpetuity, which he could not enjoy as a natural person. The sovereign of England is an example of a corporation sole. There have been few instances of corporations sole in this country. 

A corporation aggregate is one which is or may be composed of more than one member, and is almost invariably the type of corporation created in the various states. 

A corporation aggregate does not become a corporation sole because all the shares of stock become vested in one person. Very commonly, one person incorporates, satisfying statutory requirements as to the number of incorporators by having relatives, employees, or friends act as "dummy' incorporators, and issuing to them a nominal number of shares of stock. After incorporation, the real incorporator sometimes acquires the few shares held by the "dummies,” but this does not convert the corporation into a corporation sole. § 8. Domestic and foreign corporations. A domestic corporation is one organized in the state with reference to which one is speaking. A foreign corporation is one organized under the laws of another state or government. For example, in Kentucky, a domestic corporation would be one organized under the laws of Kentucky; whereas a corporation organized in Michigan would be a foreign corporation in Kentucky.

A corporation doing business in another state is generally required to appoint a representative in that state, upon whom service can be made; to file a copy of its charter and by-laws and a certificate setting forth such information as the location

CORPORATIONS 

of the principal office, the names and addresses of its officers, the date of its annual meeting, the amount and kind of its capital stock. Drastic penalties are imposed in many states for the failure of a foreign corporation doing business there to comply with these requirements. "Doing business" requires something more than isolated transactions or the sending of traveling salesmen who solicit orders which are filled and sent from the home office. Generally, for a corporation to be held to be doing business, it must at least have a branch office in the state.

Not uncommonly, persons desirous of incorporating will select as the state of incorporation the one having the most favorable laws for organization, then transact business in other states as a foreign corporation. The laws of Delaware and New Jersey are popularly regarded as favorable for incorporation.

Formation of Corporation § 9. Organization under general laws.-The states have general corporation laws prescribing the requirements with which persons forming corporations must comply. Usually, these requirements will vary not only between the states, but also within a state, depending upon the type of corporation to be formed. Thus, the requirements for incorporating a business corporation might differ from those for incorporating a college fraternity.

Prior to the general corporation laws, persons desiring to incorporate merely petitioned the state legislature for the enactment of a special law creating the corporation. 

§ 10. Procedure for incorporation. The requirements and procedure for incorporation vary so widely, depending upon the type of corporation to be organized and the laws of the state of organization, that it is impossible in this text to do more than to outline some of the salient features of incorporation. These are as follows: (1) Preparation of application for a charter. The application may consist of one or more papers known by such names

IN GENERAL 

211 as agreement of association, articles of organization, and the like. The application must be executed by at least the required number of incorporators. It must contain such information as the name of the corporation, the location of its principal office, the objects of the corporation, a detailed account of the kinds of capital stock to be issued, the names and residences of the incorporators, the names of subscribers to the capital stock, a description of the consideration received by the corporation for stock issued at once, how much stock is to be issued at once, and so forth. The organization papers must comply in all respects, both as to form and contents, with the statute under which the corporation is to be formed, as must also the incorporators with respect to number, capacity, residence, and so forth. (2) The application, accompanied by payment of the fee for incorporation, is usually filed with the secretary of state. (3) A charter is delivered to the incorporators after the papers constituting the application for incorporation have been examined and approved. 

§ 11. By-laws.-By-laws are the rules enacted by a cor poration for the purpose of regulating its affairs. In the case of cities, these regulations are called ordinances. 

By-laws are drawn by the members of the corporation, usually at the organization meeting. They may be altered, amended, or repealed from time to time by the body having the power to enact them, usually the stockholders, but by no one else unless this power has been specially delegated. 

Thus, the directors of a corporation would have no power to alter by-laws unless the stockholders had delegated to them the power to do so.

The by-laws correspond roughly to the statutes of a legislature; the charter, to the constitution of a state. 

By-laws usually relate to such matters as stock certificates, the fiscal year, officers and their election, powers and duties of officers, contracts of the corporation, stockholders' meetings, directors' meetings, alteration of by-laws, and so forth. 

The following are examples of some of the provisions which might be found in by-laws:

CORPORATIONS 

(1) The fiscal year of the corporation shall begin on the first day of January in each year and end upon the last day of December next succeeding. (2) The officers of the corporation shall be a president, a treasurer, a clerk, and a board of not less than three nor more than seven directors. (3) All bonds, deeds, and contracts of the corporation shall be executed by the president and the treasurer. (4) Notice of any annual or special meeting of the stockholders shall be given by the clerk at least seven days before such meeting. (5) These by-laws, or any of them, may be altered, amended, added to, or repealed, by vote of a majority of the stock outstanding and entitled to vote, notice of the proposed amendment having been given in the call of the meeting. § 12. Effect of by-laws.-By-laws are binding upon the stockholders and officers of a corporation so long as they are not contrary to the charter or law, do not violate public policy, and are reasonable.

Third persons dealing with a corporation are not bound by by-laws the provisions of which they have no knowledge.2 

They may rely upon the apparent authority of officers and agents of corporations, notwithstanding the possibility that in a particular case the by-laws may restrict the apparent authority. § 13. Promoters.-A promoter is one who performs the duties incidental to the organizing of a corporation and the procuring of subscriptions for its stock. 

A promoter occupies a fiduciary relationship to subscribers and to the contemplated corporation. This relationship imposes upon him the duty of full disclosure of all material facts, and of utmost good faith. For example, a promoter may not sell to the corporation his own property under the guise that he is selling it as agent for another. Also, he may not make a secret profit by representing to the corporation that the property which he is selling to the corporation cost 

2 Hagerstown Brewing Co. v. Gates, p. 373,

IN GENERAL 

213 more than the price paid by him. However, he may make a profit on his contract with the corporation if he discloses all material facts relating to the contract and obtains the consent of the members of the corporation. 

§ 14. Liability upon contracts of promoters.-A promoter is personally liable upon all contracts entered into by him in his own name prior to incorporation. But if he enters into a contract on the credit of the future corporation he is not personally liable. It is generally a question of fact whether or not the promoter has made himself a party to the contract. 

A corporation is not liable upon contracts made in its name prior to incorporation. The rule has been stated as follows: A corporation comes into the world "unburdened by prenatal obligations."

The reason the corporation cannot be held liable upon the theory that the promoter was acting as its agent is that the corporation was not in existence when the contract was made, and one may not act as agent for a non-existing principal. 

Nor will ratification by the corporation bind it upon contracts made before its formation. It is an elementary principle of the law of agency that a necessary condition to ratification is that the principal must be in existence at the time the act of the alleged agent is performed.

However, a corporation adopting a contract entered into before its organization is liable upon it. By adopting the contract, the corporation makes itself a party to it. The adoption may be express, as by vote of the stockholders, or it may be implied, as when a corporation receives the benefits of a contract made before its organization. Thus, a corporation receiving and using goods purchased for it before its formation has been held bound upon the contract by adoption. § 15. Subscription to stock of corporation to be formed.— 

Ordinarily, a subscriber may withdraw any time before acceptance of his subscription to stock of a corporation to be formed. Since the corporation is not in existence, the subscription, like any other offer, is merely a continuing offer which may be revoked before acceptance. When the cor-

CORPORATIONS 

poration is formed and accepts the subscription, a binding contract is created.

However, a subscription may be so worded that it is binding upon the subscriber without the acceptance of the corporation. For illustration, the subscription may state that the promise of the subscriber is made in consideration of the promises of other subscribers to purchase stock.

A subscription to stock of an existing corporation creates a contract either if it is accepted by the corporation or if the subscription itself is an acceptance of an offer previously made by the corporation.

CHAPTER II  Stocks and Bonds 

§ 1. In general.-Membership in stock corporations, we have already seen, is acquired by ownership of one or more shares of its capital stock. These shares may be purchased by subscription from the corporation or by transfer from the owner. 

§ 2. Distinction between capital stock and capital.—Capi tal stock is the amount of capital a corporation is authorized by law to receive for its stock from subscribers for purposes of the corporation. Thus, a corporation with a capital stock of $10,000 is authorized to receive from stockholders that amount with which to do business. The capital stock of a corporation remains invariable unless changed by the corporation with legislative authority. 

The capital of a corporation consists of its net assets; that is to say, the property actually owned by the corporation. 

The capital of a corporation fluctuates, since its assets may be increased by surplus profits or may be diminished by losses. 

For example, a corporation has a capital stock of $20,000, which is paid in full by the subscribers. The first year the corporation makes a profit of $5,000. The capital stock remains $20,000, but the capital is now $25,000. 

The authorized capital stock may consist of issued and unissued shares, the issued stock representing those shares which have been issued and are outstanding, including treasury stock; and the unissued stock representing those shares which the corporation has authority to issue but has not as yet done so. § 3. Shares and certificates of stock.—A share of stock is a definite portion of the capital stock of a corporation. It represents simply a proportional interest in the concern. 215

CORPORATIONS 

A share of stock is intangible personal property. Sales of stock are within the Statute of Frauds if the purchase price of the stock exceeds the amount-$500 in most states-stated in that part of the statute which relates to sales of personal property. Consequently, it is prudent to reduce to writing agreements to purchase stock.

A certificate of stock is an instrument of the corporation, under seal, certifying that the person therein named is entitled to a certain number of shares. § 4. Corporate bonds.-A corporate bond is an instrument, under seal, in which the corporation promises to pay to another a designated sum of money, with interest. 

The number of bondholders of a corporation are usually so large that when bonds are secured by a mortgage upon corporate property, the bondholders are incapable of acting individually with reference to taking the mortgage and foreclosing it in event of default. Consequently, a trustee is selected to act for the bondholders with reference to the mortgage. The corporation and the trustee execute an instrument known as a trust deed or trust indenture, in which the corporation transfers the property to a trustee upon certain conditions. The trust deed usually recites that the transfer is made as security for the payment of the bonds; gives the trustee power to sell the property, upon default, in payment of the bonds, and to apply the net proceeds towards payment of the amount due upon the bonds; and provides that the surplus is to be turned over to the corporation. § 5. Distinctions between shares and bonds. A share of stock represents part ownership of a corporation, whereas a bond evidences a debt of the corporation. A stockholder is not entitled to receive anything from the corporation unless a profit is made and dividends are declared; a bondholder is entitled to the payment of principal and interest, at maturity, irrespective of whether the corporation has made a profit. A stockholder generally has the right to vote; a bondholder has no right to vote. There are other distinctions between shares of stock and bonds, but those stated are the most important.

Kinds of Stock § 6. Common and preferred stock. Common stock is stock which has no preference over any other class of stock; preferred stock is stock having one or more preferences over common stock. In other words, if a corporation has two classes of stock, one of which has certain priorities not possessed by the other, the former will be called preferred stock and the latter common stock. If there is only one class of stock, it is called common stock, "common" signifying in this connection that all holders enjoy, pro rata, equal rights, without priorities among themselves.

A holder of preferred stock is in no sense a creditor of the corporation. In some respects, his position may be less advantageous than that of a holder of common stock, since very often preferred stock may not carry the power to vote and may be retirable by the corporation by contract. § 7. Common preferences of preferred stock. The preferences of preferred stock are generally determined by the incorporators when the corporation is organized, and must be recited in the proper corporation papers. Usually, they are also set forth in the preferred stock certificate so that the holder thereof may know the priorities his stock possesses. 

Preferences commonly possessed or conferred upon preferred stock are as follows: 

(1) Preference as to dividends. This means that a dividend at a designated rate, such as 6 per cent, shall be paid upon the preferred stock prior to the declaration of a dividend upon the common stock. Preferred stock always has this preference in the absence of provision to the contrary. (2) Cumulative as to dividends. This means that if the dividends due in any year upon the preferred stock are not declared and paid, the arrearage must be declared and paid from earnings of subsequent years. Preferred stock is deemed cumulative in the absence of a provision stipulating whether it is cumulative or non-cumulative. (3) Participating with common stock in remaining dividend.

This usually means that if the stipulated dividend is declared

CORPORATIONS 

upon the preferred stock and an equal amount is declared on the common stock, the preferred stock shares equally with the common stock in any further distribution of profits. 

Thus, if a dividend of 6 per cent is declared upon 6 per cent participating preferred stock and a dividend of 6 per cent upon the common stock, both classes would share equally any further dividend declared. Preferred stock is deemed participating in the absence of provision stipulating whether it is participating or non-participating, or expressly limiting the dividend to a specified rate. (4) Preference as to assets upon dissolution. This means that upon dissolution, holders of preferred stock are entitled to receive assets equal to the par value of their shares, before the holders cf common stock receive anything. If any assets remain after both classes of stock have received the par value of the shares, both classes share in the excess. Preferred stock is not deemed preferred as to assets in the absence of a provision so stipulating. § 8. Stock with and without par value.-Par value stock is stock to the shares of which a monetary value is assigned at the time of issuance. For example, a corporation may be authorized to issue 1,000 shares of common stock with a par value of $100 a share.

Stock without par value, usually called no par stock, is stock to whose shares no monetary value is assigned, the certificates merely stating the proportionate interest thereby represented. Only in a small number of states are corporations permitted to issue stock without par value. The value of no par stock is ascertained at any time by its market value.

The advantage of stock without par value is that the public purchasing such stock is not deceived as to the worth of the stock by a statement of monetary value. No value being assigned, a prospective purchaser is more apt to investigate the stock for the purpose of determining its real value. 

The disadvantage of stock without par value is that a corporation may issue such stock for any kind of consideration, and the purchaser is given no assurance from the stock

itself as to how much consideration was received. In the case of stock with par value, there is some assurance that the corporation had at one time assets equal to the par value of the shares, since a corporation selling par value stock must generally receive consideration of a value equal to the par value of the shares. 

§ 9. Treasury stock.-Treasury stock is stock which has been issued by a corporation for value and reacquired by the corporation as a gift or by purchase. While in the possession of the corporation, treasury stock carries no voting power, nor does it participate in dividends. § 10. Payment for stock.-Generally, stock may be paid. for in cash, property, services, or expenses. A corporation may not, as a general rule, lawfully issue stock without receiving in return payment therefor in money or money's worth, or a valid obligation to pay. 

The consideration received by a corporation for the issuance of par value stock must in most states be equal in value to the par value of the shares. For example, a corporation may not issue ten shares of its stock of a par value of $100 for an automobile worth $200. Various methods are employed in the states for determining whether property received by a corporation is equal to the par value of the stock that is issued. The two principal methods are as follows: 

True value rule. By this rule, the purchaser of par value stock must pay the par value thereof in money or money's worth. Whenever by fraud, accident, or mistake this has not been done, the stock is deemed unpaid to the full extent of the difference and the holders are liable to creditors for this difference, even though the directors acted in good faith in making the valuation. This rule is in force in about seven states.

Good faith rule. By this rule, the valuation made in good faith, and not the true value of the property or services, determines whether the stock is deemed fully paid as against creditors. If the directors or the state commission making the valuation has acted in good faith and without actual

CORPORATIONS 

fraud or intentional overvaluation, the stock is deemed fully paid for. This rule is in force in about twenty-four states. § 11. Watered stock.-Watered stock is stock which has been issued as fully paid and non-assessable, when, actually, the full par value has not been paid to the corporation. Stock may be watered, owing to various causes: A corporation may have issued a share of a certain par value at a discount—that is, upon payment of only a part of the par value; or a corporation may have issued stock the par value of which exceeded the fair value of property given in payment. Again, a corporation may have issued par value stock as a bonus for the sale of some other stock. In all these cases, the stock is said to be watered; that is, the par value of the stock exceeds the fair value of the assets which it represents. 

Corporations may issue stock for which payment is to be made in cash installments; but such stocks would not be watered stock unless the full price agreed upon is less than the par value of the stock. § 12. Rights of creditors when stock is watered or not fully paid for.-Creditors of an insolvent corporation may compel payment of the balance due from holders of watered or partly paid-for stock. As to stock only partly paid for, the claim of the corporation for the balance of the price is an asset of the corporation which creditors should be allowed to reach and apply in payment of corporate debts. As to watered stock, the right of creditors to compel payment of the full par value has been based by the courts upon different theories. Some courts say that since the purchase of watered stock is illegal, it is only proper that the payment should be treated as a payment on account and the stockholder should be held liable at the request of creditors to pay the balance. 

The "trust-fund doctrine" of some courts is that the capital stock of a corporation is a trust fund for the benefit of creditors, giving them the right to enforce full payment for the capital stock. Still another theory for giving creditors a 3 

1 Harrison v. Armour, p. 374. 

2 Gates v. Tippecanoe Stone Co. et al., p. 375. 

Upton, Assignee v. Tribilcock, p. 376.

right to recover from holders of watered stock is the "holdingout" theory that the corporation, in issuing stock as fully paid when it is not fully paid, has made a misrepresentation which has injured its creditors. 

A transferee for value without notice of watered stock or stock not fully paid for is not liable to creditors of the corporation; but a transferee with knowledge of the facts, or one who has not given value for the stock, is so liable. § 13. Payment on call.-A call is an assessment on shares of stock for unpaid installments of the subscription price. Stock may be issued upon an agreement that the price, or installments of it, shall not become due until a call is made. 

The call is made by the directors of the corporation. 

§ 14. Method of transferring stock. The steps in the transferring of stock are ordinarily the following: (1) The stockholder indorses his name in blank upon a form on the back of the certificate; (2) he delivers the certificate so indorsed to the transferee; (3) the transferee delivers the certificate to the corporation; (4) the corporation cancels the certificate surrendered and issues a new one, specifying the name of the transferee as owner.

Once a stock certificate is indorsed in blank, it may be transferred from person to person merely by delivery, like bearer negotiable paper.

As between transferor and transferee, a transfer is complete and title passes upon delivery of the certificate properly indorsed. But to secure rights as a stockholder, the transferee must have the corporation record the transfer upon its books. Otherwise, he is not entitled to receive any notices of meetings and the dividends that are declared upon his stock. 

Sometimes a transferor, delivering a certificate, executes on a separate piece of paper, an assignment and power of attorney to record the transfer, instead of indorsing the form on the back of the stock certificate. This method is convenient for transferring a stock certificate as collateral security, because upon payment of the loan the certificate may be returned to its owner in its original form.

CORPORATIONS The Uniform Stock Transfer Act, regulating the transfer of stock, is law in many states. The principles above mentioned are found in this Act. 

§ 15. Liability of transferee to corporation.-A transferee of stock is liable to the corporation for an unpaid subscription, unless he relies in good faith upon a recital on the certificate that the stock has been fully paid for. In this latter event, the corporation would be estopped to claim that the stock had not been fully paid for. Dividends § 16. In general.—A dividend is a fund set apart by a corporation, from profits, to be distributed to stockholders. 

Until a dividend is declared, a stockholder is not entitled to share in the profits of the corporation. 

Dividends may be declared only out of net profits. In determining whether there are net profits, the directors must make provisions for current expenses, indebtedness, and depreciation. A dividend declared from capital stock is illegal, and creditors may recover the amount thereof from stockholders. After directors have duly declared a dividend payable at a future time, they may rescind their vote before the dividend becomes payable, provided that they have not made the declaration public and have not set aside a fund for payment of the dividend.

When a dividend has been declared and is due, it is the absolute property of stockholders and they may sue to recover it. § 17. Kinds of dividends.-Dividends may be classified as follows: 

Cash dividends. These are the usual kind. Commonly, the amount of the dividend is a certain per cent of the par value of the stock. 

Scrip dividends. These are paid in scrip or in certificates entitling stockholders to the right therein recited sometimes the right to receive cash at a future date, sometimes the right to convert the certificate into stock or bonds of the corporation. Commonly, a scrip dividend is issued to anticipate the conversion into cash of property representing profits.

Stock dividends. These are dividends paid in new or unissued stock of a corporation, the stock representing accumulated profits over and above the capital stock. This type of dividend is commonly declared by corporations which desire to use their earnings and profits for expansion of the business rather than for cash dividends. In many states, all stock dividends are treated as principal and all cash distributions as income, where the stock is held in trust. 

Property dividends. A property dividend is one consisting of specific property of a corporation, such as desks distributed to its stockholders by a corporation manufacturing desks. 

§ 18. Declaration of dividends. The declaration of divi dends is within the discretion of the board of directors. The discretion of the directors is wide and the courts will not generally interfere with their decision unless they are guilty of fraud, neglect of duty, or abuse of discretionary powers.

The discretion of the directors is not so wide in the declaration of dividends upon preferred stock. Such dividends should be declared when there are net profits available to pay them. $ 19. Persons entitled to dividends.-Persons whose names are carried on the corporation's books as stockholders at the time of declaration are entitled to a dividend declared, irrespective of when the dividend is payable. A transferee who becomes such after the declaration is not entitled to a dividend, even though it is paid after the transfer has been effected. Of course, this rule is subject to the agreement of the parties and to the rules of the stock exchange in which a sale is made.

If the directors specify a group of stockholders to whom a dividend shall be paid, such as "stockholders of record on 

June 15," these persons will be entitled to the dividend, irrespective of a transfer before the time of payment.

CHAPTER III STOCKHOLDERS, DIRECTORS, AND EXECUTIVE OFFICERS 

Stockholders 

§ 1. In general. Stockholders have no part in the management of a corporation. The management is intrusted to the board of directors and such other officers and agents as the corporation has authority by law to appoint. Only to the extent that stockholders vote at stockholders' meetings, electing officers and voting upon fundamental matters affecting the corporation, do they influence and control management of a corporation.

Such fundamental matters as increasing or decreasing the capital stock, selling all the property of a corporation, and amending the by-laws must be submitted to the stockholders for consideration. The directors have no power to decide such questions. § 2. Right to dividends.—A stockholder has a right to receive a dividend declared upon his stock by the directors. 

This point was discussed more fully under the subject of 

Dividends, Chapter II, Section 16. 

A stockholder also has the right to receive his proportional share of the proceeds of capital on termination of the corporation, after payment of the debts of the corporation. § 3. Right to inspect books.-A stockholder usually has the right to inspect corporate books and records at a reasonable time and place. But in doing so, he may not impede the conduct of corporate business. § 4. Right to attend meetings and to vote.-Generally a stockholder has the right to attend all meetings of the stockholders and to cast his vote in the determination of all questions submitted to the meeting. Holders of preferred 226

STOCKHOLDERS 

227 stock have the right to vote unless this right is restricted at the time of issuance of the stock. 

Business commonly transacted at stockholders' meetings is the election of directors and of any other officers who, under the by-laws, are to be elected by the stockholders; the hearing of reports of officers; the confirming and ratifying of the acts of officers; the voting upon increasing or decreasing capital stock; the amending of the by-laws or organization papers; the authorizing of the officers to perform certain acts; and any other important matters affecting the welfare of the corporation. Even matters which lie within the province of the directors and officers, such as important contracts, are commonly submitted to the stockholders for authorization or ratification so that there may be assurance of their approval. § 5. Meetings of stockholders. The by-laws usually specify in detail as to the notice, the place, the kind, and the time of stockholders' meetings. A meeting which is not called and held in accordance with by-laws is invalid and all business transacted at such a meeting is without legal effect.

Generally, by-laws provide for the holding of an annual meeting at which the directors and certain other officers are elected and any other necessary business is transacted. 

Special meetings may be called from time to time by the persons and in the manner specified in the by-laws. 

Notices of all meetings must be given to stockholders as directed in the by-laws, and the notice must set forth the business to be transacted at the meeting. Notice will be dispensed with if it is waived by a stockholder in the manner provided in the by-laws. 

A stockholder may attend a meeting personally, or he may be represented by an authorized agent, known as a proxy, who may vote in his place. The instrument appointing the agent is also known as a proxy.

Business cannot be transacted unless a quorum is present. 

The by-laws or statutes usually provide how much stock shall constitute a quorum. Usually, a majority of the stock constitutes a quorum.

CORPORATIONS 

The minutes of the meeting are the record of the business transacted, kept by the clerk or other proper officer. 

§ 6. Voting at stockholders' meetings.-Generally, a stockholder is entitled to cast as many votes as the number of shares he owns.

Cumulative voting in elections is authorized by the statutes of some states and by some by-laws. Under this plan, a stockholder may cast one vote for each of his shares for each director to be elected, or he may cast all his votes for one director. Thus, if five directors are to be elected and a stockholder owns fifteen shares, he may cast fifteen ballots for each director, or seventy-five ballots for one director. The object of cumulative voting is to enable a minority to secure representation upon the board of directors. If the minority stockholders are sufficiently numerous and cast all their ballots for certain directors, they are sure to secure representation. 

A voting trust is an agreement whereby some or all of the stockholders transfer their stock to a person, known as a trustee, for the purpose of voting the stock, the stock to be retransferred upon demand or at the expiration of a certain period. The object of a voting trust is to enable the stockholders to control the corporation by having their ballots cast in concert. 

§ 7. Right to preference in sale of additional capital stock. When the stockholders have voted, and the state has given its permission to, an increase in capital stock, the stockholders have first choice to subscribe pro rata to the additional shares. Only if stockholders do not exercise this right may the corporation sell the shares to persons who are not stockholders. § 8. Right to prevent ultra vires acts.-A stockholder may prevent the corporation or its officers from committing ultra vires acts. Any act committed by a corporation beyond the power given to it in its charter is said to be an ultra vires act. The remedy of a stockholder in such cases is first to protest to the proper officers of the corporation, and then, if 

¹ Jones v. Morrison, p. 377.

DIRECTORS 

229 the result is ineffective, to petition a court of equity to enjoin the commission of the unauthorized acts. 

§ 9. Right to enforce claims of the corporation.-Gen erally, a stockholder may not himself enforce a claim of the corporation, because the corporation is an entity distinct from its stockholders. This rule is applied even though a stockholder may own a substantial amount of stock in a corporation and is injured by a decline in the value of his shares, because of the failure of the corporation to enforce its claim. 

However, when a stockholder has requested proper officers to enforce a claim of the corporation and they have unreasonably refused or neglected to act, the stockholder himself may bring a suit in equity against the obligor and against the corporation. In this case, the corporation, although it is a defendant in name, will recover as if it were the plaintiff, if the suit is successful. 

§ 10. Statutory liability of stockholders to creditors.- 

By statute in many states, stockholders of certain corporations, such as insurance companies, banks, and trust companies, are liable to creditors for a sum in addition to the par value of their shares. This is referred to as the double liability of certain stockholders. Directors § 11. In general. The directors are charged with the management of a corporation. In effect, they constitute a committee selected by the stockholders for the purpose of attending to the details of corporate management. 

The by-laws usually determine such matters as the number of directors, their term of office, whether or not they must be stockholders, the kinds of notices to be sent to stockholders and the time for sending these notices, the manner of holding meetings, the powers of the directors, how many shall constitute a quorum for the transaction of business, and so forth. 

Directors must act as a board and not individually. The business of the board is recorded in its minutes, kept by the clerk.

CORPORATIONS 

Directors may not delegate to others their discretionary duties, except that in some states they are empowered by statute to elect from their number an executive committee to whom they may delegate the management of the current and ordinary business of the corporation. A director may not be represented by proxy at a meeting of the directors. 

§ 12. Powers of board of directors. The board of direc tors has power to enter into contracts and to perform acts usually incidental to the management of corporations. Thus, the directors may employ agents, borrow money for corporate purposes, execute negotiable paper, give mortgages upon corporate property, execute leases, sell corporate property, and so forth.

Directors, however, may not perform ultra vires acts; nor may they increase or reduce capital stock, make or amend the by-laws unless authorized to do so, impose restrictions upon the capital stock, or sell the business and good will of the corporation. 

§ 13. Fiduciary position of directors.-The directors occupy a fiduciary relationship to the corporation and stockholders. This relationship prevents directors from making a secret profit in transactions relating to the corporation. For example, if X promises to pay D, a director of a corporation, $1,000 to vote in favor of a contract X desires to have the corporation enter into, D is not entitled to receive this fee.

However, directors may enter into contracts with the corporation even though they benefit personally, if the contracts are fair and there is full disclosure of all material facts. 

For example, D, a director, could sell to the corporation a parcel of land worth $1,000 for a price of $1,000, upon which he is making a profit of $100, if the purchase is advantageous to the corporation and D discloses the profit he is making. 

§ 14. Liability of directors to corporation.-A director is not liable to the corporation for damage occasioned in the performance of his duties so long as he acts reasonably and in good faith. This is generally the test applied in determining his liability, although some states require that he act only in

EXECUTIVE OFFICERS 

231 good faith. For any losses caused while acting unreasonably, willfully, or in bad faith, a director is liable to the corporation.2 

§ 15. Liability of directors to third persons. By statute, directors performing certain improper acts are liable to third persons injured thereby. Thus, directors, except those voting contra, may be liable to creditors to the extent of a dividend, the payment of which would render the corporation insolvent or bankrupt. Directors making or assenting to a loan to stockholders or to themselves may be liable to creditors injured thereby. Directors signing false reports as to the condition of the corporation, which they knew or reasonably ought to have known to be false, may be liable to persons extending credit in reliance upon said reports. Directors may be liable if stock is issued in violation of law. 

The foregoing are liabilities very commonly imposed upon directors, as well as upon other officers of the corporation; but the statutes of a particular state must be consulted to ascertain accurately the law of that state relating to liabilities of directors and officers.

Executive Officers 

§ 16. In general. The ordinary executive officers of a corporation are a president, a treasurer, and a clerk. The incorporators, if they desire, may provide in the by-laws for such additional officers as one or more vice presidents, an assistant treasurer, a secretary, a chairman of the board, a general manager, and so forth.

The term of office of executive officers, as well as of the directors, is usually one year, or until successors are elected. 

The statutes and by-laws prescribe whether the officers, or certain of them, shall be elected by the stockholders or by the directors. 

§ 17. Powers of executive officers. The powers and duties of executive officers are generally described in detail in the by-laws.

The power of an officer to bind the corporation is governed largely by the law of principal and agent. Irrespective of 

2 Hun v. Cary, p. 379.

CORPORATIONS 

whether an officer has express authority in the by-laws or otherwise to act for the corporation, the corporation will be bound if the officer acts with implied or apparent authority. 

Whether an officer has implied or apparent authority depends upon all the facts of the particular case: the customary duties of such officer, the kind of contract, the importance of the undertaking, the extent of knowledge of the third person as to the facts, and so forth.

CHAPTER IV POWERS OF A CORPORATION 

§ 1. In general. Since a corporation is a creature of the state, it has only those powers conferred upon it by the state. 

Acts or contracts of a corporation in excess of these powers are said to be ultra vires.

The powers of a corporation may be divided into three classes: (1) express powers in the charter; (2) implied powers from the charter; (3) powers incidental to or conferred expressly upon all corporations. 

§ 2. Express powers in charter. The express powers of a particular corporation are those that are expressly enumerated in the charter of the corporation. For example, the charter of a corporation organized to deal in automobiles might contain the following powers:

To manufacture, purchase, sell, or in any other way to deal in automobiles and motors of all kinds whether operated by steam, electricity, gasoline, or any other form of power, and any and all parts thereof, and all appliances and accessories that enter into the construction of or are necessary for the use and operation of automobiles and motors, and generally to carry on any business incidental to the purposes stated. 

The incorporators generally set forth in the organization papers the powers they desire to have conferred upon the corporation. If these powers meet with the approval of the state, the secretary of state merely writes them into the charter which is issued to the corporation. 

§ 3. Implied powers from charter.—The implied powers from the charter consist of powers to do what is reasonably necessary and convenient in order to carry out the express powers enumerated in the charter.¹ Thus, the powers of a 

1 Brown and Another v. Winnisimmet Company, p. 381. 234

POWERS OF A CORPORATION 

235 corporation organized to deal in automobiles, set forth in the preceding section, do not include the powers to employ salesmen to sell cars and to send advertising matter through the mail to promote sales. But the corporation would have these powers impliedly, for they are reasonably necessary and convenient in order to carry out the express power to sell automobiles. § 4. Powers incidental to or expressly conferred upon all corporations. Certain powers have long been regarded as incidental to corporate existence. These powers are usually enumerated in the corporation laws of the states; but whether or not so enumerated, corporations are generally held to possess them. The following list of such powers may vary somewhat in the states: (1) To have perpetual succession unless the period of duration is limited in the charter. (2) To sue and be sued in its corporate name. (3) To have capital stock. (4) To have a seal. (5) To elect necessary officers, fix their compensation, and define their duties. (6) To hold, purchase, convey, mortgage, or lease real or personal property for purposes of the corporation. (7) To make contracts, incur liabilities, and borrow money. (8) To make by-laws not inconsistent with state laws. (9) To be dissolved. 

§ 5. Particular powers considered.—A corporation does not have implied power to enter into a contract of partnership, because corporations are not bound by any acts except those of their duly authorized officers and agents. Also, corporations may not enter into combinations if the object is to carry on an unauthorized business.

By the weight of authority, a corporation cannot take and hold stock in another corporation unless the power has been conferred expressly in the charter or by statute, or unless it is necessarily implied from its express powers. In any state, a corporation does not have this power if the object of acquiring

CORPORATIONS 

the stock is that of engaging in an unauthorized or an illegal business. The law of a particular state must be examined in connection with this power. 

The weight of authority is that a corporation may in good faith and for fair consideration purchase its own stock from profits and surplus, provided stockholders and creditors are not injured thereby. The stock so purchased is known as treasury stock, and may be reissued by the corporation. 

§ 6. Notice of powers of corporation.-Persons dealing with a corporation are charged with notice of its powers, whether or not they have actual notice. The reason is that the organization papers and charter of a corporation, setting forth its powers, are public records. Consequently, a person cannot plead ignorance of the powers of a corporation as he can profess ignorance of by-laws in dealing with officers and agents of a corporation. 

§ 7. Who may complain of ultra vires acts.-Stockholders may bring a bill in equity to have their corporation and its officers enjoined from performing ultra vires acts, provided that they have made reasonable efforts within the corporation to prevent them.

The state, through its attorney general, may institute a proceeding known as quo warranto to forfeit the charter of a corporation exceeding its powers. A quo warranto proceeding is one requiring a corporation, which is charged with neglecting to exercise or with exceeding its franchise, to show by what authority it exercises its franchise. 

§ 8. Enforceability of ultra vires contracts.-An ultra vircs contract which is executory on both sides cannot be enforced by or against the corporation. For example, the 

X Corporation, authorized to sell automobiles, enters into a contract with T to rent and operate a moving-picture theater. 

The contract has not been performed on either side. If T refuses to perform and X Corporation sues for breach of contract, T may set up the defense that the contract is ultra vires. Similarly, if X Corporation refuses to perform, and T sues, the corporation may defend on the same grounds.

POWERS OF A CORPORATION 

237 A party to an ultra vires contract performed by the other party is generally held estopped to raise the defense that the contract is ultra virės. For example, in the illustration in the preceding paragraph, if X Corporation had used T's theater for a year without paying rental, X Corporation would be estopped to raise the defense of ultra vires when T sued the corporation to recover rental. 

In many states, a party is liable upon an ultra vires contract executed by the other party, not on the ground that he is estopped to raise the defense of ultra vires, but upon the theory that he has received a benefit for the reasonable value of which he should account, as in an implied contract. 

§ 9. Liability of corporation for torts.—A corporation is liable for torts committed by its officers or agents while they are acting within the scope of their employment. Thus, corporations have been held liable for slander, libel, negligence, conspiracy, and the like. It is immaterial that the agent of a corporation is engaged in an ultra vires act when the tort is committed, so long as he is acting within the scope of his employment.

Of course, the agent too would be liable to the injured party for the wrong committed, just as other agents are personally liable for their torts. 

§ 10. Liability of corporation for crimes.-A corporation is liable for crimes committed by its officers or agents while acting within the scope of their employment. Thus, corporations have been convicted of failing to file reports required by law, maintaining a nuisance, giving rebates to shippers in violation of law, and the like. The punishment of a corporation convicted of a crime is usually a fine, but it may be compelled to forfeit its charter.

A corporation cannot commit such crimes as larceny and murder, because the intent essential to the crime is the intent of a natural person.

CHAPTER V DISSOLUTION OF CORPORATIONS § 1. Methods of dissolution.-A corporation may be dissolved in the following ways in most states: (1) By expiration of the period stated in the charter, if any is so stated. (2) By an act of the legislature. The corporation laws of most states provide that charters granted under them may be amended or repealed by the legislature. (3) By a decree of court. A court may decree dissolution of a corporation in quo warranto proceedings instituted by the attorney general because of a corporation's violation of law, or its non-use or abuse of its franchise. (4) By vote of the stockholders. Statutes provide as to whether all or a percentage of the stockholders must vote for dissolution, usually depending upon whether the corporation is insolvent; and as to whether or not a petition to court for dissolution is also requisite. 

§ 2. Effect of dissolution on existing contracts.—Gen erally speaking, the dissolution of a corporation does not affect the validity of contracts entered into by a corporation before dissolution. Creditors of the corporation may recover damages for the breach of such contracts, the damages to be paid from the assets of the corporation. 

§ 3. Limited existence of a corporation after dissolution.- 

In most states, the continuance of a corporation for certain purposes after dissolution is provided for in statutes. Thus, a typical statute provides that a corporation shall continue for a period of three years after it would have been dissolved, except for the operation of this statute, for the purpose of prosecuting and defending suits brought by or against it; of enabling it gradually to settle and close its affairs, to dispose 239

CORPORATIONS 

of and to convey its property, and to divide its capital stock; but not for the purpose of continuing the business for which it was organized. 

§ 4. Effect of consolidation.-The effect of consolidation upon a corporation depends on the statute under which the consolidation is effected. Consolidation may result in the extinction of the constituent corporations and the creation of a new corporation; or it may result in the continued existence of one or both of the constituent corporations. If two or more corporations transfer their property to one of them, and only one continues to exist, this kind of consolidation is called a merger. 

Generally, the corporation or corporations which result from consolidation have all the rights, powers, and privileges of the original corporations, and become liable for their debts and obligations.

CHAPTER VI UNINCORPORATED ASSOCIATIONS 

§ 1. In general.—There are numerous types of associations possessing many of the characteristics of a corporation, despite the fact that they are unincorporated. With the aid of legislation and by certain forms of organization, these associations are able to attain some of such corporate facilities as (1) the power to sue and be sued in the name of the association; (2) the power to receive and convey real estate in the name of the association; (3) the capacity not to be affected by the death of a member or by the sale of the interest of a member; (4) concentration of management in a small group, who may be called directors, managers, trustees, and the like; (5) limited liability of members; and (6) transferability of interests of members.

The object of these associations is to acquire the advantages of corporate existence without suffering the disadvantages of incorporation. These associations usually take the forms of non-stock associations, joint stock companies, and business trusts. § 2. Non-stock associations. In this class are associations not organized for profit, such as fraternities, improvement associations, mutual benefit organizations, citizens' leagues, and the like. These associations may have a constitution, by-laws, a president, a treasurer, a secretary, a board of directors, and other features of corporate organization. 

Generally, the members of such associations are not liable as partners, but are liable under the law of principal and agent if they authorize the acts of the officers of the association. 

The extent to which these associations acquire other corporate facilities depends upon the agreement of the members and the legislation of the state in which they organize. 241

CORPORATIONS 

§ 3. Joint stock companies.-A joint stock company is an association of individuals organized for profit, the capital of which is divided into transferable shares. Although such companies are partnerships, they partake of the nature of both partnerships and corporations. Joint stock companies generally have by-laws, a board of directors, a president, a treasurer, and a secretary. They may sue and be sued in their own name; they may receive and convey real estate in their own name; they are not affected by the death of a member or by the sale by a member of his interest; their shares are transferable; they do not receive a charter from the state. However, members are personally liable for obligations of the company except insofar as this liability is limited by statute. § 4. Business trusts.-A business trust is an organization managed by trustees who hold and manage, in trust, property conveyed to them by the owners thereof for that purpose. 

Trusts are commonly created for non-business purposes, as in gifts of property, so that restrictions may be imposed upon the transferee's use and management of property. A trust created under a will is known as a testamentary trust. A trust created and taking effect during the lifetime of the creator is known as a living trust. 

The trust device has been employed by business associations for the purpose of attaining certain corporate facilities. 

Trusts of this kind are known by such names as business trusts, Massachusetts trusts, and common-law trusts. A trust is created by an agreement of the parties, called a declaration of trust or a trust deed.

In a business trust, the legal title to all property is in the trustees for the benefit of the members, who are known as beneficiaries, or cestuis que trust; the management rests with the trustees; the interests of the members are usually evidenced by transferable certificates; the death of a member or a sale of his interest does not affect the trust; the trustees can sue and be sued and can receive and convey property in their names as trustees.

The members of a business trust are liable as partners if they have power to participate in the management, or to con-

UNINCORPORATED ASSOCIATIONS 

243 trol the trustees or even to elect them. This is true even though the members have expressly provided in the declaration of trust that they are not to be personally liable for debts of the trust. But if the members have no control whatsoever over the business or over the trustees, they are not personally liable for debts of the trust.
