CHAPTER I BANKRUPTCY § 1. The Bankruptcy Act.-The Bankruptcy Act of 1938, a revision of the 1898 Act, governs bankruptcy in the states. 

This Act is a Federal statute and is the fifth Federal Bankruptcy Act-the first four having been repealed-to be enacted by Congress under power conferred upon it in the United States Constitution "to establish uniform laws on the subject of bankruptcies throughout the United States." Since the Bankruptcy Act is a Federal statute, it is administered in the Federal courts, and not in the state courts. The courts of bankruptcy are the United States district courts. 

§ 2. Objects of Bankruptcy Act. The objects of the 

Bankruptcy Act are for the benefit of two groups: 

Creditors. Creditors of the same class share pro rata in the assets of a bankrupt. Were it not for the Bankruptcy 

Act, a debtor might use his assets to pay one creditor in full, in preference to the other creditors. Debtors. A debtor may be very much harassed by his creditors in their efforts to enforce claims. He may constantly receive threatening letters from his creditors; his property and his salary may be attached; he may have to answer constantly to court summonses; he may be cited into the poor debtor court to answer as to his property. A discharged bankrupt is released from the payment of all except certain claims. The result of a discharge is that of removing from the debtor almost entirely the pressure of his debts. § 3. State insolvency laws.-Most of the states have insolvency laws of various kinds. These laws generally serve somewhat the same purposes as the Bankruptcy Act: namely, 247

BANKRUPTCY 

a release of an insolvent person from his debts and a distribution of his property among his creditors. The procedure under insolvency statutes of the states commonly bears a resemblance to the procedure under the Bankruptcy Act. 

The state insolvency laws are not important today because they are suspended insofar as they relate to the same subject matter and affect the same persons as the Bankruptcy Act. 

The Act takes precedence because of the power vested in Congress to enact national bankruptcy legislation. 

Officers of a Bankruptcy Court 

§ 4. Clerk. The clerk of a United States district court is an officer of a bankruptcy court. It is the duty of the clerk to receive the bankruptcy petition and certain other papers in the course of the proceedings; to collect the fee imposed for filing the petition and any other fees payable in the course of the proceeding. The clerk delivers to the referee the petition and any other papers referred to him by the court. 

§ 5. Judge. The judge of a United States district court is a judge of a bankruptcy court. Since the bulk of the work of administering estates in bankruptcy is attended to by referees and trustees, the duties of judges in bankruptcy are not so onerous as they might otherwise be. The most important function of the judge consists in reviewing orders of the referee at the request of persons adversely affected by his rulings. § 6. Referee.-A referee is an officer appointed by the court for a particular district, such as a county. A referee, it may be said, is in effect the agent of the court in administering and supervising the administration of estates arising within his district. Among the powers and duties of a referee are those of adjudging persons bankrupts or of dismissing the petitions; of examining witnesses; of taking possession of and releasing the property of the bankrupt; of declaring dividends; of furnishing information concerning estates; of giving notices to creditors; and so forth. The referee is usually obliged to employ clerks and stenographers and may charge the reasonable expense of such employment

BANKRUPTCY 

249 to the estates he is administering. Generally, the referee will require petitioners in bankruptcy to pay this expense in advance before he proceeds with his duties. § 7. Receiver.-—A receiver is an officer appointed by the court upon application of the debtor or a creditor when the court finds it absolutely necessary to appoint a receiver for the preservation of the estate. The receiver takes charge of the estate until a trustee is appointed. Ordinarily, it is not necessary to appoint a receiver. § 8. Trustee. A trustee is an officer appointed by the court, pursuant to the recommendation of creditors, to administer a particular estate. The trustee is elected by the creditors at their first meeting; the appointment is subject to the approval of the court. In the event of a contest for the appointment, a majority in number and amount of all claims allowed and represented at the meeting governs. Among the duties of the trustee are those of collecting and reducing to money the property of the estate and closing it up as expeditiously as possible; of furnishing information concerning the estate; of keeping regular accounts; of giving a detailed statement of his administration to the creditors; of making final reports and filing final accounts with the court; of paying dividends after declaration by the referee; and so forth. § 9. Outline of proceeding in bankruptcy. The principal steps in a proceeding in bankruptcy are as follows: (1) The filing of the petition praying for the benefits of the Act in a court of bankruptcy. If the debtor files the petition, he becomes known as a voluntary bankrupt. If the creditors file the petition, the debtor becomes known as an involuntary bankrupt. (2) The adjudication as a bankrupt. A debtor filing the petition is adjudged a bankrupt, as a matter of course, generally as of the date he files his petition or shortly thereafter. A debtor against whom a petition has been filed has the right to contest the petition at a hearing. If he does not prevail or if he defaults, he is then adjudged a bankrupt. (3) The filing of schedules by the bankrupt, listing in detail his creditors and assets. A voluntary bankrupt must file

BANKRUPTCY 

these schedules with his petition. An involuntary bankrupt must file them within five days after adjudication. Upon application of the bankrupt, the court may extend the time for the filing of schedules. (4) The first meeting of the creditors. After adjudication of bankruptcy, the court (referee's office) sends a notice of the adjudication to the creditors, whose names are taken from the bankrupt's schedule, notifying them also of the time and place of the first meeting of creditors at which they may prove their claims, appoint a trustee, and examine the bankrupt. Generally, about the only business transacted at the first meeting is the appointment of a trustee. (5) The collection of the assets of the bankrupt by the trustee. The trustee is under a duty, immediately upon his appointment, to collect all assets of the bankrupt. Generally, his first act is to examine the bankrupt diligently as to all his property, compelling the bankrupt to turn over to him all property which is not exempt. The trustee may sue to enforce the bankrupt's claims against other persons and may defend on order of the court any suit pending against the bankrupt. (6) The filing of proofs of claim by the creditors with the referee. These must be filed within six months after the adjudication of bankruptcy. A creditor does not receive a dividend from the bankrupt's estate merely because he is listed as a creditor. To receive dividends, if any are declared, the creditor must seasonably file his proof of claim, which consists of a statement under oath, in writing, signed by him, setting forth among other information the claim and the consideration therefor.

It is one of the duties of a bankrupt to examine the correctness of all proofs of claim filed against him. 

Proofs of claim are generally allowed if no objection is raised to them. 

(7) The declaration of dividends. Of course, dividends are declared upon claims only when there are sufficient assets in the bankrupt's estate to warrant such declaration. A series of dividends of, say, 10 per cent may be declared upon the

BANKRUPTCY 

251 claims if the estate warrants. Dividends are declared by the referee and are paid under his direction. (8) The discharge of the bankrupt. The adjudication of bankruptcy of any person other than a corporation operates as an application for his discharge. A corporation may file an application for discharge within six months after adjudication. 

The application for discharge is set down for a hearing at which the trustee or other parties in interest may contest the granting of a discharge. The bankrupt will be discharged unless it appears at this hearing that he has committed certain acts enumerated in the Bankruptcy Act. A bankrupt may not be discharged: if he has unjustifiably destroyed, falsified, concealed, or failed to keep books and records; if, within a year preceding the filing of the petition, he transferred or concealed his property with the intent to defraud creditors; if he has been granted a discharge in bankruptcy six years previous to his present declaration of bankruptcy; if he has refused to obey any lawful order of the court or to answer any material question approved by the court. There are other acts which will prevent a bankrupt from obtaining a discharge, but these are the more important ones. 

If a bankrupt is discharged, he is released from all debts which might have been proved against him, with certain exceptions to be discussed in a later section. If the bankrupt is not discharged, he remains liable upon his debts, notwithstanding the bankruptcy proceedings. The only effect of the proceedings in the latter event is that of dividing the bankrupt's property among his creditors. § 10. Who may become a bankrupt.-Any person, except a municipal, railroad, insurance, or banking corporation, may become a voluntary bankrupt. 

Any person owing $1,000 or more can become an involuntary bankrupt, except the four kinds of corporations enumerated above; and except non-business corporations, farmers, and wage earners (those earning $1,500 or less per year).

BANKRUPTCY § 11. Essentials of an involuntary petition.-The creditors' 

petition against a debtor must be filed by three or more creditors if they number twelve or more; but it may be filed by one creditor if there are less than twelve creditors in all. The claims of the creditor or creditors filing the petition must aggregate $500 or over. The petition must allege, among other things, that the debtor owes debts to the amount of $1,000; that he is insolvent; and that he committed an act of bankruptcy within four months of the date of the petition.

A person is deemed insolvent under the Bankruptcy Act whenever the aggregate of his property, exclusive of property he may have transferred or otherwise dealt with to defraud creditors, is not, at a fair valuation, sufficient in amount to pay his debts. § 12. Acts of bankruptcy. The act alleged in the creditors' petition must have been committed within four months of the date of the petition and must have consisted of the debtor's having done one of the following: (1) Conveyed, transferred, concealed, or removed, or permitted to be concealed or removed, any part of his property with intent to hinder, delay, or defraud his creditors, or any of them.¹ (2) Transferred, while insolvent, any portion of his property to one or more of his creditors with intent to prefer such creditors over his other creditors. (3) Suffered or permitted, while insolvent, any creditor to obtain a lien upon any of his property through legal proceedings and not having vacated or discharged such lien within thirty days from the date thereof or at least five days before the date set for any sale or other disposition of such property. (4) Made a general assignment for the benefit of his creditors. (5) While insolvent or unable to pay his debts as they mature, procured, permitted or suffered voluntarily or in- 

1 In re Condon, p. 385.

BANKRUPTCY 

253 voluntarily the appointment of a receiver or trustee to take charge of his property. (6) Admitted in writing his. inability to pay his debts and his willingness to be adjudged a bankrupt on that ground. § 13. What property of bankrupt passes to the trustee.- 

The trustee acquires title by operation of law to all property of the bankrupt, except that which is exempt as of the date of adjudication. The bankrupt must turn over or account to the trustee for all his property as of such date, even though the trustee is not appointed until some months later; but any property the bankrupt acquires after the date of adjudication belongs to him and is not a part of the estate. 

The property of a bankrupt which is exempt under the Act is that which is exempt under the laws of the state in which the bankrupt resides. There is considerable variance among state laws as to what exemptions are allowed debtors. 

Property commonly exempted in states consists of homesteads, furniture up to a certain value, wearing apparel, implements and materials used in trade up to a certain value, fuel, provisions up to a certain value, books up to a certain value, and some insurance policies. 

If an insurance policy is not exempt, the bankrupt may retain it by paying to the trustee its cash surrender value. 

The trustee acquires title to the bankrupt's property, subject to any valid liens encumbering it. § 14. Right of trustee to avoid preferences of bankrupt.—

A trustee may avoid and recover the property or its value if the bankrupt has made any one of the following transfers: a transfer within one year before bankruptcy (a) if made without fair consideration while insolvent; (b) if made without fair consideration, leaving unreasonably small capital for business; (c) if made without fair consideration by debtor who believes he will incur debts beyond his ability to pay; and (d) if made to hinder, delay, or defraud creditors. 

The trustee may also avoid transfers by the bankrupt in fraud of creditors whenever they were made; but he may not avoid other transfers or payments made by the bankrupt upon secured claims.

BANKRUPTCY § 15. Validity of attachments made before bankruptcy.- 

Generally speaking, attachment, judgment, or other judicial liens acquired by creditors within the four months' period are dissolved; those acquired prior to the four months' period are valid. § 16. Debts which may be proved.-Debts founded upon an open account or upon contracts, express or implied, may be proved against the estate, as may debts which are a fixed liability, as evidenced by a judgment or written instrument, absolutely owing at the time of the filing of the petition, whether or not then payable. These are the most important of the provable debts. The fact that these debts may be unliquidated (unascertained in amount) does not prevent proof of them, since they may be liquidated in such manner as the court may direct.

An unliquidated claim for damages arising out of a tort committed by the bankrupt is not provable; except that a claim for negligence may be proved if suit thereon was instituted prior to and is pending at the time of the filing of the bankruptcy petition. But a claim arising out of any tort, reduced to judgment before the filing of the petition, is provable. For example, B negligently operates his car, running into and injuring T. The claim of T arising out of 

B's tort is unliquidated and may not be proved against B's estate if B goes into bankruptcy; nor is it affected by B's discharge. But if T recovered judgment upon this claim against B, or brought suit upon it, before the filing of the petition, T could prove the claim against the estate. § 17. Secured claims.-Creditors whose claims are secured may be allowed for only such sums as are owing over and above the value of the security. § 18. Rights of creditor to set off claim.-A creditor may set off against his indebtedness to the bankrupt his provable claim against the bankrupt. A creditor so setting off his claim becomes to that extent a preferred creditor. § 19. Claims which have priority in payment. Certain claims against the bankrupt's estate are entitled to priority over other claims. These claims are paid in full in the order of

BANKRUPTCY 

255 their priority.

The order of priority and payment is sub stantially as follows: 

(1) Costs of preserving and administering the bankrupt's estate. (2) Claims of workmen, clerks, and the like, not exceeding $600 to each claimant, which have been earned within three months before the filing of the petition. (3) Reasonable expenses of creditors who have secured refusal of arrangement or wage-earner plan, or who have prevented discharge in bankruptcy. 

(4) Taxes. 

(5) Debts entitled to priority under United States law and rent for three months before bankruptcy if entitled to priority under state law. (6) Claims of general creditors. § 20. Claims not affected by a discharge in bankruptcy.- 

Claims which may not be proved against the estate are naturally unaffected by the bankrupt's discharge. 

A bankrupt is released by his discharge from all provable claims, with certain exceptions. The more important of these exceptions are as follows: 

(1) Taxes. 

(2) Claims for the obtaining of property by false pretenses or false representations, or for willful and malicious injuries to the person or property of another, or for alimony, or for maintenance or support of a wife or a child. (3) Claims not scheduled in time for proof, unless the creditor had notice or actual knowledge of the bankruptcy proceedings. (4) Claims arising out of fraud, embezzlement, misappropriation, or defalcation while one is acting as an officer or in any fiduciary capacity. (5) Claims for wages due to workmen, clerks, and the like, earned within three months prior to bankruptcy. 

Also, as pointed out in the part on Contracts, a new promise by a discharged bankrupt to pay a debt is binding upon him without consideration. In some states, the new promise is required to be in writing in order to be enforceable.

BANKRUPTCY § 21. The 1938 revision of the Bankruptcy Act. In 1938, the Bankruptcy Act was reenacted in its entirety, with extensive changes in many of the provisions. Fortunately, this revision was made in the framework of the Act of 1898, much of which remained unchanged; with the consequence that there has been substantial continuity in much of the bankruptcy law and practice. The revised Act has been referred to variously as the Chandler Act, the Amendatory Act, and the Amendment of 1938. 

The principal purposes of the 1938 revision were: clarification of the law, improvement of administrative processes, and the broadening of provisions for the relief of debtors. 

Some of the important "debtor relief" chapters of the 1938 Act will be discussed in the sections that follow. § 22. Arrangements.-A debtor may make an arrangement with his creditors for the settlement or satisfaction of or the extension of time for payment of his debts. The petition for an arrangement may be filed originally by a debtor or may be filed by him in a pending bankruptcy proceeding. 

Only a debtor who is insolvent or unable to pay his debts as they mature may file this petition; and only if all the debts are unsecured. This relief is available to any person who can become a bankrupt—an individual, a partnership, or a corporation.

The arrangement proposed by the debtor may treat all debts on a parity, or it may divide the debts into classes, and deal with the different classes in different ways and upon different terms.

The creditors affected by the arrangement, or their representatives, have full opportunity at a meeting called for the purpose to examine the bankrupt, to investigate the merits of the arrangement and to present objections. 

The arrangement must be confirmed by the court if it is accepted by all the creditors, and found to be made and accepted in good faith. If a majority in number and amount of the creditors approve the arrangement, the court may confirm the arrangement if satisfied that it is fair and equitable and is for the best interests of the creditors,

BANKRUPTCY 

257 

§ 23. Real property arrangements. An individual or partnership but not a corporation-may file a petition for an arrangement for the composition of debts secured wholly or in part by real estate. The debtor must be insolvent or unable to pay his debts as they mature. 

Although the debtor is required to set forth the terms of his proposal in the petition, the creditors may later submit a counter proposal. § 24. Wage earners plans.-A wage earner whose total income does not exceed $3,600 may file a petition, setting forth a plan for the composition or extension of his debts, excluding those secured by real estate. The debtor must subject his future earnings to the supervision and control of the court, thus preventing attachments by creditors and insuring an equitable distribution of his earnings among creditors.

The expense of this proceeding is small, the wage earner being required to pay a filing fee of only $15 and to deposit not more than $15 for the expenses of the referee. The other expenses are paid from the debtor's future earnings. § 25. Corporate reorganizations. If a corporation is insolvent or unable to pay its debts as they mature, a petition for reorganization may be filed by the corporation, or by three or more creditors whose claims aggregate $5,000 or over, or by an indenture trustee of outstanding securities. The petition may be filed originally or in a pending bankruptcy proceeding. The relief provided for corporations in the 1938 

Act is more comprehensive and flexible than that provided in Section 77B of the old Act. 

Possession of the corporation is ordinarily given to a trustee appointed by the court, but may be given to the debtor if the indebtedness is less than $250,000. 

A plan of reorganization must be submitted by the trustee; or if the debtor is in possession, the debtor or a creditor or a stockholder or an examiner may submit a plan. If the court approves the plan, after a hearing, any interested party nevertheless may raise objections to confirmation of the plan. 

The court must confirm the plan if satisfied, among other things, that the plan is fair and equitable, and is proposed and accepted in good faith.

TORTS

CHAPTER I TORTS § 1. Foreword.-The subject of torts is not generally included in books on business law. Probably the reason for the omission is that one does not associate the subject matter of torts with the legal problems of a business man quite so readily as the subject matter of contracts, agency, and the other subjects which have been discussed in this text. While conceding that emphasis should be placed upon the points which have heretofore been treated in this text, the author believes that problems involving torts arise with sufficient frequency in the private and business life of business men to warrant some consideration of the subject matter and scope of the law of torts. This chapter merely enumerates the principal torts, with such description of them as will enable the reader to understand in a general way what conduct or omission to act constitutes a particular tort. The laws of a particular state may vary from the general principles stated in this chapter. 

§ 2. Definition.-A tort may be defined as a breach of a duty fixed by law, not arising from contract, for which the injured party may bring an action for damages. The duty may be imposed by statute or under principles of common law.

Thus, the rights of a party arising out of a tort are to be distinguished from rights arising out of a breach of contract. 

Either right, however, entitles the injured party to recover money damages.

The most important torts, for the commission of which an injured party may maintain an action for damages, are described in the sections that follow. § 3. Assault and battery.-An assault takes place when one person consciously directs force towards another, causing 263

TORTS 

him reasonably to entertain fear. Thus, if A wields a stick over B's head as though he were going to strike B, and B, as a reasonable man, thinks he will be struck, this act is an assault. 

But if A, in wielding the stick, were to say, "I will strike you if I see you here again," this would not be an assault, even though B was afraid, since a reasonable person in B's position would know from A's language that he was not going to strike; or if B were beyond the reach of A, B's apprehension would not be reasonable because a reasonable man in his position would know that A was unable to strike him. 

A battery takes place when a person intentionally inflicts force upon the person of another without consent or justification. Thus, if A, while walking along a sidewalk, deliberately pushes B, a stranger, into the street, A would be guilty of battery. The least touching of another in anger or with hostile intent is a battery.

An assault and battery occurs when a person has committed both an assault and a battery. It has been held that an assaulted person cannot maintain an action for fright alone, but he may, if the fright is accompanied by some physical injury, however slight.

An assault and battery is a crime as well as a tort. The state may prosecute the offender for his crime, and the injured party may also sue him civilly to recover damages for the tort.

A party sued civilly for assault and battery may justify his action if he can prove that he acted in self-defense. A person threatened with violence by another may use reasonable force to defend himself. If he uses more force than is necessary for this purpose, his action is not justified. 

§ 4. False imprisonment.-False imprisonment consists of imposing, by force or threats, an unlawful restraint upon a person's freedom of locomotion. For example: A seizes B by the arm and says, "You will not leave until I let you go"; or

A, pointing a gun at B, says, "You will remain in this room all day."

If a person can justify his restraint of the liberty of another by showing that he acted with legal authority, the imprison-

TORTS 

265 ment will not be false. Thus, a police officer may arrest a person for whose arrest he holds a warrant. 

One who has been falsely imprisoned may recover damages from the person who has committed the tort. 

The general rule is that a police officer can arrest without a warrant if he reasonably believes a person has committed a felony, whereas a private individual may arrest only when a felony has been committed and he reasonably believes that the person arrested committed it. A person may arrest another without warrant, to prevent the commission of a felony. The general rule is that an officer has no authority to arrest for a misdemeanor without a warrant, unless the offense is committed in his presence. A private individual may not arrest for a misdemeanor without a warrant, except in the case of a breach of peace committed in his presence. 

These rules are subject to statutory variations. 

The state laws, in describing a particular offense, usually declare whether it shall be considered a felony. The statutes of some states define a felony as an offense punishable by death or imprisonment in a penitentiary or a state prison. 

The word felony implies a crime of a graver or more atrocious nature than that designated as misdemeanor. 

A police officer has the right to summon and require the assistance of as many bystanders as may be necessary to enable him to perform his duty in making an arrest. § 5. Negligence.-Negligence is the failure of a person to exercise the care of a reasonably prudent man under the circumstances.¹ Generally speaking, a person who by his negligence causes injury to another is liable.

Negligence may consist of the performing of an act without due care; or it may consist of a failure to act when one is under a duty to act. For example, a person may be guilty of negligence in operating his car or in failing to move his car when it is in the path of another. 

To recover for a damage, a person must prove that it was caused by the negligence complained of. Thus, if A operates 

1 Raymond v. Portland R. Co., p. 389. Hutchins v. Inhabitants of Penobscot, p. 390. Lundy v. Southern Bell Telephone and Telegraph Co., p. 391.

TORTS 

his car so negligently that he is about to run into a tree, and just before he hits the tree B negligently runs into him, of course A cannot recover from B for the damage caused by collision with the tree.

The general rule is that a person injured by the negligence of another cannot recover if he himself was contributorily negligent; that is, if his negligence also contributed to his injuries. For example, A, while driving, negligently runs into and injures B, who is crossing the street. If A can show that B was crossing the street without looking to see whether any cars were approaching, he may be able to defeat recovery by B. This rule is not in force in some states. 

A child is bound to exercise the care of an ordinary prudent child of his age, development, and capacity. If he does not exercise such care, he is liable if his negligence causes injury to another; and his contributory negligence will bar recovery by him for the negligence of another. § 6. Deceit (fraud). To recover for deceit, a person must prove (1) a false representation of material, existing fact, (2) known to be false by the person making it, (3) made with the intent that it should be acted upon, (4) reasonably relied upon by the party to whom it was made, (5) to his damage.

The elements of deceit were fully discussed in Chapter IV of Contracts, under the heading of Fraud. Fraud and deceit are frequently used interchangeably, although fraud is the term generally employed in connection with the remedy of rescission of a contract obtained thereby, and deceit the term used in connection with the alternative remedy of an action for damages for the tort committed. It was pointed out in the discussion of fraud that an injured party may elect to (1) rescind the contract, or (2) bring an action for damages, or (3) set up the defense of fraud in an action brought against him to enforce the contract. 

§ 7. Conversion.-Conversion is an unauthorized assump tion and exercise of the right of ownership over goods of another. Thus, if A, without B's authority, sells or rents 

B's furniture, A would be guilty of conversion; or if A were

TORTS 

267 to attach B's furniture as the property of C in a suit against 

C, he would be so guilty.

The intermeddling or the taking of the property of another is not always conversion. It must appear either that there was an intent to deprive the owner of his property permanently or temporarily, or that upon demand of the owner there was neglect or refusal to deliver it. Thus, in a case in which an officer asked an owner to remove his goods from the land of another and the owner refused, and the officer then removed them, the officer was held not to have converted the goods.

Generally speaking, the innocence or good faith of the one converting the property of another is immaterial. Thus, if 

A, not knowing that a car which he purchased was stolen from B, sells it to C, he is nevertheless liable to B for conversion. 

The measure of damages for conversion is the value of the property at the time it was converted. If the owner wishes, he may bring an action of replevin to recover the property rather than an action to recover money damages for conversion.

If the taking of the property of another is accompanied by an intent to steal, the taking will be a crime as well as a tort. § 8. Trespass.-Trespass is any entry upon real estate, or any interruption of the possession of or any injury to personal property, without lawful authority. Thus, if A walks across B's land without authority, B may sue him for trespass; or if A takes and uses B's car without permission, even for a short time, B may sue him for trespass. In all cases it is immaterial that the trespass is unintentional. 

The entry upon land of another may be justified in certain cases, as when an officer enters to execute legal process; or a creditor, to demand money payable; or a landlord, to prevent waste; or when a guest enters an inn. 

The owner of real estate has the right to use reasonable force, but no more, to remove a trespasser. Only reasonable force may be used to remove trespassing animals. They may not be killed unless killing is necessary for the preservation of one's life or property.

TORTS 

A person who trespasses after he has been notified or warned not to trespass may by statute in many states be prosecuted criminally. The notice not to trespass may be given orally or in writing. 2 

§ 9. Slander and libel.-Slander is the making of oral false statements, in the hearing of another, which tend to injure a person's reputation. Libel consists of the writing of such statements, and the reading of them by a person other than the one defamed. In other words, slander is oral defamation and libel is written defamation.

Defamation may be said to be that which tends to bring a person into hatred, ridicule, or contempt; or which tends to exclude him from society. For example, to call a person, orally or in writing, a liar, a thief, a hypocrite, or the like, would be defamation. Printing a caricature of a person might also be held defamation.

To recover for slander, a person must show that he has been damaged by it, or that the defamation either: (1) charges him with commission of a felony or crime involving moral turpitude; or (2) charges him with having a loathsome disease; or (3) makes a charge tending to cause his disinheritance; or (4) makes a charge tending to injure him in his business or profession.

A person sued for slander will not be held liable if he can prove that the defamatory statement is true or that he was privileged in making it. Thus, members of Congress and state legislatures, while acting in their official capacities, have the defense of privilege; also, judges, parties, and counsel have this defense as to relevant statements in judicial proceedings.

Fair comment may be made about anyone or anything placed before the public for public consideration, provided such comment is not made maliciously. Thus, one may criticise a book placed on public sale, or a candidate for public office.

In an action for libel, the injured party, to recover, does not have to prove special damage, as in certain cases of slander, 2 Sheffill & Wife v. Van Deusen & Wife, p. 392,

TORTS 

269 Truth is a defense, as in slander, but not if the libel was published maliciously. Privilege is likewise a defense in an action for libel. Libel may constitute a crime as well as a tort. 

§ 10. Malicious prosecution; abuse of process.—Malicious prosecution consists of prosecuting a person (1) with malice, that is to say, with malevolence or recklessness; and (2) without probable cause, meaning the want of sufficient ground for belief in the guilt of the person prosecuted. To recover for malicious prosecution, the injured party must be able to establish in his suit that the prosecution terminated in his favor. Thus, A, because of a grudge against B, swears out a warrant for B's arrest for stealing A's car. A's car was in fact stolen, but he had no real ground for suspecting B of the theft. B is acquitted of the charge of larceny. B may now maintain an action against A for the tort of malicious prosecution.

Abuse of process consists of making an attachment or arrest, in the course of a judicial proceeding, with malice or without probable cause. The proceeding may be civil or criminal. For example, A, who has a claim against B in the amount of $100, brings suit against B and, to vent his spite, attaches B's bank account to the amount of $1,000; or, A, with no claim at all against B, brings suit, attaching B's bank account. 

§ 11. Slander of title.-Slander of title consists of making a false statement disparaging the quality of a person's property or his title thereto. To recover, the injured party must be able to establish that he sustained damage and that the statement was made maliciously or recklessly. For example, A owns a store which B has agreed to buy. C, who is hostile to A, with the intention of injuring A, tells B that the store has not operated at a profit for five years. This statement is untrue. A may maintain an action against C for slander of title if, as a result of C's statements, B refuses to purchase the store. 

§ 12. Interference with contract. The malicious pro curing of the breach of a contract, with knowledge of the contract, is an actionable tort. Also, a court of equity may

TORTS 

enjoin one who attempts or threatens to procure such breach. 

For example, A is an accountant working for B under a contract for one year. C, knowing about this contract, and acting solely for the purpose of injuring A, persuades B to discharge A without cause, and to employ X in his place. A would have a claim against C for procuring a breach of the contract.

Also, the procuring of a refusal to contract, maliciously and without justification, may be a tort when it is done with knowledge that persons habitually deal with each other or are about to enter into contractual relationship. Thus, it might be held actionable for a union to persuade an employer not to hire a workman he was about to employ. Also, a court of equity might enjoin such interference with the relations of the employer and the employee. 

§ 13. Misuse of trade name. The misuse of a trade name consists of a person's adopting a name or a symbol so resembling one which he knows has acquired a reputation in the market that the public will be misled. For example, A is a manufacturer of "Keystone Cigars" and his brand of cigars is well known to the public under that name. B proceeds to manufacture a brand of cigars which he labels "Keystone 

Maid Cigars." A might recover damages from B in tort, or he might have B enjoined from using that name. § 14. Conspiracy. Conspiracy is a combination of two or more persons to accomplish an unlawful purpose, or a lawful purpose by unlawful means. Thus, an employer injured by a combination of employees calling an illegal strike might maintain actions of tort against the participants; also, a storekeeper might maintain an action of tort against a combination of other storekeepers who seek to promote their business by injuring his credit and business. Conspiracy may constitute a crime as well as a tort. 

§ 15. Alienation of affections.-Alienation of affections consists of the enticement of a husband or a wife, resulting in loss to the spouse of the husband's or wife's society and conjugal affections. Thus, Dixon and his wife are happily married. Bowen persuades Dixon's wife to run away with

TORTS 

271 him. Dixon may maintain an action against Bowen for the tort of alienation of affections. 

§ 16. Nuisance.-Nuisance consists of acts or conduct materially interfering with ordinary physical comfort or human existence, or materially detrimental to the reasonable use or value of property. Thus, if A plays his cornet loudly in his back yard for hours at a time, his neighbors might maintain an action for damages for the offense, or they might have A enjoined by a court of equity from continuing the nuisance. 

§ 17. Damage by animals.—The owner of a wild animal, such as a lion, is absolutely liable for the damage caused by it. 

But the owner of a domestic animal, such as a horse, a cow, or the like, is not generally liable for damage caused by it unless it can be proved that the owner knew about the vicious nature of the animal or was negligent with respect to it. In many states, the owner of a dog is held liable for the damage caused by it, irrespective of his knowledge as to its vicious propensities.

REAL PROPERTY

REAL PROPERTY CHAPTER I IN GENERAL 

§ 1. Real and personal property defined. Real property consists of land and anything attached thereto. Thus, a parcel of land is real property; also, a building erected upon it, a fence surrounding it, clothes poles imbedded in the back yard, or a furnace imbedded in the cellar. Real property is also defined as property which is of a fixed, immovable nature. 

Personal property is property of a movable nature, as an automobile, a watch, or furniture. Articles of personal property are commonly called chattels. 

All property may be broadly classified as either realty or personalty. Some property may change from real to personal when it becomes detached from land, and from personal to real when it becomes attached to land. Thus, a tree is real property while it is attached to soil, but when cut down it becomes personal property. If a tree is cut into lumber and the lumber used in constructing a building, the lumber becomes real property because it is part of something attached to land.

Growing crops are considered personal property for the purpose of sales thereof either by the owner or by a sheriff at a judicial sale. A sale of real estate includes crops; but a tenant is entitled to his crops unless they mature after termination of his tenancy. § 2. Tests for determining whether chattels have become incorporated into realty. When the following tests are satisfied, chattels may be said to have lost their identity as personal property and to have become realty by reason of incorporation therein: (1) when the chattels are actually annexed to realty or something appurtenant thereto; (2) when they are appropri- 275

REAL PROPERTY 

ated to the use or purpose of that part of the realty to which they are connected; (3) when the person annexing them intends to make them a permanent part of the realty, his intention being gathered from (a) the nature of the articles affixed, (b) his relation to the realty and the articles, (c) the structure and mode of annexation, (d) the purpose or use for which it is made.

In the determination of whether chattels have become incorporated into real estate, all the circumstances of the particular case must be considered in the light of the foregoing criteria. It is a mixed question of law and fact. In particular cases, a scenic railroad, and a steam engine that was affixed to masonry in the floor of a building, were held to be real property.

The general rule is that personal property which has become incorporated into real property belongs to the owner of the realty, irrespective of who owned the personal property before such incorporation. § 3. Fixtures. The term fixture is most commonly used to designate articles of personal property which, although affixed to real estate by a tenant, may be removed by him. 

A trade fixture is an article affixed to rented premises by the tenant, to be used in connection with his business. 

Examples of fixtures are house furnaces, water tanks, boilers, doors, and blinds.

Generally, a tenant may not remove fixtures which have been so affixed that their identity is lost, or that they cannot be removed without material injury to the real estate itself. 

The following have been held not to be removable by tenants in the particular cases in which the question arose: doors, blinds, boilers, steam engines, water tanks, railroad ties, and house furnaces.

Generally, a tenant may remove those fixtures which are manifestly furniture, such as counters bolted to the floor or mirrors fastened to the wall; or fixtures which are not so attached that their identity has been lost, such as an oil heater used by a store for demonstration purposes and attached to the building only by a water pipe; or fixtures

IN GENERAL 

277 which may be removed without material injury to the real estate itself, such as a machine fastened to the floor by bolts, and not designed especially for use on the premises. 

In every case, all the circumstances must be considered in the determination of whether the fixture is one which may be removed.

In any case, if a tenant has a right to remove a fixture, he must exercise this right during his term. If he fails to remove fixtures before his tenancy expires, title to them passes to the landlord. 

§ 4. Reasons for distinguishing between real and personal property. The following are some of the reasons why it may become important to determine whether property is real or personal: (1) In a sale of real estate, personal property would not pass to the grantee unless it was incorporated therein. Thus, in the sale of a parcel of land, standing trees would pass with the land to the grantee, but not trees cut prior to the sale and lying upon the land. (2) The owner of personal property may lose title to such property by reason of its becoming affixed to real estate, as when a tenant of premises so affixes chattels that their identity becomes lost or they cannot be removed without material injury to the real estate. (3) When a person dies without leaving a will (intestate), his real property passes to his heirs and his personal property to his administrator. If he dies leaving a will (testate), his real property passes directly to the devisees named therein and his personal property passes in the first instance to his executor, who transfers it to the legatees after administration of the estate. (4) At common law and by statute in most states, a wife has an estate by dower and a husband an estate by curtesy, each in the other's real estate, but not in personal property. (5) Real property must be transferred by a deed-a written agreement that is signed, sealed, and delivered.

Personal property may be transferred merely by delivery of the property with the intent to transfer title.

REAL PROPERTY Methods of Acquiring Title to Real Property 

§ 5. By deed. Usually, title to real estate is acquired by a deed in which the owner transfers his title to another. The person making the conveyance is called the grantor, and the person to whom it is made the grantee. 

A deed is a sealed instrument containing a contract or covenant. The ordinary meaning of the term, particularly in real estate transactions, is a written instrument, signed, sealed, and delivered, by which one person conveys land to another.

The principal kinds of deeds by which title to real estate is conveyed are known as warranty deeds and quitclaim deeds.

Either type of deed is sufficient to transfer a grantor's title to real estate. The chief distinctions between them are as follows: (1) In a warranty deed the words of grant are generally, "I, A B, . . . do hereby give, grant, bargain, sell, and convey unto the said C D . . . "; and in a quitclaim deed, “I, A B, . . . do hereby remise, release, and forever quitclaim unto the said C D ... (2) The grantor's covenants of title are different in warranty and in quitclaim deeds. 

In a warranty deed the grantor usually covenants substantially as follows: that at the time of the delivery of such deed (1) he was lawfully seized in fee simple of the granted premises; (2) the granted premises were free from all encumbrances; (3) he had good right to sell and convey the same to the grantee and his heirs and assigns; and (4) that he will, and his heirs, executors, and administrators shall, warrant and defend the same to the grantee and his heirs and assigns against the lawful claims and demands of all persons. 

In some states the grantor in a quitclaim deed covenants substantially as follows: that at the time of delivery of such deed (1) the premises were free from all encumbrances made by him; and (2) that he will, and his heirs, executors, and administrators shall, warrant and defend the same to the grantee and his heirs and assigns forever against the lawful claims and demands of all persons claiming by, through, or under the grantor, but against none other.

IN GENERAL 

279 In many states, statutes provide that certain covenants of title, as, for example, the aforementioned warranty covenants, shall be implied from the use of particular words in conveyances of realty. The purpose of these statutes is to shorten the language in deeds by rendering it unnecessary to recite each time the covenants accompanying a warranty or quitclaim deed. The statutes of a particular state should be consulted on this point. § 6. Formalities attending deeds.—A deed must be signed, sealed (in most states), and delivered, in order to be valid. 

Sometimes deeds are delivered in escrow; that is to say, the grantor delivers the deed to a third person to be delivered by him to the grantee upon the occurrence of a specified condition, such as the payment of the price. If the condition is not fulfilled, the conveyance is ineffective because of the absence of delivery.

The grantee is entitled to record his deed in the registry of deeds of the county in which the land is situated. The recording of a deed serves as constructive notice to everyone of the title acquired by the grantee, since all persons are charged by law with notice of all records in the registry, pertaining to the land in question. By the same token, persons are not charged with notice of a deed which is not recorded, so that an unrecorded deed is effective only between the grantor and grantee and as to those who have actual notice of it. Consequently, a grantee should at once record the deed received by him.

In some states, the grantor must acknowledge before a notary public that the deed is his free act and deed. 

§ 7. Examination of title by grantee.—A grantee should have the title to real estate he is purchasing thoroughly examined by a competent attorney to make sure the title is good. A grantee may not rely safely upon apparent ownership of the grantor, for a wide variety of defects may exist in the latter's title. These defects may be discovered by an examination, at the registry of deeds, of records of all transactions relating to the title. If the records at the registry do not disclose defects, a grantee may safely purchase, for a

REAL PROPERTY 

bona fide purchaser for value without notice is not affected by unrecorded transfers.

Common defects in title, for which a grantee should particularly search, are the following: (1) Deeds of successive grantors may not have accurately described the real estate. (2) Certain deeds may not have been executed properly. 

Some grantor may not have signed, sealed, or acknowledged his deed. (3) Some deed in the chain of title may have imposed restrictions upon the use of the real estate, such as a restriction that no building should be erected upon a parcel except a dwelling house set back at least twenty feet from the sidewalk. (4) Former owners of the real estate may have mortgaged it and the mortgage may still be outstanding and unpaid as a matter of record. (5) The city or town in which the real estate is situated may have imposed some kind of assessment upon the real estate, such as that for betterments or for taxes which have not been paid. (6) A creditor may have brought suit against an owner of the real estate, attaching the real estate, and the lien may still be outstanding as a matter of record. (7) Materialmen or mechanics, improving buildings upon the real estate, may have filed claims of liens against it. (8) An owner may have gone into bankruptcy, in which event title to the real estate may have passed to his trustee in bankruptcy and the bankrupt may have been without power to convey it. (9) The land may have been owned by several persons and all of them may not have joined in a deed conveying it. (10) A wife may not have joined in a deed releasing her dower interest in the property, or a husband may not have joined in one releasing his curtesy interest. (11) A former owner of the land may have died and his estate may not have been properly administered, in which event the title of the heirs or devisees might be defective. 

Thus, the validity of a title is not determined solely by what has happened to the land while it is owned by the person granting it, but by all the transactions and occurrences appearing of record during ownership by successive owners. 

Consequently, it is very risky to purchase real estate without

IN GENERAL 

281 checking thoroughly every reference to it in the records at the registry of deeds.

A person examining a title generally makes a written summary or abstract of every paper he finds in the records relating to the particular parcel to which he is examining the title. 

This summary is called an abstract of title. It is carefully preserved for future reference in the event that the report of the examiner concerning the title is ever questioned, and in the event that the examiner is ever requested to examine the same title again. 

§ 8. Acquisition of title by will or by descent.—An owner may in his will devise his real estate to such persons as he desires. In this event, the devisees acquire title to the real estate upon the death of the testator, subject to the property's being used by the executor to pay debts of the estate if the assets are insufficient for that purpose; also subject to the claim of a surviving spouse for dower, curtesy, or any statutory share the spouse may have in real estate of a deceased wife or husband.

If an owner of real estate dies, leaving no will (intestate), his real estate descends to his heirs-at-law. The heirs-at-law of a person are designated by statute in a particular state. 

Usually, they consist of (1) the surviving wife or husband and children or issue of deceased children; (2) if there are none of this class, the parents of the deceased owner; (3) if there are none of the two previous classes, the brothers and sisters of the deceased owner or issue of deceased brothers and sisters; (4) if there are none of these three classes, the relatives nearest to the deceased owner in degree of relationship. 

§ 9. Acquisition of title by adverse possession.—A person may acquire title to land (1) by actual, open, and notorious possession; (2) held adversely to the owner; (3) for a continuous period of twenty years, unless the period is made shorter by statute. This method is called acquiring title by adverse possession or by prescription.

Obviously, a tenant whose possession is merely permissive cannot acquire title, irrespective of the length of time he remains in possession of land.

REAL PROPERTY 

The periods of time land is adversely possessed by several different persons may be tacked on one to the other if there is privity between them, as when one adverse possessor conveys to another his interest in the land. 

Acquisition of title by adverse possession is permitted because of the public policy of not disturbing one who has been in long-continued possession of land as an owner. § 10. Other methods of acquiring title.-One may also acquire title to land by purchasing the interest of the owner at a judicial sale conducted by a sheriff to satisfy a claim of a creditor of the owner; or by purchasing at a tax sale held by the town or city in which the land is situated to satisfy its claim for taxes imposed upon the land. 

One may also acquire title to land by accretion, as when a person owns land bordering upon a river and soil is washed onto his land from adjacent property by action of the water. 

Estates in Real Estate 

§ 11. Estates classified according to duration.-A feesimple estate is absolute ownership of real estate, entitling the owner unconditionally to dispose of the property during his lifetime, the property upon his death descending to his heirs or passing to his devisees.

A life estate is an estate the duration of which is limited to the life of the person holding it or to the life of some other person. Both fee-simple and life estates are referred to as freehold estates, the term denoting estates held for an uncertain period as distinguished from leasehold estates, which are held for definite periods. 

A leasehold estate is an estate acquired in real estate by lease from the owner. The duration of this estate is determined by the terms of the lease. These estates will be considered more fully in the next chapter. 

The estate which remains after the creation of a life estate or a leasehold estate is called a reversion if it is to revert to the original owner after termination of the life or the leasehold estate, and a remainder if it is to pass to a person other than

IN GENERAL 

283 the owner. Thus, if A conveys a life estate in his property to 

B, A has a reversionary interest in the property. A remainder is created if A conveys his property "to B for life, remainder to C." 

§ 12. Homestead estate. A homestead estate is an artificial estate created by statute to protect the possession and enjoyment of an owner against claims of his creditors by exempting the property from execution and forced sale so long as it is occupied as a home. The exemption is generally granted to the head of a family and the amount of the exemption is fixed by statute. Generally, a husband may not convey his homestead estate unless his wife consents, joining in the deed. § 13. Estates by dower and by curtesy.-An estate by dower is the right of a wife surviving her husband to hold for her life one third of the real estate owned by her husband during marriage. An estate by curtesy is a similar right given to a surviving husband.

A wife or a husband acquires these estates the moment the spouse becomes the owner of the real estate, but the estate does not vest in enjoyment unless the wife or the husband having the estate survives. 

A wife or a husband may release her or his estates by dower or curtesy by joining in a deed conveying the property, or by a subsequent deed.

Dower and curtesy are regulated by statute in the various states. § 14. Easements. An easement is a right acquired by one person by deed or by prescription¹ to use in a certain way the land of another in which he has no estate or interest. 

For example, the owner of land may grant to another the right to use his alleyway, or the right to construct poles upon his land.

An easement is acquired by prescription when a person has made open and notorious use of land, adverse to the owner, for a continuous period of twenty years. 

1 Parrott v. Stewart et al., p. 395.

REAL PROPERTY 

An easement of necessity exists when one person conveys a part of his land to another and the only method of reaching the part conveyed is by passage across the land retained by the grantor. § 15. Joint tenancies and tenancies in common. Two or more persons owning land jointly generally own either as joint tenants or as tenants in common. 

In a joint tenancy, each owner is regarded as owning a single estate in the whole property, whereas in a tenancy in common each owner is regarded as owning a certain undivided interest in the whole property, as an undivided one-third interest when property is owned by three persons having an equal interest in it.

These types of ownership are created by the grantor's specifying in the deed, or the testator's specifying in his will, which tenancy he desires to create. The law regards a tenancy in common more favorably than a joint tenancy, with the result that if a grantor or testator does not specify which type of tenancy he creates, the law will presume that a tenancy in common was intended. 

The principal distinctions between these two kinds of ownership are as follows: (1) In a joint tenancy, the property, upon the death of one joint tenant, passes to the others; whereas in a tenancy in common, the interest of a tenant in common passes upon his death to his heirs-at-law or his devisees. (2) A conveyance by a joint tenant of his interest to a third party destroys the joint tenancy and creates a tenancy in common.

A tenancy by the entirety is joint ownership of real estate by husband and wife. It is created by words in a deed or will expressing such intent. Ordinarily, a conveyance to a husband and wife as joint tenants makes them tenants by the entirety. The characteristics of tenancy by the entirety are as follows: (1) Upon the death of one spouse, the survivor acquires title to the whole. (2) Neither spouse can convey his or her interest in the property in such manner as to defeat the title of the survivor to the whole estate.

CHAPTER II LANDLORD AND TENANT § 1. Creation of the relationship. The relationship of landlord and tenant is contractual. The contract by which the relationship is created is called a lease. A lease may be defined as a conveyance of land or tenement to a person for life, for a term of years, or at will, in consideration of the payment of rental or some other compensation. The term lease is commonly used to designate the written instrument by which the relationship of landlord and tenant is created. 

In most states, statutes provide that an oral lease for a period longer than that stated in the statute is void. Statutes so providing are not uniform with respect to the period for which oral leases may be made. In many states, the period is one year; in other states, the period is longer. In some states, an oral lease creates only a tenancy at will. 

An oral executory agreement to give or to enter into a lease, as distinguished from a present oral demise for a term to commence at a future date, is within the Statute of Frauds unless the Statute expressly excepts such agreements. 

In cases in which a lease is required to be in writing, a lease signed by the lessor and delivered to the lessee, who does not sign, is binding upon both parties-especially when the lessee has entered into the use and occupation of the premises. 

Leases customarily contain many provisions, called covenants and conditions, inserted for the protection of the lessors. 

The reason these provisions are inserted is that it is the lessor who generally draws the lease and his rights are more apt to be infringed in the course of the tenancy than those of the lessee. It cannot be emphasized too strongly that a lease is just as binding as any other contract, and a lessee should not execute a lease until he has familiarized himself with every provision of it. If the lease contains provisions to which the 287

REAL PROPERTY 

lessee objects, he should either require the lessor to strike out such provisions or refuse to sign the lease. 

§ 2. Kinds of tenancies.-The following kinds of tenancies may be created:

Tenancy for a specified number of years, such as a tenancy for three years.

Tenancy from year to year. Such estate is for the period. of a year, and further periods of a year, unless terminated by either party's giving due notice to quit. This tenancy may be created expressly by agreement; or by implication, as when property is occupied generally under a rent payable yearly, half yearly, or quarterly; or when a tenant holds over after the expiration of his term without having entered into a new contract, and pays rent. In some states, a tenancy from year to year may not be created merely by a tenant's holding over after the expiration of his term unless there is an express agreement to that effect. 

Tenancy at will. A tenancy at will is a tenancy which continues until it is terminated by the will of either the landlord or the tenant. A tenant occupying premises under an invalid written lease, or a tenant occupying under a lease which is not for any definite period, is deemed a tenant at will. 

A tenancy at will is implied when a tenant occupies the premises and the landlord accepts rental under no express agreement.

Tenancy at sufferance. A tenant at sufferance is a tenant who wrongfully holds over after the expiration of his term. 

The distinction between him and a trespasser is that he enters the premises lawfully, whereas the trespasser does not. A tenant at sufferance may become a tenant at will if the landlord accepts rental from him without reserving his rights to remove him. 

§ 3. Liability of landlord to tenant for personal injuries. 

The rights of landlord and tenant are governed primarily by the terms of the lease or agreement into which they enter. 

It is customary to state in the lease the rights and liabilities of the parties in considerable detail.

LANDLORD AND TENANT 

289 In the absence of an express representation that the premises are fit for habitation, a landlord is not ordinarily liable to a tenant injured by reason of the defective condition of the premises. A tenant takes the premises in the condition in which he finds them when he enters. There are two exceptions: (1) A landlord is liable to a tenant for injuries caused by concealed defects, not discoverable on reasonable inspection, about which the landlord knew or ought to have known-for example, a defective cesspool. (2) A person leasing furnished rooms is in some states held impliedly to warrant that these are fit for habitation. § 4. Repairs. In the absence of agreement, a landlord is not bound to make repairs upon the premises.¹ Here again, the tenant takes the premises in the condition in which he finds them. Even if the premises are damaged by fire, the landlord is under no duty to repair the damage. 

In the absence of agreement, a tenant is not under a duty to make repairs except those necessary to keep the buildings upon the premises wind- and water-tight, such as the replacing of broken windowpanes, the repairing of leaking pipes, and the like. A tenant is not obliged to make repairs of a substantial or lasting nature, such as the constructing of a new roof or the rebuilding of walls. 

A tenant is under a duty to return the premises to the landlord in the same condition that he obtained them, reasonable wear and tear excepted. § 5. Liability of tenant for waste.-A tenant is liable for any waste (destruction) committed by him upon the premises. 

Thus, a tenant who destroys a building upon the premises would be liable to the landlord for any damages. § 6. Subletting and assignment by tenant. In the absence of agreement, a tenant may assign his lease or may sublet the premises for a part of his term, but he himself remains liable upon the lease unless the landlord agrees to release him and to accept the assignee or sublessee in his place. However, 1 Whitehead v. Comstock & Company, p. 396.

REAL PROPERTY 

leases usually provide that the lessee may not assign his lease or sublet without obtaining the written consent of the lessor. 

The lessor may be held to waive this provision if he knows about the assignment or subletting and raises no objection. § 7. Improvements by tenant. In the absence of agreement, improvements made upon the premises revert with the premises to the landlord, as explained in Chapter I. However, the tenant may, during his term, remove fixtures not so annexed as to lose their identity, and fixtures which can be removed without material injury to the premises. § 8. Liability of tenant for rent. A tenant is liable for rent in accordance with the terms of his lease or agreement. 

In the absence of agreement the only remedy of a landlord for recovery of rental in arrears is that of bringing suit for the amount due. In most states, a landlord has no lien upon the property of a tenant for rental in arrears; nor may a landlord oust a tenant except after giving notice or by bringing a proceeding for possession provided for by statute. 

In the absence of agreement, a tenant is not excused from paying rent by destruction of a part of the premises if some part remains upon which the lease may operate. Thus, if A leases a house and land from B and the house is destroyed by fire, A continues to be liable for the full amount of the rental. 

But if A leased an apartment in a building and the building was destroyed, A would be relieved of his liability to pay rental, for there would be nothing upon which the lease could operate.

A tenant has a defense to a claim for rent when there has been an eviction, though from only a part of the premises. 

Actual eviction is physical deprivation of the whole or a part of the premises, as when a landlord builds on land, adjoining the demised premises, a wall encroaching even several inches on the demised premises. A constructive eviction consists of intentional acts by a landlord not amounting to expulsion, but substantially diminishing the tenant's enjoyment of the premises, as when a landlord intentionally refuses to perform his agreement to supply the tenant with hot water, or when a landlord causes a din, intending to disturb the tenant.

LANDLORD AND TENANT 

291 When there has been an eviction, a tenant may abandon the premises, refusing to pay rental; or he may remain in possession, refusing to pay rental, except that if the eviction is constructive he is liable for a proportionate part of the rental. 

A tenant may not refuse to pay rental merely because a landlord has failed to perform an ordinary covenant in the lease, such as a covenant to make repairs. The reason is that the promise of a tenant in a lease to pay rental is independent of the promise of the landlord to do certain things. (See 

Contracts, Chapter VIII, Section 7.) But if a tenant is sued by his landlord for rental, he may bring a cross-action for violation of the landlord's agreement. 

§ 9. Termination of the relationship.—The relationship of landlord and tenant may be terminated in one of the following ways: (1) By expiration of the term specified in the lease. (2) By mutual agreement of the parties. (3) By a notice to quit for non-payment of rent. The requisites of such a notice are usually set forth in statutes. (4) By surrender of possession by the tenant, if it is accepted by the landlord, as when a landlord accepts the keys from a tenant without reserving his rights. (5) By a statutory notice, in the case of a tenancy at will, in many states. Also, in many states, a tenancy at will terminates by operation of law upon the death of either party or upon a sale or lease of the premises by the landlord.
